en: Kṛṣṇayajurvedīya Ekāgnikāṇḍa. Published under the authority of His Highness the Maharaja of Mysore, 1902. This *Ekāgnikāṇḍa*—also known by the synonymous title *Mantraprapāṭhaka*—is divided into two sections (*prapāṭhakas*) and consists of a collection of mantras employed in the *Gṛhya* (domestic) rites. This *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* is included within the renowned corpus of the Yajurvedic recension known as the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*.

For example, in this branch (śākhā), within the seven books (kāṇḍa) known as the *Saṃhitā*, there are 44 *prapāṭhakas*; in the *Brāhmaṇa* consisting of three books, 29; in the *Kāṭhaka*, 3; in the *Āraṇyaka*, 8; and in the *Mantra-prapāṭhakas*, 2. In total, the number of *prapāṭhakas* is eighty-two.

Although some here, following Mādhava’s commentary on the Veda, consider the *Taittirīyopaniṣad*—consisting of three sections (*prapāṭhaka*)—to be the "three folds" (*trivalī*), and thus justify the number eighty-two by combining it with the two mantra-sections of the *Āraṇyaka*, which has ten sections;

Nevertheless, since even according to the commentaries composed by Bhaṭṭabhāskara and others, the *Taittirīyopaniṣad* is understood to consist of only one prapāṭhaka, the count of eighty [sections] would be untenable without the inclusion of two mantra-prapāṭhakas; therefore, the inclusion of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* here is indeed necessary.

For this very reason, the statement in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī* cited in the introduction to Bhaṭṭabhāskara’s commentary—"Now follows the section on the single fire (*ekāgnikaṇḍa*), as well as the Vaiśvadeva mantras found in the section on the fire (*agnikāṇḍa*); for these, the Viśvedevas are the seers"—is consistent. Furthermore, since the expression "two times eighty" is not mentioned anywhere in the works of Mādhava and others, it is appropriate to conclude that, according to their view, the Yajurvedic tradition consists of four times eighty [sections].

This is because the argument—that the *Kāṇḍika-kāṇḍa* does not fall within the scope of the Vedic revelation (*āmnāya*) as established by the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī*—is untenable. By this [argument], it is also refuted [to claim] that these final two *praśnas* in the *Āpastambīya-kalpasūtra*, consisting of thirty-two *praśnas*, are merely places where Āpastamba has arranged his own *Gṛhya-mantras* known as "Khilas" (supplements) in a specific sequence for the sake of easy comprehension by people like us, following a particular order.

For this very reason, the usage [of terms] such as "with the former" or "with the latter" is easily established in the *Gṛhyasūtras*. Among those, in the *Kalpasūtras*, there are thirty-two sections (*praśnas*): the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* (New and Full Moon sacrifices) in the fourth section; the *Cayana* (Fire-altar construction) in the sixteenth and seventeenth sections; the *Āgrayaṇa* in the ninth section; the *Vājapeya* in the eighteenth section; the *Agnihotra* in the sixth section; the *Sautrāmaṇī* in the nineteenth section; the *Nirūḍhapaśubandha* (Independent Animal Sacrifice) in the seventh section; the *Aśvamedha* (Horse Sacrifice) in the twentieth section; the *Cāturmāsya* (Four-Monthly Sacrifices) in the eighth section; and the *Dvādaśāha* (Twelve-Day Rite) in the twenty-first section.

[Prāyaścitta, 9th; Ekāha Agniṣṭoma, 10–13; Satra, Paribhāṣā, and Pravaras, 24th; Rātrisatra, Āgrayaṇa, Dākṣāyaṇa, Cāturmāsya, etc., 14th; Paitṛmedhika, 26–27; Soma Gṛhya, 28th; Prāyaścitta and Dharma, 29–30; Pravargya, 31st; Mantra-prapāṭhakas, 31–32. Thus, there are thirty-two sections in total. It has been made clear that the statement by some—following the lead of others—that [the work] consists of thirty-two sections is an improper assertion based on mere conformity to tradition.

Neither Āpastamba nor any other commentator has stated that the *Kalpasūtra* consists of thirty-two chapters; thus, even if it were limited to thirty chapters, there would be no contradiction with the *Āpastambīya Kalpasūtra*. Furthermore, since there is no possibility of including those respective mantra portions within the *Kalpasūtras* of Baudhāyana, Āśvalāyana, and others, to claim their inclusion in the *Prākṛta* (archetypal) version would contradict the established style of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras*.

Furthermore, if Āpastamba were the author or the compiler of the mantras, he would have composed or arranged them according to the sequence beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and so forth, rather than following the mixed-up order starting with marriage (*vivāha*) and the like. Therefore, the Mīmāṃsakas conclude that he merely composed the Sūtras in accordance with the recitation already established by an unbroken tradition that is without beginning or end.

Furthermore, in the commentary on the sūtra "Having fed the boy, [he should recite] the first Yajus of the Anuvāka," found in the tenth section of the fourth chapter of the Gṛhyasūtra, Sudarśanācārya himself—while explaining that the mention of the *anuvāka* here is intended to indicate that these [mantras] are only those recited in the Gṛhya-mantras and not those situated in the Kalpa-sūtras, and that their purpose is stated as being for recitation in the Brahma-yajña and other such rites—has already refuted this dispute; so enough of further elaboration.

This single-kāṇḍa [section] has been published together with either the commentary of Mādhava or that of Bhaṭṭabhāskara. However, one should not entertain any doubt as to whether Bhaṭṭabhāskara composed the commentary on this kāṇḍa; for indeed, in his *Pitṛmedhabhāṣya*, having first cited the mantra "mātā rudrāṇām," he stated: "The portion beginning with 'mātā' and ending with 'utsṛja' belongs to the *madhuparka*."

Furthermore, that *madhuparka* mantra is recited only in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* and nowhere else. Moreover, this other distinction is understood from the statement in Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s commentary: that the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* was spoken and recited here before the *Āraṇyaka*, and it must likewise be studied by students in that same manner. It is also probable that this commentary by Haradatta does not differ significantly from the commentary of Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara.
For we have found, in a certain ancient manuscript, that Haradatta’s commentary on the Pitṛmedha-prapāṭhaka is virtually indistinguishable from Bhaṭṭabhāskara’s commentary.

In a very old manuscript of Bhaṭṭabhāskara’s commentary on the *Taittirīyāraṇyaka*, located within the treasury of the Uttarādimaṭha and brought from Narasīpura, written in Devanāgarī script, on folio 98, immediately after the words: “Thus ends the third prapāṭhaka in the Yajurvedabhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭabhāskaramiśra,” there follows: “Having prostrated before Mahādeva, the wise Haradatta now provides an exposition of the Paitṛmedhika mantras.”

Beginning with these words, the commentary on the *Paitṛmedhika-mantras* is seen to have been written. This [manuscript] is for the most part indistinguishable from the commentary of Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara; it is extant up to the end of page 116, reaching as far as the commentary on the thirteenth mantra of the fifth section (*anuvāka*). Following that, there is a loss of folios until the commencement of the commentary on the *Upaniṣads*. As for this visible commentary on the *Akārikā-kāṇḍa*, one should not doubt that it belongs to Haradatta himself.

This is evident from the observation of the verse beginning with "In the beginning, having prostrated... and ending with "...is prescribed. This same meaning is also determined by the *Mādhavīyadhātuvṛtti*; for in that commentary on the roots, under the root *piś* in the *tudādigaṇa*, it states: "This [root] also occurs in the sense of illuminating (*dīpanā*).
Thus, regarding the passage 'May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms' (*tvaṣṭā rūpāṇi piṃśatu*, 1.13), Haradatta says: 'The root *piṃś* [means] illuminating...'"

The statement from the *Ekāgni-kāṇḍa-bhāṣya*, "Because it is seen [in the scripture] here: 'The Pitṛs, performing the *paitṛmedha* rite, reached the sky by means of the non-asterisms (*anakṣatrebhiḥ*)'", has been cited. Furthermore, it should not be understood that this Haradatta was merely a commentator on the *Āpastamba Śrauta-, Gṛhya-,* and *Dharma-sūtras*; rather, he was also the author of the *Padamañjarī*, which is a commentary on the *Kāśikāvṛtti*.

This is because of the unanimity of purpose regarding the unique rule concerning the separate employment of the final vowel *a* at the end of the formula for returning a greeting (*pratyabhivāda*), as found in the *Dharmasūtra*—in the passage "and [the name] is purifying, but not [ending] in *asraḥ*"—and in the *Sūtrapadamañjarī* on the rule "in the case of a Śūdra," which establishes that same point. However, we are unable to specifically determine the chronological period of this Haradatta.

In general, however, we determine that he lived after Sāyaṇa Mādhavārya—the author of the Vedabhāṣya, Dhātuvṛtti, and other works—and before Medhātithi, the renowned commentator on the Manusmṛti who composed the Manubhāṣya.

For this very point is indicated by the author of the *Manubhāṣya* in the second section (khaṇḍa), under the thirty-third sūtra of Haradatta’s commentary on the *Paribhāṣāsūtras*: "And this meaning has been shown by the author of the *Manubhāṣya*: 'There is another governing rule (*adhikāra*) regarding the performance of marriage, but there is no recurrence of the previous governing rule'? Thus he cites the *Manubhāṣya*. In this *Ekāgnikāṇḍa*, such a dispute is observed here and there regarding the division of mantras and their application (*viniyoga*). And that [dispute] is elaborated upon in works such as the *Tātparyadarśana*.

In this case, however, regarding the mere application [of the rule], another opinion has been explained; Haradattamiśra himself will demonstrate it in various places. At the time of editing this first book (*ekāṇḍa*) along with its commentary (*sabhāṣya*), the following were the manuscripts used as reference copies: 1. A manuscript printed in Madras city, written in Telugu script (*āndhrākṣara*). 2. A palm-leaf manuscript belonging to Subrahmaṇya Śāstrins of Kadiramaṅgalam in the Tanjavur district. 3. A palm-leaf manuscript belonging to Puṣṭasāmi Śrautins of Mysore. 4. S. [Fragmentary manuscript].

The manuscript of Veṅkaṭarāma Śāstrin (No. 9) and five manuscripts of Aśvatthanarasiṃha Śāstrin of Mysore (Nos. 6–10), all written on paper, are preserved in this very library. Among them, No. 137 (Ā. Śuddha) is a clean copy; No. 601 (Pra. is moderately clear; and these four (Nos. 650, Ā. 108, 0. Ā., and 1.1") are not very clean. Having consulted these ten manuscripts, this work has been edited. May there be peace.

2011 195 Oṃ. Salutation to the Supreme Self (Paramātman). In the Śrī Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda, in the Ekāgni-Kāṇḍa, begins the first Prapāṭhaka.
Aditi, grant us your favor; Anumati, grant us your favor; Sarasvatī, grant us your favor; O God Savitṛ, impel [us].
Now begins the commentary on the Mantra-Prapāṭhaka composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, the wise Haradatta correctly provides this commentary on the mantras of the Ekāgnikāṇḍa.

In this regard, the teachers first recite the Vaiśvadeva mantras. It is stated therein that there is sprinkling (pariṣecana) on both sides—“just as before. Those mantras for the sprinkling should be explained first. Aditi is the mother of the gods; O Aditi, grant your approval (*anumanyasva*). Grant permission for the rite being performed by me. Anumati is the goddess who grants consent; she is the moon when it is nearly full. O Anumati, grant your approval. Sarasvatī is the deity of speech; this is her vocative address.

O Sarasvat, give your approval! [The form] *Sarasvate* follows the Vedic rule of *guṇa* substitution. O God Savitar, you who grant permission for all things, impel us as well; grant us your leave. Om! To Agni, Svāhā! To Soma, Svāhā! To the Viśvedevas, Svāhā! To Dhruva Bhūma, Svāhā! To Dhruvakṣiti, Svāhā! To Ayukṣiti, Svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! Aditi, approve this! Anumati, approve this! Sarasvat, approve this! O God Savitar, you have granted your impulse.

Now follow the Vaiśvadeva mantras. Regarding the employment of these mantras, there is the rule: "For twelve days one should sleep on the ground," and so forth. "Employment" (upayoga) means the acquisition of knowledge preceded by observances. The vow belongs to the performer alone; however, some maintain that it applies to the wife as well. *Om agnaye svāhā*. Just as *om* is a syllable of permission (*anujñākṣara*), so too the utterance *svāhā* is for the purpose of offering the oblation (*havir-pradāna*). *Somāya svāhā*. Some do not study this mantra. *Viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*. To all the gods.

To the eternal, to the one of uniform form, to that which is devoid of increase and decrease; to the vast, to the infinite, to Brahman. "The Infinite indeed is what one should desire to understand," so says the *Chāndogya*. To the one whose abiding, motion, and pervasion toward the entire range of effects are constant and immovable—to that Brahman, the one of constant abiding (*dhruvakṣiti*). Likewise, to the one of unfailing abiding (*acyutakṣiti*). Likewise, to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Rudra is Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. He is called Sviṣṭakṛt because he makes the sacrifice well-offered (*suhuta*); to him. As before, the sprinkling around (*pariṣecana*) is performed.
You have permitted; you have granted leave. You have impelled; you have given consent. End of the first section of the first chapter.

To Dharma, Svāhā! To Adharma, Svāhā! To the Unseizable, Svāhā! To the plants and their guardians, Svāhā! To the Rakshasas and their guardians, Svāhā! To the domestic animals, Svāhā! To those who dwell in the place of rest, Svāhā! To the lords of the place of rest, Svāhā! To all beings, Svāhā! To him who desires, Svāhā! To the intermediate space, Svāhā! That which moves, that which stirs, and that which exerts itself—this is the portion of Name; to Name, Svāhā! To the Earth, Svāhā! To the Intermediate Space, Svāhā!

Svāhā to Heaven! Svāhā to Sūrya! Svāhā to Candramas! Svāhā to the Nakṣatras! Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Bṛhaspati! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Svāhā to Brahmaṇaspati! Svāhā to the Pitṛs of the firm foundation! Homage to Rudra, the Lord of Beasts; svāhā! To those beings who roam by day and by night, bringing this offering, may they depart! Svāhā!

Now follow the mantras for the offering of the *bali*: "To Dharma and Adharma, well-known; and to the Waters. Likewise, "and to the Herbs and Forest Trees. Here, the presiding deities of these respective things are understood. "To the Rakṣasas and the Divine Folk (*devajana*). This refers to those who are the attendants of the Rakṣasas and the gods. "To the Household Deities (*gṛhyā*). Those that exist in the house are the household deities, well-known from the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*); to them. "To the Quarters (*avasāna*). A quarter is a house; the plural number is used with reference to its constituent parts.

To the deities presiding over those respective locations; to the lords of the resting places, the protectors of the dwellings; to all beings, *svāhā*! To all those beings indeed—*svāhā*! To Kāma (Desire)—Kāma is well known. Thus also for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). That which moves, that by which the door is closed—the messengers (*preṣyāḥ*). To them I bring an offering, desiring prosperity; may the Lord of Prosperity bestow prosperity upon me, *svāhā*.
Hari Oṃ! "May the two paths be auspicious for one who is meditating"—this is what is said. Or rather:

that which trembles in the world at the time of dissolution, and that which moves and exerts itself—this is a portion of *Nāman* (the Name), whose nature is to bend [toward all things]; to that *Nāman*, Svāhā! Earth and the other elements are well known. Just as there is the utterance of *svāhā* for the gods, so there is the utterance of *svadhā* for the ancestors. *Namaḥ rudrāya paśupataye*: salutation to Rudra, the Lord of creatures (*paśu*). Creatures are those with two feet and those with four; [salutation] to their Lord. Those beings who roam about...

To those beings who roam about, moving here and there by day and by night, desiring an offering—[namely] to Vituda, the son of Kubera; for it is seen in another mantra that "to Vituda, the son of Kubera" [is the recipient]—to those who are his servants, to them I bring an offering, desiring prosperity. May that Vituda, the lord of prosperity, bestow prosperity upon me.

By this [text], it is shown that the offering (*bali*) is indeed at night alone, because of the statement, "At night, indeed, with the best [portion], [the offering is] aerial," and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), "Desiring the offering at night. Others, however, explain the particle *eva* as having its position shifted, saying, "At night, with the best [portion] alone"; for them, there is a cessation of other offerings at night. Some, desiring the offering by day, offer the offering by day through modification (*ūha*), because of the observation in the Āśvalāyana [Gṛhyasūtra]: "To those who roam by day" [indicates] by day, and "to those who roam by night" [indicates] at night.

Now, the wedding mantras: he recites the *prasugmantā* verses over the excellent suitors who have been sent forth—namely, "O ye who go forth well. "O ye who go forth well (*prasugmantāḥ*), may you proceed with great ease toward the bridegrooms; may you be gracious to us. May Indra take pleasure in our offering when he partakes of the Soma juice. May the paths by which our friends come for the sake of the bride be thornless and straight. May Bhaga lead us all together."

While you are meditating—at the very same moment, that is, immediately after meditation—O friends, proceed with great excellence toward the bride’s father and other relatives who are to be chosen as suitors, by means of the best and most excellent paths. Indra also is a companion here; thus he says: "Both [of us] are ours. According to the rule *asmado dvayośca*, the plural form is used for two.

Indra takes pleasure in—the meaning is that he approves of—the union, the pair, of me and my daughter. Why? Because he perceives the food consisting of Soma-juice; that is, he understands: "These two, being united, will sacrifice to me. (Note: The genitive case in *saumyasyāndhasaḥ* is used in the sense of the accusative.)

"Thornless and straight, thornless and straight"—[this is said] for those going to the maiden's house. May these paths, their roads, be thornless—devoid of thorns, pebbles, and the like—and straight. By which paths our friends, these well-wishers, go toward the bride's father and others who are to be chosen (*vareyaṃ*) for the maiden; and may Aryaman and Bhaga lead us two together, bring us together, and unite us.

"O gods, may our *jāspatya*—the state of being husband and wife—be perfectly well-governed and firmly established. Having seen [the bride] herself, one should mutter the third verse: "abhrātṛghnīm. "O Varuṇa, bestow upon this bride that auspicious mark (*lakṣmī*) which is 'not killing her brothers' (*abhrātṛghnī*). [The form *lakṣmyam* is derived from *lakṣmīm*; the absence of the *pūrvasavarṇa* vowel and the substitution of *yaṇ* occur according to the rule *vā chandasi*. "And you, O Bṛhaspati, bestow that auspicious mark which is 'not killing her husband' (*apatighnī*). "O Indra..."

O Savitṛ, bestow that Lakṣmī who is the destroyer of childlessness; and you, bestow the Lakṣmī who is the soul of all. The meaning is: act in such a way that she does not suffer the death of her brother or other relatives.

*Yasasya*. [The reading] "the vowel *o* is Vedic" is an additional reading; in that case, the mantra-reading would be *samyasya*: "O Gods, may there be good fortune for this woman. O Bṛhaspati, grant her a wife who is not a slayer of brothers, nor a repeller of Varuṇa; one who is not a slayer of sons, O Indra—may Fortune attend her! Be one whose eye is not evil, a repeller of enemies, auspicious, well-disposed toward kinsmen, and full of splendor. May she be a mother of living sons, beloved by the gods, and pleasant; be gracious to our bipeds and gracious to our quadrupeds. I consecrate her. (1)

Having seen it herself, she should recite the third [verse]: *abhrātṛmnīm*. O Varuṇa! Bestow upon this bride that fortune which is "without a brother" (*abhrātṛmnī*). [The form *lakṣmyam* is derived from *lakṣmīm*; according to the rule "vā chandasi," there is no substitution of the preceding vowel with its homogeneous counterpart, but rather the *yaṇ*-substitution. Bestow that fortune. O Bṛhaspati! And you, bestow that fortune which is "without a husband" (*apatimnī*). O Indra! You, bestow that fortune which is "without sons" (*aputraghnī*).

"O Savitṛ! Bestow upon her Lakṣmī, who is the soul of all; that is to say, act in such a way that she does not meet with death from her brother or others. [The bridegroom] should gaze at her with the mantra "Aghora... Gazing (*samīkṣaṇam*) means examining her limb by limb. "O bride, may you have eyes that are not terrible (*aghoracakṣuḥ*), and may you be one who does not fall away (*apātikī*). Be auspicious (*śivā*) toward your husbands"—the plural number refers to the group including the husband's brothers-in-law and others—"be auspicious toward me, your husband, and toward your brothers-in-law and the rest."

Be well-disposed and full of splendor! She who has been born is indeed the "life-giver" (*jīvasṛḥ*). She who desires the gods as objects of worship is "one who loves the gods" (*devakāmā*). Be pleasant—that is, praiseworthy—in every respect; this is connected with the word "be" (*bhava*) everywhere. Be auspicious for our bipeds; and be auspicious for our quadrupeds—be the bringer of happiness. [One should draw it] toward oneself, saying: "This do I..."

In you, O wife-killer, dwells misfortune; that I designate. Living, they cry out; they depart upon their paths. Men have meditated upon a long course. That which is dear to the fathers, whom they have sent forth—joy for the husband, offspring for the embrace. May he drive away the cruel one; may he drive away the waters.

"O bride! That ill fortune (*alakṣmī*) which is the slayer of your husband—[the short vowel *i* is used here by Vedic license]—that I point out; having wiped it away, I cast it out. The meaning of the word "this" (*idam*) is that this very act of casting out the *darbha* grass is the casting out of ill fortune itself. Just as this ill fortune is being cast out, so too is this [act] performed.

At the time of separation from the beloved, when the kinsmen are weeping, there is the recitation: *jīvāṃ rudanti* ("They weep for the living"). Āśvalāyana maintains that this refers specifically to the weeping of the maiden herself; as he says: "When she is weeping, [one recites] *jīvāṃ rudanti*? They weep with reference to this very living maiden. *Dhvare*—for *dhvara* is an act of injury. At a time free from injury, they bewail her, they undergo a reversal; they grieve at a place where there ought to be joy. These [kinsmen], long-lasting (*dīrghī*), [extend] their *prasitim* (rope/continuity) over a long period of time.

May the men—the kinsmen of the bride—be mindful of our unbidden bond of affection; may they contemplate it. Those who have agreed to this marriage-rite, who have impelled and set it in motion—what kind of rite? One that is "vāma" (desirable) for the fathers, worthy of being sought by the ancestors; and one that brings forth for my husband a son who is the very form of happiness. [The plural "janayaḥ" is used in place of the singular genitive "januṣaḥ," meaning "of her birth."]

"Let the people who are relatives of the bride, having performed such a marriage ceremony, not weep upon embracing their daughter-in-law for the sake of that embrace—meaning, let them not weep when considering our future long-lasting bond of affection.

Let the Brāhmaṇas lead her forward with a bath; let the waters flow without killing the heroes. Let them quickly go around the fire of Aryaman, while the mother-in-laws and the brothers-in-law look on. In the hole of the wagon, in the hole of the chariot, in the hole..."

"One who possesses the mantra should say: 'Let it wash away' (*vyukṣat*). Elsewhere, the root *ukṣ* has the meaning of sprinkling; here, however, it should be understood in the sense of removal. And the fifth [conjugational] suffix (*lakāra*) is used. Let that which is harsh in the waters depart; let the waters flow out, let them rise up! Why is this requested? So that the Brāhmaṇas may bring the water for the bathing of this bride. [The form] *avīratrīḥ*: by the rule 'In the Veda, there is optionally [the substitution of] *jasi*,' the preceding vowel is substituted."

The sons are heroes, possessing the nature of that wealth; other ways of conduct than that are "heroless ways. The waters flow forth [with the word] *avīran*. It is stated again with the intention of expressing the qualification "heroless" (*avīram*).

The placing of the *darbha* grass upon the head of the bride with the verse beginning "Aryaman" (*aryamṇaḥ*): Aryaman is the Āditya; by his grace, may these [fires] quickly encircle this wedding—may they stand surrounding it, having formed a circle, just as this [grass] has been made circular. And having gone around, let them wait and look on. Who? The mother-in-law, the mothers, the brothers-in-law of my bride and myself, and the brothers of my bride and myself.

Upon that [yoke-pin], he establishes the southern hole of the yoke-pair with the formula: "In the hole of the cart. Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend: There was a certain maiden named Apālā who suffered from leucoderma (śvitri). No one would marry her. A constant desire arose in her mind: "How may I worship Indra? Once, having descended into a river for the sake of bathing, she was being carried away by the current;
while keeping that very desire in her mind, she was brought by the current to a place where...

O Indra, Lord of Śacī, you have thrice bestowed Apālā upon me, radiant as the sun. May the golden-hued [waters] be auspicious; may the waters be peaceful for me. May the earth be auspicious, and may the food of the bull be auspicious. May the waters be peaceful, and the heat be peaceful.

He saw me; having crushed him with his teeth, he offered that froth (*ramam*) to Indra. Having drunk it, Indra discharged water through the three holes—the two of the chariot’s pole (*anas*) and one of the yoke—and having thrice purified [me] with those waters, he made me radiant as the sun. This is to be seen in the verse beginning, “The maiden, weaving... (*kanyā vāsaḥ...*). The word *ratha* is used in the nominative case with the sense of the genitive; having discharged the water from the holes of the chariot and so forth, he purified [me] thrice. The appearance of the letter *r* is an archaic Vedic insertion (*chāndasa*).

Having purified and cleansed her, O Lord of Śacī! O Indra! you made the maiden named Apālā possess the splendor of the sun (*sūryavarcasam*); the change of gender (*puruṣavyatyaya*) is Vedic; likewise, I shall do the same for her—this is the meaning.

The mantra for depositing gold in a hole is: *śaṃ ta iti*. May the gold being placed in the hole be *śam* (auspicious) for you; may they be *śam*! The particle *u* is meaningless and serves only to fill the meter. And may the waters being poured there be *śam*, that is, may they be a source of happiness (*sukham*) for you. The reading *samu śaṃ tvāpaḥ* is not well-known, but even there the meaning is the same; it is merely a transposition of the letters *sa* and *śa*. A *medhī* is a threshing-post, but here it refers to the yoke-pin (*abhidhānī*).

May Methī also be auspicious for you; likewise, may the fissure of the Yuga be auspicious. And may the waters, which purify many and possess a hundred-fold protection, be auspicious for you. Be distinct from the poison, O Viṣṭre, and then unite with your husband.
And eight [verses] beginning with "dīdhiyuḥ" are for men. || 1 ||

The golden-colored, pure, purifying waters have gone forth, leaving behind what is stagnant. May the purifier, the god Savitṛ, purify you with those waters through which the pure have passed. The repetition of "golden-colored, pure, purifying" is for the sake of emphasis. Now, immediately thereafter, at the time of sexual union, unite this body of mine with yours.
Thus ends the first section in the commentary on the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* composed by Śrī Haradatta.

In the following section are five bathing mantras beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. Those which have a golden color (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*)—that is, whose color is like gold—are of pure hue, bright, clean, and purifying; they have set forth, that is, they flow. Having left behind, having abandoned, what is blameworthy—that is, sin—the Waters proceed. For within these, hundreds of purifiers—that is, many purifying holy places (*tīrtha*)—are spread out, extended. With those waters, may the divine Savitṛ purify you.

In the second mantra, "Kaśyapa" is the name of Āditya. He is called *paśya* because he sees everything; *paśya* itself becomes *paśyaka*. There, through the transposition of the first and last syllables, *kaśyapa* is formed. This is seen in the Āraṇyaka: "Kaśyapa is the seer (*paśyaka*), for he perceives everything. And he is said to have been born from those waters as he rises in the morning. From fire...

In whom Kaśyapa was born, in whom Agni [was born]; those golden ones who have held Agni as their embryo—may those waters be gracious to us. In whose midst King Varuṇa moves, beholding the truth and falsehood of men; those golden ones who have held Agni as their embryo—may those waters be gracious to us. Whose food the gods make in heaven, which are established in many places in the intermediate space.

May those waters which have held Agni as their embryo, being golden-hued, be pleasant and auspicious to you. May the waters look upon you with a gracious eye; may they touch your skin with a gracious touch. Those waters which drip with clarity and are purifying are the very birthplace of the lightning-fire in the waters, and its maintenance is likewise therein. Golden-hued means having a beautiful color; may those waters be *śam*—that is, pleasant and bringing happiness to you. The word *syona* is also a name for happiness; there is no tautology here because of the distinction between worldly and otherworldly happiness.

The third [verse]: "Of whom the King..."—the meaning is clear. The fourth [verse]: "Of whom the gods..."—the gods dwelling in heaven (*dyusthāna*) make the waters their food, which they consume in the sky. Those who have settled in many ways within the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) at the sacrifices; those who have taken the raw embryo, having assumed the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍabānala*); "those," and so forth—the rest has been explained. "May they with auspiciousness..."—O bride! May the waters look upon you with an auspicious eye, and may they touch your skin with an auspicious body, dripping with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

"May they be pleasant to us. "O lover of songs, may these songs encompass you on every side; may they increase your long life, and being pleasing, may they be dear to you. [The verse] beginning with "āśāsāna" is this one. "May Pūṣan lead you from here, he who milks the ghee; the pure ones... and so forth. This has been explained.

"The wearing of an unwashed garment [is performed] with the mantra: *pari tvā girvaṇaḥ*. O Indra! You are *girvaṇas*, one who delights in songs (*vana*); you are to be honored by songs characterized as praises, or you are the enjoyer of praises. May these my songs encompass (*pari-bhavantu*) you; the root *bhū* preceded by *pari* signifies acceptance (*parigraha*). May they accept you from all sides (*viśvataḥ*), everywhere, just as this garment surrounds [the body]—this is the intended meaning. Of what sort are you?"

To the one who approaches elders and venerable teachers—what kind of words? Words that are "anuvṛddhayaḥ": *anu* is a prefix denoting sequence; *vṛddhayaḥ* means increased or extensive; let those which are *juṣṭayaḥ*—meaning they should be cultivated or resorted to by you—be so. Let them be served by you.

"Seeking the bond of the yoke. Desiring good cheer, joy, offspring, prosperity, and well-being for her body, this bride stands here having become devoted to Agni. "I bind this woman with the bond of the yoke" means I fasten her for the sake of a well-performed act, namely the meritorious rite called marriage. *Kam* is an expletive; it means so that there may be happiness. Then he leads her toward the fire, saying: "May Pūṣan [lead] thee. Pūṣan is the Sun.

Bestowing hope, mental well-being, progeny, and prosperity upon our bodies—being devoted to Agni’s vows, may she come to us for the sake of our welfare. (Ṛgveda 1.1.10) Taking you by the hand with the Aśvins, I lead you forward on the chariot so that you may become a mistress of the household, possessed of sons, and a radiant queen over this dwelling. (Ṛgveda 10.85.36)
And may they be present in the future as well. || 2 ||
Soma first obtained [her] as Gandharva; the highest [Agni] obtained her. Agni is your third husband; your fourth is born of man.

May he lead you from this place to the vicinity of Agni, taking you by the hand. Having been led from here, having had the oblation performed for you, and being carried away by means of a chariot or similar vehicle, may the Aśvins carry you forward and grant their consent; for this very consent of theirs constitutes their act of carrying you away. And then, go to my house, so that you may become the mistress of the house, just as the mistress of the house has gone.

"Having gone there, O mistress who has mastery, having become the sovereign, speak toward the *vidatha*—that is, the sacrifice—and its subject matter; speak directly. Thus ends the second section. At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, there is a consecration with the following two verses: "Soma was the first," etc. Soma was the first to find you; after him, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu found you; thirdly, Agni is your husband.

"Born of man"—I am born of man, your fourth (*turīya*) husband. This very meaning is stated with a slight distinction: "Soma gave... Soma gave, has given, or may give wealth (*rayi*). [This is explained] in the *Saṃvyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*: "Soma gave, the Gandharva gave, Agni gave; he gave me wealth, sons, and this woman."

"I take your hand for the sake of noble offspring, so that you may reach old age with me as your husband. Aryaman, Savitṛ, and Puraṃdhi—the gods have given you to me for the household. Those were the former people where the ancient sacrifices were established; there Mūrdhanvat Saubhrava offered to the gods in the beginning. Regarding that [act] from which the term "taking the hand" (pāṇigrahaṇa) for marriage arises, there are four mantras, beginning with "I take your hand": "I take your hand"—I grasp your hand.

For what purpose? For the sake of having good offspring (*suprajāstva*). "One who has good offspring" is *suśrajā*; the state of being such is *suprajāstva*. The lengthening of the vowel is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Furthermore, I take [her] so that you may become one who reaches old age (*jaradaṣṭi*) together with me. That which makes manifest the attainment of the state of old age is *jaradaṣṭi*. *Purandhi* means "possessing many thoughts" (*purudhī*), i.e., possessing great wisdom or great capacity for action; this is an adjective applied to each of [the qualities] beginning with fortune (*bhaga*).

Others, however, consider this to be a designation of Indra. "The gods, beginning with Bhaga, gave you to me"—for what purpose? "For my *gārhapatya*, for the state of a householder. The particle *le*—that is, *hai*; the word *ha* is meaningless. Those [gods], beginning with Bhaga, were the former people.

Those ancient people, the first-bearers who were the performers of marriage in the primordial time, where the cows were placed and established in the household; and where Saubhava Mūrdhanvān stood, the first among the gods, he scorched intensely on all sides before the gods. Subhra is Aditi—she whose two ears are beautiful; her offspring [is this]. [In the third section of the first chapter: "O Sarasvatī, O most auspicious one, O possessor of strength, may this [offering] reach you."

I sing forth that you, the foremost of all existence: "He who goes to all the quarters, pervading every direction, the golden-handed Āditya, the son of Ira, the descendant of Subhra—his head is the *mūrdhan*; by this, his preeminence is indicated; he is *mūrdhanvān*, meaning possessed of preeminence. Or, Agni is the *saubhrava*, and he is *mūrdhanvān*, as praised in the verse beginning with ‘*agnirmūrdhā*’. Thus says Āśvalāyana: ‘The two *saṃyājyā* verses for the Virāj are *agni-mūrdhanvat* and [the other]’."

The phrase "pūrvo devebhyaḥ" is well-connected [to the context], because it is seen in another mantra: "Agni is the mouth, the first of the deities. One should apply the meaning as follows: "To that Gārhapatya fire where those [deities] such as Bhaga and others reside, they gave you; therefore, I take your hand. Regarding the word "Sarasvatī":

O Sarasvatī! You too, protect this taking of hands with excellence! O fortunate one! O possessor of strength (*vājinīvatī*)—here "strength" means food—or rather, "possessor of praise" (*vājinī*), for you possess both oblations and hymns! We sing forth to you, who are at the forefront of all that exists, of all beings; we sing forth, we praise you with excellence. [The form *pragāyāmasi* is derived from the root *gai* with the suffix *asi* following the rule *idanto masi*.]

Saṃ. 4-4-4: "He who goes... This Pavamāna follows all the quarters and intermediate directions; he goes in succession. "Hiraṇyahastaḥ" means one whose hand holds gold to be given to the gods; thus he is Hiraṇyahasta. "Airammaḥ": *irā* is food; he who measures (*mimīte*) or prepares that food is Airammaḥ. He is the friend of Agni. For they address Agni as the "friend of Vāyu. May he who is thus [Vāyu] make you mindful with mantras.

"May Viṣṇu follow you for one step for food; two for strength; three for sacred observance; four for prosperity; five for cattle; six for the seasons; seven for the seven Hotṛ-priests—may Viṣṇu follow you. Be a companion with seven steps. May Vāyu, who has been [born], make you one whose mind is fixed on me. Then he causes her to take seven steps toward himself, saying: "One for food... and so forth.

"May Viṣṇu follow you for this purpose: so that there may be food for you, strength, ritual action, and the state of being a source of bliss. "Food" (iṣ) means nourishment. "Strength" (ūrj) means power. "Ritual action" (vrata) means duty. "A source of bliss" (mayobhūḥ) means one who brings about happiness; the state of being such is "the state of being a source of bliss" (māyobhavam), for that purpose—as Āśvalāyana says, "for the sake of that which is to become a source of bliss. [This applies] to five animals, to six seasons, and to seven [groups]; in all cases, the phrase "may Viṣṇu follow you" is to be supplied. [The officiants are] the Hotṛ, the Praśāstṛ, and the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin.

The Śīpivitṛṇṇa, the Neṣṭṛ, the Acchāvāka, and the Āgnīdhra—these are the seven *hotṛ* priests. Accordingly, the Brāhmaṇa states: "Therefore, for the Saumya Adhvara, the sacrificial rite, the seven *hotṛ*s utter the *vaṣaṭ* call facing eastward. For the purpose that these [priests] may be present for you in the performance of the sacrifice, may Viṣṇu follow after you.
"You who have taken seven steps are indeed 'Seven-stepped' (Saptapadā); being such, you are Saravā."

"Be! Let us be seven-stepped. [The dual ending] *-au* becomes *-ā*. "With seven steps, you and I have become friends"—the verb *babhūviva* (we two have become) has its prefix *vi-* elided according to Vedic usage. [First Prapāṭhaka, Third Khaṇḍa, Verse 17: "Let us two, the bright ones, radiant and well-disposed, carry [the sacrifice]; dwelling together for the sake of food and vigor, let our minds be united, our vows be united, and let our thoughts be made one. "You are she; I am he. You are she; I am he. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

May I attain friendship with you; may I not be separated from your friendship, nor become alienated or set apart. And may you not be estranged from my friendship. "Let us two come together! (samayāva)—this is the form of the root *i* preceded by *sam* in the imperative mood; it means "let us meet. Let us form a resolution (*saṅkalpa*) that "this and this must be done. Being well-disposed toward one another (*sampiyau*), being mutually united, shining through mutual support because of our similar relationship, and being of good mind (*sumanasyamānau*), that is, becoming well-disposed.

This word *bhṛśādi* is Vedic, characterized by the absence of elision of the *s*. The connection is as follows: "O you two who dwell together for the sake of nourishment (*ūrj*), experiencing it together. I shall "unite our minds" (*samākaram*); because of the multiplicity of activities, there is a plurality of minds, and I bring them into harmony. Likewise, I shall "unite the vows" (*vratāni*); that which is to be performed by you according to dharma, that shall be performed by her as well.

Likewise, in the phrase "samucittāni," the syllable *u* is meaningless (*anarthaka*), because the mind has already been mentioned; here, the external sense organs are the "minds" (*cittāni*), and these too he made equal. "Sā" and "tvam" are designations for the *ṛc*, and "amaḥ" is the designation for the *sāman*. This is seen in the *Vṛhad-Brāhmaṇa*: "The *ṛc* was named Sā, and the *sāman* was named Ama. "Tvaṃ sā asi" means "You are she"; "ṛṇase" means "I am Ama. At the time of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination), the *ṛ* becomes *ū*. However, among the *Vṛca*s, the reading is "amo'ham. For this very reason, it is stated again for the sake of clarity: "Amaḥ aham asmi" means "I am Ama," and "Sā tvaṃ" means "You are she."

Em. Vā. 3-2-23. The eighteenth section, containing large letters, is in the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikāṇḍa*: "I am heaven, you are earth; I am the seed, you are the womb. I am the mind, you are speech; I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛk. Come to me as my devoted wife, O Sūnṛtā, for the sake of obtaining a son, for the sake of obtaining prosperity. || 3 ||
And six in front, three.

"Obeisance to Soma, the knower of birth; obeisance to the Gandharva, the knower of birth. The meaning is: "Just as the *Ṛk* and the *Sāman* are mutually connected, so too are we two. Here, the intended sense is the relationship of superiority and inferiority (*auttarādharya*), with "Heaven" being myself and "Earth" being you. "I am the seed (*retaḥ*)," which is a metaphorical identification of the cause with the effect; "you are the bearer of the seed (*retobhṛt*)," meaning you are the receptacle for the seed infused by me. "I am the mind (*manas*)," and "you are speech (*vāk*)," meaning that just as speech articulates what has been conceived by the mind, so too is there harmony between us two.

"I am Sā (Speech), who am unattached; being such as I am, may you be devoted to me and favorable toward me. For what purpose? 'puṃse putrāya vetave'—in order to obtain a male son, for the sake of attaining both prosperity and a son. The repetition of the word 'son' is for the sake of emphasis. Come! You are dear speech, and because of that truthfulness, you are addressed as 'Sūnṛte'!"* *The repetition of "putrāya" is for the sake of emphasis. * *The address "Sūnṛte" is due to her connection with that [truthful] speech.

Thus ends the third section in the *Ekāgni-kāṇḍa-mantra-vyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. Next follow the sixteen principal offering mantras (*pradhānāhuti-mantra*): "To Soma, who has obtained a bride; to Gandharva, who knows womankind; to Agni, who knows womankind—svāhā! To Agni, who knows womankind—svāhā! "The maiden, going from her fathers to the world of her husband, has entered the consecration (*dīkṣā*). May she be gracious. Svāhā! "May he release her from the name of the mortal; may he make her well-bound for the immortal."

"Just as this woman, O bounteous Indra, may attain many sons and be fortunate, so do you, O bounteous Indra, make her possessed of many sons and fortunate. Bestow upon her sons who are difficult to overcome; make her husband the eleventh. 'Agni is the first of the deities. [The word] *kanyalā*—the word *kanyā* itself is [the base], while the sound *la* is an augment."

"From her father's family, going to the world of her husband—that is, departing for her husband's family—the maiden *avādāsthu* [abandoned] the *dīkṣā*, the vow of a maiden. [The form] *avādāsthu* is the third person singular aorist (*luṅ*) of the root *dīṅ* (meaning "to perish"), with the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) implied; the change of *t* to *th* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The meaning is that she has caused [the vow] to perish, i.e., she has abandoned it. Regarding *preta*: Indra is the one being addressed, because of the connection with the vocative "O Indra" (*indra mandriḥ*).

There is a transposition of genders. O Śūdra! O Mīḍhvān (the bountiful one), O showerer with rain! Release this bride from here—from the father’s family—and do not release her from there—from the husband’s family. Rather, bind her firmly; bind her well in that husband’s family. So that she, being firmly bound, may become possessed of good sons and good fortune. Regarding the word "imām" (this): O Indra! O Mīḍhvān! Make this bride possessed of good sons and good fortune.
"Bestow upon her ten sons; establish them, and make me the eleventh. "Agni!"—let Agni come forward. Of what nature is he? He is the first among the deities. 20.

May *Soma* release her offspring from the noose of death. May King Varuṇa grant his consent so that this woman shall not weep for the loss of her grandson. May the Gārhapatya fire lead her progeny to a long life, for she whose lap is never empty shall be a living mother. May she awaken to the joy of seeing her grandson. Let no cry of lamentation arise in your house at night; let your kinsmen sleep elsewhere.

"May King Varuṇa and Agni take heed of this act being performed, so that this woman, having been released, shall not weep—shall not shed tears—on account of her grandson, that is, on account of the calamity concerning her son. 'This one' refers to this bride; may the Gārhapatya fire—the nuptial fire associated with the master of the house—protect her. May it protect not only her, but may it also lead her offspring to long life."

What more need be said? May the lap be not empty; may the son’s circle be complete; and may the mother of living sons rejoice on account of her sons. May this daughter-in-law awaken from sleep to the joy of a grandson—awakening toward the joy of a grandson. "May there be no noise in your house": O daughter-in-law! May no clamor or outcry arise in your house at night; let all those who weep lie down elsewhere than with you.

And you, having become one with disheveled hair and scattered locks, O woman with disheveled hair, cover your breast! Living for a hundred years, shine forth in the world of your husband, beholding your offspring as they grow toward beauty. May Heaven protect your back; may Vāyu protect your thighs; and may the Aśvins support your breasts. May Savitṛ protect you from above. Bṛhaspati shall protect the garment you wear, and the Viśvedevas shall protect you from behind. [May he remove] childlessness and the death of the husband. End of the fourth section of the first chapter.

"Do not weep; do not strike your breast—let that not befall you. Shine forth in the triple abode, O radiant one, sustaining offspring and food. May neither the loss of a husband nor the loss of a son be the cause of your weeping; let neither of these two happen to you. "May heaven protect your back"—may the sky protect the upper part of your body. "May Vāyu protect your chest"—may the wind protect your torso. And may the Aśvins protect your two breasts.

May Savitṛ protect the suckling son; and may Bṛhaspati protect you as you put on this garment—with the verse for the putting on of the garment, "O lover of hymns, may songs encompass thee" (RV 10.96.1)—from that [evil]. May the Viśvedevas protect you from behind. Regarding the term *aprajastām*: she who has no offspring is *aprajā*; the state of being such is *aprajastā*. That [state], namely the death of a grandson (*pautramṛtyu*)—the mortality related to a son—or even (*uta vā*) the sin (*pāpmānam*), [may they ward off].

"I release this bond from the two-footed one. O Varuṇa, hear this my prayer. Having heard it, grant me prosperity this very day. Just as people, having released a sound from their heads, fasten it upon trees and such, so too do I act. "O Varuṇa, hear this my call!"—O Varuṇa! Hear this my invocation. And having heard it, grant me well-being this very day. Desiring to protect you, I, being one who seeks to preserve, yearn for you; I sing and praise you. "That [bond] of yours... [and so forth].

O Varuṇa, O you of wide renown, O you worthy of praise by many, O you who are to be lauded! Do not steal away our life-span. Being free from anger and devoid of malice, be mindful—be aware—of that which is desired here in this rite. That which I have just mentioned, I entreat you for it; with the sacred word (*brahman*), with a mantra, praising you and offering oblations, everyone indeed seeks that very thing. Thus, this *ṛc* has been arranged here out of conformity with its meaning, even though it was [originally] displaced.

"O Varuṇa, hear my call within the *irbha* [grass]; be gracious and have mercy. Seeking your protection, I sing your praise. (Saṃhitā 2.1.1) *The fourth section of the first chapter.*

7. ... [I] implore you: "Thou art ours, O Agni," "So thou art ours, O Agni," "Thou art foremost, O Agni," "Thou art the foremost, O Agni. O Agni! O Knower, the perceiver of all, may you remove—that is, cause to fall away—the wrath (*heḍas*) of the god Varuṇa which is directed toward us. This form is derived from the root *yaj* (or *yat*), used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*) with the optative suffix (*liṅ*), and is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The meaning is: "May you sacrifice it away"—that is, may you cause it to be cast down, so that it becomes directed downward.

O Agni! You who are the best sacrificer (*yajiṣṭha*), the most excellent bearer (*vāḍhetama*) of the oblations, shining intensely (*śośucāna*), [burn away] all (*viśvā*) hostilities (*dveṣāṃsi*) directed toward us from our enemies—the fruits of enmity such as slaughter, imprisonment, and so forth. Such as you are, O Agni, endowed with these aforementioned qualities, you are the lowest (*avama*), that is, the fundamental source (*mūlabhūta*) of the gods.

"Agni is the foremost of the gods; Viṣṇu is the highest"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. O Agni, through your protection (*ūtī*), be most near (*nediṣṭhaḥ*) to us. "May you, O Agni, knowing [the way], ward off from us the wrath of the god Varuṇa. Being the best sacrificer, the greatest bearer of oblations, and shining brightly, do so for us. "O Agni, may you be our protector, most near to us at the dawning of this light. Being gracious, release us from Varuṇa's fetters; accept our offerings, be merciful, and be easy for us to invoke. O you who are to be invoked by the devotees, or rather, you who are the one to whom the devotees turn—with *ayās* (unwearied), being *ayās* (unwearied)—the elision of the letter *s* is Vedic. Being such, you have been placed and fixed within our minds; the ellipsis is "you are," meaning "we fix you within our minds. *Ayāsan ayāssan*: the elision of *s* is as before. Carry the oblation given by us to the gods; as such, bestow healing medicine upon us.

Thus ends the fourth section in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. [The bridegroom] does not speak of longevity while on the way to the wedding procession. [He recites: "May he who has longed for me [grant it], together with the bridal procession (*vadhū*). May he give back the wife to us, O Agni. (RV 10.85.26). He makes her step upon a stone: "Step upon this stone... (RV 10.85.34).
