O bride! Do not step upon this stone; and as you step upon it, may you be as firm as this stone is firm. Steadfast in your heart, do you overcome those who desire battle, those who seek to fight—overcome them, having struck them down, and conquer those who challenge you, those who attack you. The offering of parched grain (*lājahoma*): "This woman... This woman speaks softly, coaxing her relatives, while scattering the parched grains, pouring them out. What does she say? "May my husband have a long life."

What is the meaning of *keo'rthaḥ*? It means: "May she live for a hundred autumns," that is, may she live for a hundred years. The mantras for the circumambulation are: *tubhyam agre*. O *Agra*! To you, *Agra*, at the beginning of time, they led [her] around together with the *vahatu*. *Sūrī* is the name of the daughter of Savitṛ, the presiding deity of marriage. *Vahatu* is the name for the woman’s property obtained from the father's family. The word *punaḥ* has the same meaning as the word *adya* (today).

"Today, indeed, give the wife to our husbands; grant her along with offspring. [The word] "again" (*punar*) means the same thing as before. May the one whose head is the seed bestow her together with long life. May he who is her husband attain long life. [May we cross over] a hundred autumns, and may we, through you, cross over our enemies as if crossing a stream of water. "I step upon this stone. Now the maidens worship the divine Aryaman.

This god, the Adhvaryu, has brought back this bride once more to her husband’s house, just as the bird brings the fire-stick (*araṇi*) back to the fire. And with you, O Viśva, may we stand firm like a stone. You become Aryaman through your speech; may he who is the husband of this bride be long-lived. What is the meaning? May he attain a hundred autumns; may he enjoy a hundred years. “Viśvā” [means...]

He opens [the door]! O Lord, protected by you, may we cross over our enemies and the hostilities of those who hate us; may we pass beyond them as easily as bulls and others pass over the streams of water, just as rain-showers are surpassed [by the strength of the bull]. Regarding the word *ātiṣṭhāmam*: this has been explained. The second *lājahoma* (oblation of parched grain) is with the verse beginning *aryamaṇam*. He who is quickly sought after (*aryate*) is Aryaman, namely Agni. Or, Aryaman is the well-known deity. Formerly, maidens sacrificed to him; having performed that sacrifice, they obtained husbands.
Even now, that sacrifice is considered by Lāja to be unimpaired and unhindered by anyone; the divine Aryaman, having departed, shall eat this [offering] well, and so forth—this has been explained.
"To you first"—this has also been explained.

First Prapāṭhaka, Fifth Khaṇḍa. O you who possess self-power (*svadhāvat*), you bear a name that is radiant; they anoint you like a tree well-smeared with milk. When you make the husband and wife of one mind, it is for you that they have first led [the bride] around. Again, O Agni, the giver of wives, may we all be yours. "I release you from the bond of Varuṇa. This is the third offering of parched grain (*lājahoma*): "You are Aryaman. You are Aryaman, the giver; for according to the Śruti, "He who indeed gives is Aryaman."

O noble one! You alone are the giver; for you support—meaning you nourish—the name of maidens, which signifies bowing down, as well as food accompanied by *svadhā*, and gold (*svar*) for the sake of heaven (*svarga*). Since maidens, food, and heaven all incline toward men through your power, you alone are Aryaman; this is the meaning. And they sprinkle [offerings] unto you alone.

By what means? By means of "cows" (*gobhiḥ*); here the word for the material cause (*prakṛti*) is used in the sense of its product (*vikāra*), as in the mantra: "Mix the exhilarating [Soma] with cows" (*gobhiḥ śrīṇīta matsaram*). It is not well-placed in the tree by means of products of the cow such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like. The negative particle *na* placed first is used in the sense of negation; the placement after the word is used in the sense of comparison. Just as one sprinkles water upon a tree that has been well-placed, well-deposited, or established, so it is here. Since you, O Lord, make the husband and wife *samanasā*, of one mind.

Saṃ. 2-3-4: "The mantras for the circumambulation again are: *tubhyam agre* and so forth; their meaning has already been explained. With the next two [verses], he unfastens the girdle (*yoktra*): *pra tvā muñcāmi*. I release you from the noose of Varuṇa. This very unfastening from the girdle, I perform as a protection for you in this world, together with [the other]. I loosen this bond of Varuṇa which the benevolent Savitṛ has fastened upon you."

I establish you in a pleasant place within the womb, in the world of the Creator, which is well-disposed and secure. You are held by iron, fashioned from iron; you are shaped by that very iron. With that bond, Savitṛ—the impeller of all, the one of good intention, good mind, or excellent wisdom—has established you in the womb, in the world of Brahman. Of what kind? In the world of the well-performed, for the world of Brahman is indeed the world of meritorious action. In that pleasant place, I, your husband, create a comfortable dwelling for you.

"By means of this unyoking of the tether, I loosen and untie this noose of Varuṇa. The noose which Savitṛ—the very gracious one, meaning the maker of happiness for his devotees—has bound, [I release]. 'In the womb of the Creator' and so forth is the same [as before]. Unharmed, meaning indestructible. This is the mantra for placing the fire at the front of the worship of the follower: *ayāśrāg*. *Ayā*..."

Thus it has been explained. O Agni! You are *ayās*—he who is *anabhiśasti*, meaning one for whom no curse (*abhiśasti*) exists; you are free from reproach. *Dīrghatamas* says [this] is the sense of being blameless (*anavadya*). The word "truly" (*satyam*) is used here with *ayās* for the sake of emphasis. The particle *iti* is used for restriction. Being such as this, you have been held—that is, meditated upon—by us with a mind that goes forth (*ayasā*) toward you, a mind that moves toward devotees.
(1-4-16, Sixth Section of the First Chapter).

Carry the oblation; with this [power], bestow healing upon us. (5) By Truth the Ādityas stand firm; Soma is supported in heaven. With your mind, carry the oblation given by us toward the gods; and you, being swift (ayās), bestow and establish healing for us. Thus ends the fifth section in the *Kāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by the venerable Haradatta. At the time of departure, [one uses] the verse beginning with "satyenottambhani" regarding the support of the chariot.

Just as this earth stands supported, propped up, and established by *ṛta*—that is, produced through [the discipline of] mind, speech, and body; and just as the sky stands supported by the sun; and just as the Ādityas stand by means of sacrifice (*yajña*), according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "*The oblation offered into the fire reaches the Āditya perfectly*" (*aprīḥ prāstāhutiḥ samyagādityamupatiṣṭhate*); and just as Soma is deposited in heaven—you, who have been propped up by us, stand. This is to be construed by supplying the remainder of the sentence.

With the two following verses he yokes the draft-animals: "They yoke... [and so forth]. Men have yoked the great, shining one; they have yoked the great horse, the ruddy one, the swift, the goer, capable of movement, who moves having bypassed—that is, passing beyond—the stationary objects that stand around him; for moving about, he indeed goes by bypassing the stationary things. In the latter half-verse, the word *yāvat* is to be supplied: "as far as the luminaries," meaning the stars.

The meaning is that in such rituals, men employ [the horse] constantly from the beginning of the *Agnikāṇḍa* with its commentary until they shine in heaven. Regarding the phrase "yoge yoge" (in every yoking): whenever the yoking of horses and so forth to the chariot and so forth occurs, then at each such time, "tavastaram" is used; here "tavi" is a Vedic root (*dhātu*) for the purpose of expressing growth (*vṛddhi*), or it has the sense of motion (*gati*). Thus, "tavaḥ" means growth or motion; however, in this context, it denotes that which possesses those qualities—namely, being exceedingly endowed with growth or motion. "Vājebāje" is a name for the gathering together.

"Wherever we encounter a confluence [of rivers], this is an elliptical expression meaning that in all circumstances and for all purposes, we—his friends who have become companions through our state of being singers—invoke Indra. For what purpose? For protection (*ūtaye*). He consecrates her as she ascends with the subsequent mantras, beginning with "suākaṃśukam."

Why is the *sukiṃśuka* chariot distinguished? It is a *sukiṃśuka*—meaning a *śalmāla* tree characterized by beautiful *kiṃśuka* (flowering) thorny *palāśa* leaves; here the word for the material cause (*prakṛti*) is used for the modification (*vikāra*). It is constructed from the *śālmalī* tree, and this serves as an illustration for any tree in general. However, others say that the construction of the chariot is based on the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of these two [verses] of the mantra.

O bride, ascend this chariot which possesses manifold forms, is golden-hued, and is of brilliant color; it is well-rolling (*suvṛt*), meaning it moves excellently, and has beautiful wheels (*sucakra*). [The hymn continues: "They yoke the steeds of the immortal one; they surround the ruddy, moving sun. The luminous realms shine in heaven" (Ṛgveda 1.50.2). "We invoke Indra, the most powerful in every endeavor and in every battle, as our friend for protection. (Ṛgveda 8.97.1)

(Śaṃ. 4.12) First Prapāṭhaka, Eighth Khaṇḍa. O bride, ascend to the world of immortality; prepare a pleasant bridal procession for your husband. Ascending to the highest place, driving away those who would attack, mount the head of your husband and shine forth with progeny. "Be a sovereign lady over your father-in-law and a queen over your brothers-in-law. Having ascended the world and the dwelling-place of your fathers-in-law, prepare a pleasant and blissful bridal procession for me, your husband; establish here on this very chariot the woman’s property obtained from the paternal family. "Ascend"—thus [it is said].

Mounting the excellent, superior chariot, ascending upward, dispersing the attackers, and casting away those who seek to fight, mount upon the head of my husband and become preeminent through progeny. And be a *virāj*. "Virāj" is the name of a meter (*chandas*) consisting of ten syllables; for thus says the Śruti: "They amount to ten; the *virāj* has ten syllables."

Just as the *virāṭ* meter consists of ten syllables, so too may you have ten sons—this is the meaning—or else, may you be resplendent (*virājamānā*). He clarifies her preeminence with the word "sovereign" (*saṃrājñī*): "Be a sovereign, beloved, among your father-in-law; be a sovereign among your mothers-in-law; be a sovereign among your husband's sister (the *nanāndṛ*, who is the brother-in-law of the bride); and likewise, be a sovereign among your brothers-in-law (the *devṛ*s, who are the husband's brothers)."
The prefix *adhi* restates the sense of the locative case. That very point is stated again: "of the daughters-in-law" (*snuṣāṇām*). [This refers to] those who are our daughters-in-law...
[End of section] from the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikāṇḍa*.
... for those [women], it is indeed the Virāj. O Nīlalohita, your ritual action (*kṛtyā*) is performed; her kinsmen prosper, and the husband is bound in bonds.
Those diseases (*yakṣmāḥ*) which follow the people as they go to carry the bride’s radiant form—[may they be removed].

May the gods worthy of sacrifice lead them back once they have departed. May you become the sovereign lord (*virāj īśvara*) over my wealth, over my husbands, over those who stand in the place of my husband, over my brothers-in-law (*devar*), over my brothers-in-law’s brothers (*devarāṇām*), and over other kinsmen born in the same household as me. [The ritualist] spreads two threads upon the path with the mantra: "Blue and red. These two threads to be spread are blue and red in color; one is blue and the other is red. What follows from that? [The action to be performed.]

The form of the sixth verse is as follows: *kṛtyā* refers to the power (*sakti*) of a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) employed by others; its "attachment" (*saṅga*), "obstruction" (*pratihati*), or manifestation (*vyajyate*) is brought forth. By means of these two verses, having become obstructed, it is unable to overcome us. Consequently, "may her kinsmen and husband prosper" (*edhante edhantām*); and regarding the bonds—that is, the objects of affection in places of confinement—he is bound, let him be bound. This is an indirect reference to himself, just as in the expression "this person said. Those two verses proceed with the subsequent ones, beginning with "those [who belong] to the bride" (*ye vadhvaḥ*). "Of the bride" (*vadhvaḥ*)...

The genitive plural form *ṣaṣṭhavacanam* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasam*). Regarding the dowry (*vahatu*)—the wealth obtained by this bride from her father’s family—of what nature is it? It is "luminous" (*candram*), meaning it produces radiance. Whatever diseases (*yakṣmāḥ*), those who are the abodes of disease, thieves, and so forth, go toward or seize people to take them away—may the gods who are worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiyā devāḥ*) lead those things back again to the place from which they came. 10) "May the paths be easy to traverse; may the enemies depart; may the swift ones run away. He who travels on an easy path finds the wealth of others. (RV 10.85.32)

"And nine [verses] beginning with *dhanaṃkhyam*. (6) "Do not find that difficult place," [it says]. Those who stand as "waylayers" (*paripanthinaḥ*), desiring to obstruct or seize the path, are the waylayers; may they not find [us], may they not catch us, may they not recognize us. Those waylayers who sit in wait or rush upon the couple—may the couple pass beyond that difficult terrain by means of these easy-to-traverse paths. "Those whose nights are hidden" (*parokṣaniśaḥ*) is as explained before.

"May the enemies, the foes, those very ones who lie in wait as waylayers, depart and go away. "I have ascended the *sugam*—the path upon which one travels with ease. I have ascended the *ariṣṭam*, the secure vehicle in which there is no injury; it does not come to harm. Not only is it not harmed, but it also finds wealth (*vasu*) for others who stand as waylayers. It is this path that I have ascended."

Thus ends the sixth section in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. The recitation for transgressing sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and so forth begins with the verse: *tā mandasānā*. This belongs to the *Āśvina* [section]. *Tā mandasānā*—those two Aśvins, being praised (*mandasānā*), are the lords (*patī*) of Manu (meaning "of the human," *manuṣaḥ*). May they protect us from the evil-minded one who stands on the path. O you two, be our refuge for long life and splendor. Beyond this lies the *Nirṛti* [section] along with its commentary, the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa*.

In the dwelling—the house—of that man who thus desires for me, you two, O speakers of speech, bestow upon me, who seeks the word characterized by praise, wealth consisting of sharp sons along with riches. Furthermore, O Lords of Splendor (*śubhaspatī*), you two create a watering place (*tīrtha*) such as a *suprapāṇa*—a place where one drinks easily—where water flows with ease; for "splendor" (*śubha*) is a name for water, and you two are the protectors of that water characterized by rain.

Furthermore, [the boatman] has seized the thief and others who were plundering. He does not address the boat that has released its chariot, saying, "This is not [mine]. This tree (*vanaspati*)—the boat being the modification (*avakāra*) of the tree—shall lead us across to the further shore of this river, so that we may reach it safely (*svasti*), meaning without destruction. *Sīrā* is a name for a river; the vowel *ā* is used here in the vocative case. O *Sīrā*, may you be easy for us to cross by means of your mouth. [Thus he addresses] the river.

The word *dvacanam* [is explained as follows]: Alternatively, it is a designation for the boat itself, meaning "one that carries well across" (*sutarā suṭu tārayitrī*), with a long vowel due to the suffix *yut*. There is also a word *āyus* ending in the vowel *ū*, according to the statement "the meter is indeed *āyus*. And it exists for the sake of speech. Having crossed over, one performs the recitation: "On its further shore" (*asya pāre*). On the further shore, on the bank of this river and so forth, the living beings (*jīvāḥ*) who have reached the state of being liberated from what was to be crossed over—may we attain that light (*jyotiḥ*) which is their life. For the sake of great well-being (*svastaye*) through Indra.

That which was without heads before the gods, which devoured the devourers—may Madhavan join the joint; may Purōvalu break it apart. May we attain the light, the fearless place; may we obtain it. May Indra and Mahan be for our greatness and for our well-being. Thus is the oblation performed when there is a transgression regarding the cremation ground and so forth, with the verse beginning "yaṣṭate cit."

Regarding the word *ppā* in the form *suluka*: it is that which exists even without (*ṛte cit*), even without the *abhiśriṭ*, that is, the substance used for anointing (*abhileṣaṇadravya*). Even without that, it exists prior to (*puraḥ*) the *jartṛ*s; this is a derivative form of the word *jatu*. In that case, where it is taught with a final *u*-vowel (*ukārānta*), there is merely the addition of the letter *r* (*repha*). But here, even the *u*-vowel becomes an *ū*-vowel (*ūkāra*). This [form] is in the instrumental case (*tṛtīyānta*), though it appears in a different form (*vyatyayena*). And because of the mention in the plural, the sense of the singular is understood.

The term *ātṛdaḥ* is derived from the root *tṛd* with the suffix *kasun* following *jatvādi*; the meaning is that they are "exceedingly sharp" even before the time at which the *jatvādi* materials pierce—that is, while they are still making the [target] pierceable.

The meaning is: "the uniter" (*sandhātā*), "the union" (*sandhi*), and "that which is to be united" (*sandhātavya*); that is, the uniter of the object to be united. "Maghavan" refers to Indra. In the word "purovasuḥ," the vowel *o* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) form of the word "puru"; thus it means "possessing abundant wealth" (*purūvasuḥ*). "The fashioner for us" (*niṣkartā*): this too ends in the suffix *tṛn*. As stated in the *Brahma-Brāhmaṇa*: "That which is fashioned (*nipkṛta*) is indeed refined (*saṃskṛta*). He is the refiner (*saṃskartā*) who restores that which was opened up, utterly destroyed, once again.

He who is possessed of abundant wealth (*puruvasu*), the bountiful one (*maghavā*), who—having first gathered even the most difficult substances such as lac (*jatū*) and the like from within—joins things that ought to be joined and restores what has been disfigured; because he acts with such intent, it is understood [that the offering is made] to him: *svāhā* to him! "O Agni, come hither! O Varuṇa, I approach you. You are our leader, O Agni; you are our leader, O Agni. You are the leader, O Agni. "The Gandharvas and the divine Apsarases who dwell in these trees, among the lords of the forest (*vanaspati*)."

"O Agni, [grant] the *iḍā* first!"—O Agni, here! Grant to me, who am calling upon you, that which is rich in deeds (*purudaṃsam*), most beautiful to behold (*atyantachāyyam*), and the constant (*śaśvattamam*) bestower of cattle (*gossanim*). Furthermore, may we have a son (*sūnuḥ*), a grandson (*tanayaḥ*), and a great-grandson (*pautraḥ*). Of what nature? "Born again" (*vijāvā*), having the inherent quality of procreation. [The suffix] *viṭ* is applied by the rule *janasanakhanakramagamemaḥ viṭ*; and by the rule *viḍūnoranunāsikasyāt*, there is the substitution of *ā* for the nasal.

What need for more? O Agni! May that *ṭubhati*—your well-known intellect characterized by grace toward devotees—be present among us (*asme*). —The five verses beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" have passed. For the transgression of milky trees and the like, there is the recitation (*japa*) of the verse beginning with "ye gandharvāḥ."

Those Gandharvas, headed by Viśvāvasu, and the divine Apsarases who dwell and reside in these trees—the Vanaspatis, the Nyagrodha, Udumbara, and Aśvattha—these indeed are the homes of the Gandharvas and Apsarases. May they be auspicious to this bride; may they not harm the bridal procession (*vahatu*), the dowry (*strīdhana*) being carried away, nor this woman being brought here. [End of] the explanatory section on the *ekāgnikaṇḍa*, 7 = for the sake of the sacrifice.

"May she who has sons, who gives milk, who brings forth offspring—may that benevolence of yours be with us. (Ṛgveda 10.85.44) These mantras are written in the [relevant] sections. Regarding the verses beginning with "yā oṣadhayo": "The herbs, the creepers, those on the dry land, and those in the forests—O bride, may they release you here, full of progeny; may the swan [carry you] away. "I bring the bridal procession with sacred prayer and houses; may Savitṛ create a dwelling for the husbands. The mantra to be recited when crossing a river: "The herbs which we have crossed... [and so on].

And those rivers, those deserts, waterless regions, those woods, and those forests—these have been mentioned as having become such [by their very nature]. O bride! May they make you possessed of offspring; this is the ellipsis. And may they release you from distress. With the following verse, he causes her to look at the bridal procession (*vahatu*); therein, the bridal procession is to be brought forward first, according to the indicative mark of the mantra. "I cause you to look—I show—the bridal procession, the wealth brought from her father's family, by means of *brahman*, that is, by means of the mantra."

"I shall cause her to look upon me with my own eyes—with an eye that is not fierce, not cruel, but gentle. Let her look with such an eye; I show her this. And whatever manifold form, consisting of various ornaments and the like, has been bound all around her by her kinsmen, may Savitṛ make that pleasant and comfortable for me, her husband. [He releases her from the veil, saying: "O Bhaga... etc.

O Aśvins! Your own benevolent favor, consisting of grace, has come toward us; it has arrived and reached us. O possessors of wealth through horses! Through our hymns and praises, O lords of riches, may our desires enter your hearts. You have become our protectors, a pair, the masters of splendor. May we, as beloved ones, reach the dwelling of the Immortal. Now may the divine Bṛhaspati, Indra-Agni, and Mitra-Varuṇa grant us well-being. May our desire come to pass.

The final two verses of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* contain an explanation: "Our desires regarding our dwellings—'may we easily reach home'—have become fixed, settled, and certain, because you two have been our protectors (*gopā*) on the path of the two worlds. O lords of the auspicious (*śubhaspatī*), companions who move together, guardians of food or water, through your favor, having become dear to Aryaman (the Āditya) or Agni, may we enter the dwellings (*duryān*). (Note: The phrase *prathamārthe dvitīyā* indicates that the accusative case is used here in the sense of the nominative; *vṛtsu* is glossed as *gṛheṣu*; *mithulā* means *sahacāriṇau*; and *aryamṇaḥ* refers to the Āditya or Agni.)
"This one" (*ayam*): this is an address directed toward the horse. O Horse! Since we have *āma* (sour milk), come here;

you, having been brought, may you roam at will for our desire (*kāmāya*). Who [is it]? This god Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, and the others, for the sake of well-being (*svastaye*)—that is, for non-destruction—being well-disposed (*saṃrarāṇaḥ*), bestowing progeny properly, sharing the labor together with progeny; that is to say, sporting with offspring. Thus ends the seventh section in the commentary on the mantras of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* composed by Śrī Haradatta.
[The eighth section of the first chapter begins.]

... by means of this [sacrifice], may this Bharṇa’s favor be victorious... he brought forth heroes. May those who consume the nourishment (*irā*) while tearing it apart be well-disposed toward me; I enter among them with a gracious mind. O Agni, bring hither the great seers, the cow, the life-force, and the skin as a covering—a skin that is a source of happiness and protection for you. Bring such a skin as this!

For what purpose? For the sake of spreading [a seat] for this woman, for the purpose of providing a substrate (upastaraṇa). The suffix *ken* is used in the sense of a gerundive (*kṛtya*). Sinīvālī is seen on the new moon day. O Sinīvālī! May this bride be prolific; may she become possessed of offspring. And may it be in the mind of the god Bhaga—that is, in his intellect which consists of grace—[that it be so]; the meaning is: "By your favor, may he too bestow grace upon her. As he leads the bride into the house, he makes her recite: "I enter the house."

Of what kind? "Auspicious" means pleasing; "sumanasas" refers to the mothers-in-law and others residing in the house who become well-disposed upon seeing the daughter-in-law; thus he calls the houses "sumanasas."

I am one whose husband is not a hero, yet my sons are heroes; though my wealth is not of that nature, through the grace of the gods and my husband’s sons, I am possessed of excellent heroes—endowed with noble protectors. Bringing nourishment (*irām*) and pouring forth clarified butter (*ghṛta*), where the *brāhmaṇas* eat and the clarified butter is poured, from there it flows hither; those houses are called "pouring forth clarified butter. [The nominative is used in the sense of the accusative. Having entered into such houses, I shall lie down with a well-disposed mind.

In the *Savyākhyānekāgnikāṇḍa*, verse 40: "May the two wives be without distress; may they give birth to offspring. May the fragrant one, bestowing blessings, attend to this sacrifice. May Agni, the protector of the house, being well-disposed, fulfill our purposes on his back. Just as Bhaga [bestows] fortune, may he grant us prosperity and offspring. Through offspring from these two, may Prajāpati [prosper]. Then follow the thirteen subsequent oblation-mantras beginning with *āganmaite*.

She has come, she has arrived at the cow-pen, the house—my queen, my wife Vaṅbhā—along with cows and horses obtained from her father’s family. "One whose husband is long-lived" is *āyuṣmatpatnī*; by this, he invokes long life for himself. By the phrase "with offspring," he invokes the attainment of heaven, for it is said, "There is no world for one who is childless"; thus, the specific injunction there is "procreating offspring. And [he says], "procreating offspring."

Having become one who possesses beautiful wealth, may this *aupāsana* fire attend upon and serve me for a hundred winters, for a hundred years; it is intended that it should be fit for the sake of Atri. This *aupāsana* fire is Agni the Householder (*gṛhapati*), the protector of my home.

May Agni—who is well-praised, whose seat is beautiful, who increases prosperity, and who bestows abundance upon me (in accordance with the statement, "One should desire glory from the Fire-god")—being such as he is, grant wealth (*rayi*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and also progeny (*prajā*) to us two, that is, to the husband and wife. [The form *dadat* is used] either as a present participle or as a subjunctive (*leṭ*). Just as he gave to Bhaga for the sake of the god Bhaga; and the mention of Bhaga is illustrative, meaning "as he did for the gods," for even the successes of the gods are born of ritual action (*karmaja*).

"O Prajāpati! For the sake of progeny—of that offspring belonging to this couple—[grant] 'auspicious ornaments' (śobhanābharaṇā; *Matsyapurāṇa-vacana*, according to the *Śabdakalpadruma*). From the two who are vigorous, let there be offspring. By that which has become the oblation (*havis*), may this [person] swell again. Regarding the wife whom they have desired for us, may those two remain right here; do not separate them from their full lifespan and fame. Grant me great protection (*śarma*)"—this is the connection through grammatical transformation.

O Indra and Agni! Grant protection such that, while both of us remain alive and active, our offspring shall not perish—grant such protection that none shall die. By this—that which is offered by me, whether as a substance already present or as an oblation obtained—may this person cause her to flourish with essence, such as clarified butter and other offerings, whom they have brought and given to him as his wife. "Arbhi—" [meaning "toward"].

"Likewise, may she increase with milk; may she increase with the kingdom, with houses, fields, and so forth. Likewise, by means of wealth (*rayi*) that nourishes many—possessing a thousandfold progeny—may this couple be independent; that is, may there be an increase in wealth such that they have no dependence on anyone else. "Thus, indeed! This is a statement directed toward one's own inner self.

"O our inner selves! Dwell right here in this house; may you never be separated, even for a moment. A full lifespan—'He lived for a hundred and sixteen years,' thus [it is said]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.16.7). 42.

"O Sādhyā, you who are established in a single place, for Indra’s well-being! Be firm and nourishing within me; Bṛhaspati has taken you with great power. With me as your husband, may you be rich in offspring; live a hundred autumns. Tvaṣṭṛ begot the wife, and Tvaṣṭṛ [begot] you as her husband. May Tvaṣṭṛ grant you both a thousand lifespans and long life. 'Hear this my cry, O Varuṇa'... 'To that I go, O Agni'... 'Be a protector to us, O Agni'... 'You, O Agni, are the first'... 'You, O Agni, are the leader'. (8)

"May you two live with offspring and cattle. (8) This is the manifestation of what is declared in the Śruti. May Indra also grant you great well-being. "Dhruvaidhi" (Be firm): O bride, you who are to be nourished by me, be firm—be steadfast—in me. Bṛhaspati has given you to me. Being possessed of offspring, live together with me, your husband, for a hundred autumns—many years. "Tvaṣṭā... (Tvaṣṭṛ... [The verse continues].

"As long as Tvaṣṭṛ indeed fashions the forms of the emitted seed," and "May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms"—Tvaṣṭṛ, who is heard in scripture as the agent in the creation of forms, that very Tvaṣṭṛ begot this wife. Likewise, Tvaṣṭṛ alone begot for her you as her protector. O my inner self! May that same Tvaṣṭṛ create a thousand lifespans, abundant riches, and long life for both of you, the two inner selves.

1–1: "imaṃ me varuṇa" and the following [verses] have been included in the *pañca* [section]. Thus ends the eighth section in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. These mantras (22–24) are written on pages 11–15;
[they correspond to] Sūtra 1.5.9: "Stay here, O cows; stay here, O progeny; stay here, O horses; stay here, O Pūrus."

"May the possessor of wealth, accompanied by sacrificial gifts, sit down here. In the lap of these [stones] for Soma, Soma is placed. Being well-established, they both proceed with the next verse while sitting upon the skin: "Here, O cows! [The meaning is: "O cows, in this house, be procreated; become numerous! O horses! O men! Be procreated"—thus it is intended. In all these cases, the *āmantrita-nighāta* (the suppression of accent on vocatives) does not occur because of the Vedic character (*chāndasatvāt*).

Right here, right now, may the abundance of wealth (*rāyaspoṣaḥ*), accompanied by faith and worthy of much giving—the swelling of riches—take its seat. Now, she who has borne only male children and whose son is living, makes her son sit on the lap of the bride with the mantra: "By Soma... The Āditya gods are our strength through Soma; through Soma is the growth of plants, for sacrifice occurs upon the increase of plants. And the earth is firm through Soma, [supported] by herbs, trees, and so forth.

"Furthermore, just as Soma was placed and deposited in the lap of these Kṣatriyas, so may this boy sit upon your lap. He gives fruits to him, saying: "You are *prasva*s. [The word] *prasva* means "those that bring forth"; O fruits! You are *sva*, you are of the nature of bringing forth. [The *s* is] a Vedic *visarjanīya*; [thus it means] "you are."

"May this bride also shine forth and flourish in this world with progeny and husband. The meaning is: "Just as you are prolific, so may she also become prolific through your favor. He recites the subsequent mantra: "iha priyam... ("May there be what is dear here in this house..."). [In this house, may there be what is dear to you... (with commentary on the various sections).

"May your joy prosper; may you increase. By this, the excellence of progeny is expressed. He speaks of the excellence of dharma: "In this house, for the sake of the status of a householder (*gārhapatya*), be watchful; be attentive in the service of guests and the sacred fires. May Prajāpati, the Ordainer, bestow a fetus upon you. O Sinīvālī, grant a fetus; O Sarasvatī, grant a fetus. May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, place a fetus within you. Just as this great earth, standing firm, holds her embryo, so may the husband enter me and pour his seed therein.

And may Dhātṛ—one of the Ādityas—or Prajāpati himself, cause that infused seed to take root and transform it into an embryo. And may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion its forms, such as hands, feet, and so forth; for Tvaṣṭṛ is the agent of shining, as seen in the mantra, "By means of the stars, the Fathers adorned the sky. Make them radiant.
"Place the embryo"—thus [is the prayer] addressed to the bride presided over by Sinīvālī and Sarasvatī.

He conceives [the fetus] in that very way. "Place it"—that is, hold it. And may the two gods, the Aśvins, who wear lotus-garlands (*puṣkarasrajau*), place the embryo within you. "The two golden fire-drills" (*hiraṇyayī araṇī*): here, the *pūrvasavarṇa* (the preceding vowel) is substituted for the third case singular ending.

With a golden womb—that is, with a generative organ similar to that—we invoke for you such an embryo as the two Aśvins produced through their effort by churning; we pray that it may be born in the tenth month. Since the Aśvins are beautiful in form, let your son also be beautiful; such an embryo shall be yours. "Yatheyaṃ bhāti" [is the mantra].

Just as the great earth stands vast and firm, so do you conceive this embryo; may it remain within you constantly for ten months. As the earth contains the seed of grain, as Dyaus (the Sky) is pregnant with Indra, and as Vāyu is the embryo of the quarters, even so do I place the embryo within you. O Viṣṇu, with your most excellent form, place a male embryo in this woman who desires a son, so that she may give birth in the tenth month.

"O Nejameṣa, now she stands just so; that is to say, she remains lying on her back. The reading *uttānatyeva* is indeed found among the Bahvṛcas (Ṛgvedins). Just as the earth, having received the seed characterized by rain poured down from the heavenly world, sustains the embryo characterized by the harvest, even so do you receive the embryo—sustain it. "In the tenth month" has been explained previously. "Just as the earth... [and so forth]."

Because fire resides within earthly things that grow in the forest, the earth is said to have fire as its embryo; Indra is the preeminent deity in the heavenly world, and he is described as her embryo; and since wind originates from the quarters of space, it is their embryo. Just as these are the embryos of these [elements], so do I place an embryo within you. "O Viṣṇu!"—O Viṣṇu, endowed with the most excellent form, place a male embryo within this woman.

In what kind of woman? In a *gavīnī*—this is a metaphor for a desirable woman (*kamanīyā*), one who is longed for (*kāmyā*), that is, one fit to be desired, meaning one who has bathed after her menses (*ṛtusnātā*). Others, however, consider *gavīnī* to be a designation for a woman’s exceptional virility (*vīryātiśaya*), based on the observation [in the Veda]: "Thy *takarī* pierces through, thy womb pierces through, thy two *gavīnyau* pierce through" (*vi te bhinadi takarī vi yoniṃ vi gavīnyau*). The meaning is: in that *gavīnī* which this woman possesses. "In the tenth month" is already explained. 60.

May he, together with his sons, prosper; may he bestow [prosperity] upon us again. Place an embryo within this womb of mine who longs for a son—an embryo that is male. Entering her womb, deposit the seed; let a male son be conceived within the womb. Let the mother bear him for ten months; let him become a hero who conquers the darkness.

"May a male embryo enter your womb, like an arrow into a quiver. [He recites] "O Nejameṣa! Nejameṣa is well-known in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as one of the *skandagrahas* (demons that afflict children). Likewise, it is stated in medical science (*vaidyaka*) regarding the affliction by the *kumāragrahas*: "And one should worship Nejameṣa. O Nejameṣa! Fly away, go far off; for you are a defiler of the embryo. If you must certainly come, come back again with your son; having taken your son, come back.

And having come, place the embryo in this womb of mine, which belongs to me and is desirous of a son. Of what kind? [In the phrase] *yaḥ pumān* ("who is a man"): O you, having opened (*vyasya*)—that is, having spread apart and expanded—the womb into which semen is being discharged by me, receive it. When that is done, let the embryo be placed within you, and let that male child be conceived. And you, as the mother, [shall bear him] for ten months; here the word *māsa* (month) undergoes the substitution *māsa-* according to the rule beginning with *pada-*.

"May she bear [the child] for ten months"—here there is a transposition of persons (puruṣavyatyaya); [thus it means] "bear [it]. And may he be born as the most heroic among his own kinsmen. "Into thee..."—let the full-grown embryo enter your womb. Like what? Like an arrow into a quiver—that is, just as an arrow enters that in which arrows are placed. And when he has completed ten months, let a hero be born to you as your son, one who has fulfilled the ten months. 13.

"I place eight embryos within you. (13) "I perform for you the rite pertaining to Prajāpati; may [the embryo] enter your womb. May he be born not deficient, complete, victorious, uncrippled, and free from the influence of Piśācas. O woman, may a son be yours; may that son be born as a man. From those [embryos], may a son be born to you—one who is heroic and endowed with valor. Thus ends the thirteenth section in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by the venerable Haradatta. "I perform... (etc.).

That is the act pertaining to Prajāpati, the work of Prajāpati, namely the emission of semen, based on the scriptural vision: "Prajāpati emitted [the seed]. I perform that for you. And from that, let the embryo enter your womb. And may it be born complete—with no missing limbs, full, with its full term of ten months—neither crippled, nor lame, nor deformed; nor one "conceived by Piśācas" (apiśācadhītaḥ)—for *dhītaḥ* means either conceived (*dhīyate*) or thought of (*dhyātaḥ*), meaning one who is not conceived or thought of by Piśācas. "May it be a male," he says.

"O woman! May a male son be born to you"—this is what is expected from what is about to be said. First, let the embryo be male; and may that male be born after him, and may the second and subsequent embryos also be males—this is the meaning. May those such auspicious, beneficial, and disease-free seeds—that is, vital powers—as well as the *ṛṣabhas*, who are like bulls capable of impregnation, produce them. Who, then, are they? Prajāpati and others, or the plants such as beans and so forth; [may they produce them] when drunk, or when pressed.

The *Ekānnikāṇḍa* with its commentary: "May the auspicious seeds, the bulls, generate for us! Those auspicious seeds which the bulls generate for us—through them may you obtain sons; may she be a mother like Venukā. May my desire be fulfilled; indeed, it is unconquered by my enemies. O God, whatever desire I cherish, fulfill that for us both. Just as sons are born one after another, so may they produce such heroic powers for us both.
Regarding the word "yāni": the aforementioned bulls [generate] those auspicious seeds.

The plural form "naḥ" is used because of the rule "asmado dvayośca" (the word *asmad* takes the plural when referring to two). Do not produce [other children] with those seeds; through them, may you obtain sons. May you, as a mother (*prasūḥ*), being prolific and like a cow (*dhenukā*), be one who is constantly suckled by your son, just as a cow is sucked by her calf. Regarding the word "kāmam": the root *prā* means "to fill"; thus, "kāmagram" means that which fulfills desires. May this rite of mine prosper (*ṛdhyatām*); may it be successful (*ṛddham astu*) and unfailing (*aparājitam eva amogham eva*) for me.

"O Deva Vāyu! Fulfill this desire of mine, make it successful—that I may give birth to a male child. Thus he is entreated, for it is the semen impelled by Vāyu that is emitted. Regarding the mantra for the "anuhava" (the muttering of a prayer) when sneezing or being called from behind: "anuhavam. Calling from behind is *anuhava*; calling from all sides is *parihava*; a censurable speech such as "cut! or "split! is *parīvāda*; and sneezing from all sides is *parikṣava*. [The mantra is: "O Vāta, do not abandon us... (RV 10.186.1). The mantra is recited.

Whatever ill-omened dream, whatever evil utterance, that I cast away as poison to the enemies. Whatever is ill-invoked, whatever is ill-summoned, whatever is inauspicious regarding birds; whatever track of a wild beast, whatever is crooked, that I cast away as poison to the enemies. *The fourteenth section in the first chapter.* 68. May I see [the enemy]. Whatever ill-omened dream, whatever evil utterance, that I cast away as poison to the enemies. Whatever is ill-invoked, whatever is ill-summoned, whatever is inauspicious regarding birds; whatever track of a wild beast, whatever is crooked, that I cast away as poison to the enemies.

"May the fire be far from you; may the axe be far from you. May the rain fall upon the windless place for you. May there be well-being for you, O Lord of the Forest; may there be well-being for me, O Lord of the Forest. Salutations to the maker of the *śakṛt* (dung), to Rudra; salutations to Rudra, the maker of the *śakṛt*. [Note: The change of the letter *v* to *p* is according to Vedic usage. Whatever bad dream has occurred, whatever evil utterance such as that which causes distress (*vaidhavya*), and whatever other such ill omen there is—that I cast away upon my enemies; I release it. [Regarding the word *yat*...]

Whatever was followed by an invocation (*anuhūtam*), whatever was carried around (*pārihṛtam*), whatever pertains to an ill-omened bird (*aśākuna*) that is not a favorable sign, and whatever transverse movement (*akṣṇayā sṛtam*)—such as the sideways running or the counter-clockwise circling—of a wild animal like a jackal and so forth, all that I give away to my enemies. "Auspicious" (*śakunam*) means a favorable omen; its opposite is "inauspicious" (*aśākunam*), meaning a bad omen. Regarding the consecration of a wondrous tree (*citriya-vanaspati*), [the mantra begins with] "From afar... and so forth: "O Tree! From afar, Agni is yours."

In this way, let even an axe be far from you! "Nivāta" means the absence of wind; when such a windless state exists, may the god rain upon you (*tvā*), lest there be the danger of breaking in the wind. Thus, may it be well with you, O Lord of the Forest (*vanaspate*)! May it be well with me too, O Lord of the Forest, through the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of you. The ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) for the dung-heap is: "Obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the dung-heap" (*namaḥ śakṛtsade*). He sits or settles (*sīdate*) in the dung-heap for Rudra; the repetition is for the sake of emphasis: "Obeisance to Rudra who dwells in the dung-heap. O dung-heap!

In the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*: "Homage be to you, O Goṣṭha (the cow-pen)! Do not harm me. Homage be to you, O Sarga (the path)! You are a thunderbolt; homage be to you! Do not harm me. 'O auspicious bird, you sing the *Sāman* chant; like a son of Brahman, you recite at the libations. May there be well-being for us, O auspicious bird! You are the Goṣṭha; you abide in the cows. Homage be to you! Do not harm me. Even the cows do not harm anything at all, and you are the Goṣṭha."

The consecration of the *sīka* (a type of garment) is with the mantra: *sīgasi*. "O *sīka*, you are the fringe (*daśā*) of the garment; you are indeed like a *sīka*; you are not a thunderbolt (*vajra*), you are not a thunderbolt; you do not attain the state of a thunderbolt"—here the elided form (*pararūpa*) is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The phrase beginning with "salutation to you" (*namaste*) has already been explained. The consecration of the bird (*śakuni*) is with the mantra: *udgāteva*. "O bird! You sing the *Sāman* like a *Udgātṛ* priest; just as the *Udgātṛ* sings the *Sāman*, so do you sing."

Furthermore, you sing, you praise, and you speak what is laudable like a son of Brahmā at the *savanas*. A "son of Brahmā" (*brahmaputra*) refers to the *Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* priest, who belongs to the class of those devoted to the Veda; just as he recites at all three *savanas* during the *ukthya* and other sacrificial forms, so do you. The word *savana* here denotes the sacrifice. Moreover, O bird! May there be well-being for us, and may you be well-disposed toward us.

Thus ends the fourteenth section in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. 65. At dawn we invoke Indra; at dawn Mitra and Varuṇa; at dawn the Aśvins; at dawn Bhaga, Pūṣan, and Brahmaṇaspati; at dawn let us invoke Soma and Rudra. At dawn let us invoke the fierce Bhaga, the conqueror; we invoke the son of Aditi, the ordainer. "I desire to partake of that fortune which is the portion of the Aśvins, the thought of the swift one, and even of the kings"—thus he says.

O Bhaga, O leader, O Bhaga, true wealth; O Bhaga, piercing open this prayer for us like a water-jar! We invoke those well-known lords of the household, the masters of food, at dawn for the sake of protection. And we shall call upon Rudra at dawn; we invoke Rudra, the winner of the morning.

We invoke—that is, we call upon—that Bhaga, one of the Ādityas, who is victorious at every dawn (*prātajit*), fierce and invincible, the son of Aditi, the Āditya who is the sustainer (*vidhartā*) of all through rain and other means. Even the poor man (*ādhaḥ*), even the hurried one (*turaḥ*)—the word *cit* having the sense of "even"—even a king, thinking himself wise, knows that Bhaga when he speaks thus. (Note: *bhakṣati* is a form in the *luṅ* (aorist) used in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative); *ādhaḥ* means "poor"; *turaḥ* means "hurrying"; *jānaḥ* means "knowing" or "wise").

How so? The meaning is: "May I enjoy the fortune (bhaga)," knowing this, everyone desires to be his devotee (*bhakta*). "O Bhaga, O Dispenser!"—O Bhaga, O Leader of all! He is addressed again and again for the sake of emphasis. "Bhaga! O Rādha"—*rādha* is a name for wealth.

O Bhaga! May this intention of mine—that "this [offering] shall overcome my rival"—and that wisdom which seeks the overcoming of the rival, protect us as we rise up; may you grant us protection in turn. O Bhaga, bestow upon us cattle, horses, and heroes; may we abide in the favor of Ṛta both now and at the present time, in the beginning of the day, in the middle of the days, and at the journey's end.

"O Maghavan, when the sun has risen, may we abide in the good favor of the gods. May Bhaga indeed be our Bhargava; O gods, may we be under his protection. O Bhaga, may all these people praise you, granting us what is desired. O Bhaga! Do you cause us to prosper with cattle and horses. O Bhaga! By your grace, may we be preeminent among men, including servants and others. [Regarding the word] "ut": *Note: The provided text contains several archaic Vedic forms and fragments. The translation reflects the intended meaning of the mantras as they appear in the context of the *Ṛgveda*.*

Now, at this time of action, may we be possessed of fortune (*bhaga*) through the god Bhaga—both at the onset of the day, even at evening, even in the midst of the days, and also when the sun has risen; *uditā* is the locative singular form of *udita*. O Maghavan! *Magha* is a name for wealth; O possessor of wealth! At the rising of what? The meaning is: may we be possessed of fortune during all three times of the sun, such as the forenoon and so forth.

Furthermore, may we abide in the benevolent thought—the gracious-minded awareness—of the gods; that is to say, by the grace of Bhaga, may other gods as well show us favor. Thus ends [the section on] Bhaga. O gods! May the god Bhaga himself, being Bhaga, be possessed of fortune (bhagavān); may he be endowed with the quality of Bhaga, meaning that his gift is indeed praiseworthy. Through that Bhaga, may we become possessed of fortune (bhagavantaḥ).

O Bhaga! I, every single person, call upon you—whoever you truly are—with fervent invocation; here there is a transposition of the grammatical person (puruṣavyatyaya). [End of] the fifteenth section of the first chapter... Some say [you are] the horse; others say [you are] the sun. [Brāhmaṇa 1.4.8]. I invoke you; O Bhaga, be our leader here.

"May all sacrifices bow down to you, O Uṣas, as Dadhikrāvan bows to the pure station. May they bring hither to us Bhaga, the finder of wealth, like swift horses bringing a chariot. May the auspicious Dawns dawn upon us at all times—rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in heroes—yielding milk and swelling from every side. Do you protect us always—[the Ṛgvedic priest] calls out. Thus it is studied by the Bahvṛcas: 'O Bhaga! may you be our leader and guide here in this ritual act.'"

"Regarding the phrase *sabhadhvārāya*: by the grace of that very Bhaga, even the dawns (*uṣasaḥ*) have bowed down for this sacrifice (*adhvarāya*), which consists of the subduing of rivals; here the imperative sense is expressed by the present tense (*laḍ*), meaning "let them bow down," i.e., "let them partake. Like Dadhikrāvan—some say he is the food (*anna*), others say he is water (*āpaḥ*)—just as he is fit for the pure place, the purified station, so too [should they be]."

Furthermore: "May they bring Bhaga—who knows wealth and bestows wealth—toward us, facing our way. Who are they? The swift, vigorous horses, just as horses draw a chariot; so it is here. The next verse is addressed to the Viśvedevas: "O Dawns, rich in horses, rich in cattle, and rich in heroes, shine forth, shine forth, become fully risen—at all times, meaning eternally."

Ghee—this is an elliptical expression including "milk, clarified butter, honey, water," and so forth—yielding from all sides, swelling and flourishing on every side; those [cows] mentioned in this hymn (68) in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* with their own praises, may they then be ours here. [Fifteen. And four more: [Fifteen. This plant, the most powerful herb, I dig up for you from the navel [of the earth], by which one drives away a rival wife, and by which one finds a husband. O high-standing, fortunate, conquering, and swift one!

"O you who have been designated as my supreme protectors, beginning with the elder brother (agrajyā), may you always protect us with blessings; guard us! Thus ends the fifteenth section in the *Ekāgni-kāṇḍa-mantra-vyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. The mantra for uprooting the plant called *pāṭhā* for the purpose of subjugating the husband: "I dig this... "I dig—that is, I uproot—this medicinal herb named *pāṭhā*. It is a *vīrudh*, meaning a plant that grows in various ways and possesses spreading tendrils."
"Most powerful" means exceedingly vigorous. By which herb one overcomes a rival wife—that is, every woman—and by which she properly finds, that is, obtains, an extraordinary husband.
The consecration of that recitation is performed with the following verses: "O thou of upturned face."

O you whose leaves are known to be turned upward, O Uttānaparṇā! O fortunate one, the cause of good fortune! O Sahamānā, who endures and overcomes the Vedic meters! O you who repel the co-wife, O Sahasvatī, the exceedingly powerful one! Drive away my rival; send my co-wife away and make me alone the possessor of this [fortune], making it unique to me.

[The section on] production. First Chapter, Sixteenth Section. "Make my husband mine alone. I am the superior; I am higher than the higher, and more exalted than those who are exalted. And she who is my rival, let her be lower than the lowest. For I do not grasp her navel, nor do I dwell among her people. I am the conqueror; you are the one who overcomes. Having become the subduer of both, may we together overcome my rival. I have placed power within you; I am the superior. Thus [ends the section].

"O superior one! O excellent one! O recitation! May I myself be superior (*uttarā*) by my very nature; furthermore, may I become even more superior than those who are already superior—the word *uta* having the sense of 'indeed' (*eva*). The Vāḍavas read it in this very way. Now, let her who is my rival be even lower (*adharā*) than those who are already low. "'Not indeed! [She says: 'I do not even utter her name. For what reason? Because she does not take pleasure in this person—this being a reference to oneself.'"

What need of more? We utterly destroy—*parāvadati* means "to drive far away," thus we utterly destroy, we cause to perish, we send away the rival wife to the furthest distance (*parāvat*), which is a name for the remote. [The mantra continues: "I am she. With the following verse, having split that [rival] into two, one should cast her down from the hands, saying: "I am she"—that is, I am the one who overcomes, the one who subdues the rivals. And in the next line: "Thou art she"—thou art the conqueror, thou art the subduer.

May we two, both of us, becoming powerful and strong, overcome my rival wife; may we subdue her. (From the *Sacyākhyānaikānnikāṇḍa*): "Over you with greater strength—I [will prevail]. May she run after me like a cow to its calf; may she run like water through a strainer. (16) "May we overcome her," and two [more]. (16) "Up has risen that sun; up has risen my glory, my splendor."

At the time of going to bed, the wife should embrace her husband with her arms, saying: "I have placed thee near. This is said to the husband: "I have placed this [wife] of thine, who is enduring, near thee; I have placed her beneath thee, and indeed I have placed her upon thee," being endowed with a mind that is most powerful and preeminent in its overcoming. And in this very manner the embracing should be performed, so that one hand is placed beneath the husband and the other above.

When this has been done, may he run toward me, toward me, like a cow toward her calf—just as a cow that has recently calved runs toward her calf; and just as water flows along a downward path, so too [may he run]. Thus ends the sixteenth section in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. For the purpose of subduing co-wives, one should worship the Sun every day with the following Anuvāka: "That Sun has risen... (*ud asau sūryaḥ*). That Sun has indeed risen.

May *bhaga*—my own inherent fortune, or the organ of generation—not abandon me. Because of the repetition of the word *ud* (to rise), the verb *agāt* (has gone) is expected [as its counterpart]. The meaning is: "Just as this sun rises, increasing in power, so may my *bhaga* also rise. For that reason, being *vidvalā*—possessing knowledge (*vit*) through this lore—I am possessed of that [knowledge]. [I am] one who has first approached her husband; I am one who is radiant, with wide eyes and a broad forehead.

"I am the banner, I am the head; I am the fierce one, the one who pronounces the verdict. My son-in-law shall do what is pleasing to me; my daughter is the sovereign. And I am she who is victorious; I have witnessed against my husband. She has overcome this form; I have become the conqueror, the subduer, the one who especially overcomes. "I am! [71]

I am the banner; indeed, I alone am the banner-like position for both parties. I alone am the head, the one occupying the position of the head. I am the fierce one, the unconquerable. *Vivācanī* means the one who causes the *vivācana*, which is the final decision or resolution. Furthermore, let my very own *kratu*—whether meaning ritual action or wisdom—the Lord (*pati*) follow (*anūvācaret*). The letter *v* is a Vedic [sandhi] form. He followed; thus the Rigvedic seers recite. Let him perform it. Of what kind? Of me who am victorious (*sehānāyāḥ*). This is a form derived from the root with the suffix *kānac* in the perfect tense.

The meaning is: "O you who are overcome or who overcome, let my husband act exactly as I have known or as I have done. She prays: "May my sons be slayers of enemies (*śatruhaṇaḥ*), that is, destroyers of their foes; and furthermore, may my daughter be *virāṭ*, that is, resplendent."

Moreover, here the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*): "May I be victorious" (*asāni*), meaning "may I be a conqueror (*sañjayā*) of my rivals. Likewise, regarding the husband, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the locative (*saptamī*); thus, it means "in the husband. Similarly, the Vedic seers recite this verse: "May my husband be the most glorious and praiseworthy," the meaning being that he should cause even me to hear [this]. Regarding the words "by which Indra": Indra became fulfilled (*kṛtī*, i.e., one who has accomplished his purpose) by means of that oblation (*haviṣā*). [Thus] I have become one who has performed that rite; indeed, I have become free from rivals among the gods.

{ These rival wives have I overcome, so that I may rule over this hero and over his wealth. (17) Two verses beginning with "astheyasām" [are added]. (17) And in heaven he became supreme; I too prepared that oblation—by the rule "mantre ghasa" etc., the form is from the substitution of *l* for *cli*, thus "akṛṣi. O gods! And then indeed I became "without rivals"—"kila" indicates renown. "Asapatnā" means without a rival wife.}

Without rivals, without adversaries, possessing purifiers—this is a Vedic shortening [of the vowel]. You are the slayer of co-wives (*sapatnī*), victorious, ever-conquering, and overpowering. [The suffix] *kanip* is added to the root *bhū*; [the *van* portion] is elided. You are of a nature to overcome; I have seized and obtained the wealth, the splendor, and the luster of all my co-wives. Just as others seize the wealth of those who are less stable than the most stable—where "those who are not stable" (*astheyāṃsaḥ*) refers to others who are more unstable than the very stable ones—their wealth is taken away by others, so it is here. Thus, [I have taken it]. *Samiti*: [This concludes the section].

These co-wives, I have thoroughly subdued; may I completely conquer these overbearing women. [The absence of the elision of the final vowel is Vedic. "This one is auspicious" (*sumaṅgalīriyam*). Just as I have known them, so may I, being overbearing, conquer these overbearing co-wives. When that is so, I shall shine forth—*virājāmi*—as the sovereign mistress of this heroic husband and of his wealth. Thus ends the seventeenth section in the commentary on the mantras of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* composed by Śrī Haradatta.

... in the eighteenth section of the first chapter: ... from the two bladder-like organs, from the two eyes, from the two temples, from the two ears, and from the chin—O Consumption, I tear away from you that which is in the head, from the brain and from the tongue. From the neck, from the *uṣṇihā* joints, from the *kīrkastā* joints, and from the *anūkyat* joint—O Consumption, I tear away from you that which is in the forearms, from the two *aślā* vessels, and from the two arms.

"From the entrails, from the rectum, from the large intestine, and from the heart; from the two kidneys, from the liver, and from the lungs—[I drive away] consumption from the bride who is seized by consumption, or from another woman such as a sister, using the roots of the *puṣkarasaṃvarta* plant with the subsequent mantras, rubbing the limbs according to their respective characteristics, and casting [the substance] out toward the west with the mantra beginning 'akṣībhyām'. The word "adhi" is redundant. I tear away your consumption located in the head; having rubbed it away, I cast it out.

Thus, following the general instruction, there is a detailed specification: "from the eyes," and so forth. The eyes and other organs are well known. *Mastiṣka* is the flesh located within the skull. Regarding "from the necks" (*grīvābhyaḥ*): the neck (*grīvā*) is the throat; the plural number is used by attributing a distinction based on its various joints. Regarding "from the *uṣṇihās*": the *uṣṇihās* are the vessels located there, and those bones situated therein are the *kīkasās*. From the spine (*anūkyāt*), that is, from the vertebral column; "belonging to the forearms" (*doṣaṇyam*) refers to what arises from the forearms (*doṣaṇoḥ*); the shoulders (*aṃsau*) and the arms (*bāhū*) are well known. Regarding "from the intestines" (*āntrabhyaḥ*): these are those [organs] in which the consumed food resides during the state of digestion.

From those entrails (*pudāni*), from the rectum (*gudanāḍī*), from the large intestine (*vaniṣṭhu*), from the entrails themselves at their thick portion, from the heart (*hṛdaya*)—that is, the lotus of the heart—from the two kidneys (*matasne*) which are shaped like mango fruits, from the liver (*yakṛt*), and from the lungs (*plāśayaḥ*). [End of section] *Savyākhyānakāgnikāṇḍa*.

I tear away from you the disease from the two thighs, from the two knees, from the two shanks, and from the two forefeet; I tear away from you the disease from the two hips and from the buttocks. From the penis, from the testicles, from the middle of the body, from the nails, and from the eyebrows—I tear away this disease from your entire self.

"From every limb, from the joints, from the marrow, from the very core, O consumption, whatever has been born in you at every joint—that [I] tear away from your entire self. From the two thighs... Thus: the thighs are well known; the knees are the joints of the thighs, from the two points of connection between the thighs and the shanks; the shanks are well known.

From the two feet, from the tips of the feet, from the two hips, from the roots of the thighs, from the *bhāsad*—the word *bhāsad* (the same as *bhasad*) is the name of a specific part in the region of the genitals; from that [region] comes dissolution. Others say it is from the navel or from the circle of the anus. "From the *mehana*"—*mehana* means the organ of generation. From "making firm" (*valaṅkaraṇāt*), there is the substitution of *la* for *na*; this is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). The followers of the Ṛgveda read the word with the letter *na*.

"Vana" means "adorning" (*vanana*); that by which something is adorned is an "adornment" (*vanaikaraṇa*). For the entire world is brought under control by such adornment. [The word *mehanāt*] refers to such an adornment. Others, however, say the division is *u alaṅkaraṇāt*; from the region of the girdle (*mekhalā*) as an ornament, and "hair and nails" are well known. From every part of the self—both those mentioned and those not mentioned—tear away this consumption (*yakṣma*). [This is expressed by the phrase] "from limb after limb."

From every limb, from all the hairs, and from every joint and every articulation—whatever consumption (*yakṣma*) has arisen, [drive it] away from "every [limb]," as previously explained. [First Prapāṭhaka, Eighteenth Khaṇḍa. "Give away the variegated garment, O Śābalya; distribute wealth among the Brahmins. For what wife, having become a worn-out rag, would enter her husband? That body becomes unseemly, pale, and wretched, when the husband wraps his own limb around the garment of his wife."

This is cruel, harsh, and bitter (verse 75): "O lover of songs (*girvaṇas*), that bridal garment which was wrapped around you with the words ‘*pari tvā*’—that very thing he should give to the one who knows the rite of marriage (*vidē vivāha-karma-vidē*) with the verse ‘*uttarābhiḥ parādehi*’ [RV 10.85.28–32]. Abandon the *śābalya*, the garment of variegated color; O Brahmins, distribute the wealth (*vasu*), having divided it, and go away! But what is the reason for abandoning the garment? It is said: This bride (*jāyā*), having become a footed sorcery (*paddhatī kṛtyā*), enters the husband.
She speaks unseemly things (*aślīlati*). By means of this evil sorcery (*amuyā pāpayā kṛtyayā*), she has entered him."

The husband’s body becomes unseemly, devoid of splendor, and harsh (*ruśatī*). *Ruśati* has the sense of "injuring" (*hiṃsā*), and the agentive suffix is used in the passive sense by way of grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*). Thus, it also means "being injured. Under what condition does all this occur? It is said: if the husband, with his own limb—the body—desires to cover (*abhidhitsati*) the garment of the bride (*vadhvā vāsasā*), wishing to clothe himself in the bride’s garment; for such a wearing of the bride’s garment is indeed wicked, and therefore it must not be worn even when accompanied by a mantra. Furthermore, the garment itself is censured as "cruel" (*kūra*).

Cruel, causing destruction, pungent, causing pain, like poison that is not [properly] prepared (*apaṣṭavat*), or as if mixed with poison—such a garment is indeed censurable; it is not fit for eating, nor is it fit for use. To whom, then, is this suitable? He says: to the Sun (*sūrya*).

In the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*: Therefore, this [should be] for one who possesses the two-fold knowledge; he who possesses direct knowledge should accept this: "Command, expansion, purpose, and the unfolding [of meaning]; behold the forms of Sūryā—those I now disclose to you. (18)

From Akṣobhya, from the necks, from the intestines, from the thighs, from the penis—[the verses] beginning with "prasugmantā," the eighteen [verses], the golden-colored ones, the fifteen, that which is the first, the sixteen for the sake of hair, the eighteenth for the knower of birth, the deity of marriage; even though this collection of mantras was seen by her, it begins with "prasugmantā" and ends with "avamanta."

He who would know—that is, understand—this [garment] directly, clearly, word by word, accent by accent, syllable by syllable, according to its meaning and its application, he alone should accept it; he is worthy of accepting it. Furthermore, regarding the censure and the description of the garment: "āśasana" means causing injury, such as with a stake; "viśasana" means the cutting apart of hides, such as with a knife; and furthermore, "adhi" is a meaningless prefix. "Vicartana" means the removal of the hide from elsewhere. Such is this garment; it is not [to be accepted].

The connection is that one should accept [them]. Now, how is it that no harm comes to him? It is said: "Behold the forms of Sūryā; for they belong to Sūryā. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 5.1.1). [First Prapāṭhaka, Eighteenth Khaṇḍa.

In the morning, at the time of eating, one should offer four oblations for the rising sun; the sun has twelve visible forms, and the Brahmin recites [the hymn] regarding them as Brahman—so how could there be any suspicion of harm in this? The word *uta* is used in the sense of "correctly," since particles have multiple meanings. Thus, this handing over of the bride’s garment (*vadhūvāsas*) must be performed with a word ending in the dative case; and so Āśvalāyana says at the end of the marriage rite: "One should give the bride’s garment to the knower of Sūryā. Others, however, say that this garment of one seized by consumption (*yakṣma*) is taught here as being to be given to a physician.

By the word *sūyā* as well, those very same mantras are intended. Thus ends the second section, [numbered] 78, in the *Ekādhikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra. "O Vāyu, with warm water, let Aditi shave the hair; let them moisten it for life, for long vitality, and for splendor. May the knower [of the rites] long behold the sun; with that, may the Brahmins shave this [hair] for his life. Now follow the mantras for the initiation (*upanayana*). Therein, one pours warm water into cold water with the mantra beginning "with warm" (*uṣṇena*).

"O Vāyu! Having taken warm water with warm water, come, arrive! For what purpose? 'May Aditi shave the hair'—this indicates Aditi's role as the benefactor in the shaving; likewise for Vāyu in bringing the water. With the following [verse], he moistens the head of the boy: 'May the waters moisten [it]'—he moistens the head of this student. May they moisten it, may they soften it, so that he may live, for the sake of living."

For how long a time? For a long life—a hundred years plus sixteen is a long lifespan—for the sake of splendor (*varcasa*), that is, for radiance, for a long duration (*jyok*) to behold the sun, so that he may live for a long time; for as long as he is thus, he becomes possessed of sight and endowed with splendor—may it [the razor] cut [the hair] accordingly. With the following verses, the teacher shaves in each direction. Therein, in the eastern direction, [he uses] "with which he shaved... That is, with which razor Savitṛ [shaved] King Soma's...

The learned one, skilled in the barber’s craft, shaved the head of Varuṇa. With that razor—by way of its lineage—or with such a razor, O *brahmāṇaḥ*, O Brāhmaṇas who perform the *puṇyāhavācana* ceremony, [shave] this head of this boy. (First Section of the Second Chapter). With that by which Pūṣan shaved the head of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra for the sake of their longevity—with that, for his longevity, for prosperity, and for well-being, shave this head! May his sight be unimpaired, just as it was when he was born. With that by which Pūṣan shaved the head of Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra for the sake of their life-span—with that, for his life-span, for excellence, and for well-being, [shave him].

"By that [means] by which he may further pass his transgressions and long behold the sun—with that, for his life, for the sake of heaven, and for prosperity, do you shave him. The meaning is: "With that by which Pūṣan [shaved] Bṛhaspati, Agni, and Indra for their longevity, with that I employ you for my shaving"—that is to say, "With your permission, I shall shave him. Shave him in such a way that, upon being shaved, this young boy, Yajñaśarman, may become long-lived, reaching old age, and one who eats until he is full.

"O Asu!"—here, the naming of the young student (*māṇavaka*) is indicated by the nominative case. Now, from the south: "With which [razor] Pūṣan..."—"With which razor"—this has been explained. "With that razor, shave his head for long life. This is an internal exhortation to the self within the body: "O my inner self within the body! Shave [it] for the sake of good renown (*sauślōkya*). *Mujheoka* means ill-repute; its state is *sauślōkya*. The meaning is: "so that this person may possess good fame. And "for well-being (*svastaye*), that is, for non-destruction."

Now, as for the phrase "afterwards, by which more": by which razor this young boy has already moved, he shall move even more. This is the fifth *lakāra* (the optative suffix). He should move most extensively; he should move surpassing all [others], and for a long time (*jyok*), he should gaze upon the sun. The lengthening of the vowel in both instances is Vedic (*chāndasa*). The rest, beginning with "by that," is explained. 80. [End of] the section on the single razor with commentary.
