Therefore, I consecrate you with this life-span and splendor, so that you may be long-lived and full of vigor. When they trim [the hair] with the razor, making it well-formed and beautiful, with lovely locks of hair—purify the head, do not diminish his life-span; do not harm him. Having risen, at the impulse of King Varuṇa and by the command of Bṛhaspati, [he trims] the hair from the northward—with that by which he prospers. The first half has been explained.

"With that razor, I shave your head, O [Name]!"—this is the designation of the name, addressed in the vocative case, such as "O Jñaśarman! Just as when the shaving is performed, you shall be endowed with long life and luster, and remain well-disposed for a long time (*jyok*), so do I shave you. Here too, the fifth *lakāra* (the optative) is used; it means "I shall shave. Then, the teacher consecrates the barber who is performing the shaving with the following verse: "With the razor... and so forth.

When, with a razor that is sharpened, keen, well-fashioned, and beautiful in form—intending to express the agency of the one who performs the act of cleansing—you shave his hair with such a razor, then, by virtue of the word "when" (*yadā*), the word "then" (*tadā*) is to be supplied. At that time, cleanse his head; make it pure so that the hairs become rootless. This is the meaning. "Do not harm his life-span"—thus they pray, because shaving is inherently auspicious.

And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "What indeed is this uncovered vessel? It is the earthenware pot. Now follows the mantra for depositing [the water]: "Having shaved the hair... (*uptvāya keśān*). Having shaved (*uptvāya*)—[the word] *ūrā* means "shaved"—the hair (*keśān*). Whose [hair]? Of King Varuṇa. By what? By the waters (*āpaḥ*) completely (*niśśeṣam*). [End of] the second section of the second chapter. (Note: The text provided contains citations from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, specifically 1.10.8.)
That was the splendor of the fires; from them he discovered the treasure manifoldly, between heaven and earth, the waters, and the light.

"O God, granting life, grasping old age, with a face anointed with ghee and nourished by ghee, drinking the ghee and the lovely nectar of the cow in the beginning—like a father [protecting] his son, O Bṛhaspati, protect us. What did they do? They found the "nidhāna," the receptacle for those hairs (the term *lyuḥ* is used in the sense of location). That place where they are deposited, they obtained in many ways—that is, in various manners—in due order (*anukrameṇa*).

*Kala*? [The offerings are placed] in the intermediate space between heaven and earth (*dyāvāpṛthivī*), that is, in the atmosphere; the *sruks* [are placed] in the heavenly world (*svargaloka*). Thus, there is a distinction of locations according to the distinction of times. In the same way, it should be applied as: "I too place [the offering] at the root of an *udumbara* tree or upon a clump of *darbha* grass. Thus ends the placement of the fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*) with the mantra "O giver of life... in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍamantravyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta.

O God! O Foremost One! You are the giver of life; you are old age, and "jarā" is praise. While this [root] *gṛ* elsewhere has the sense of "uttering," here it should be understood in the sense of "accepting"—that is, "accepting the praise. You have a face of ghee (*ghṛtapratīka*). The root *ghṛ* means "to flow" and "to shine"; *pratīka* is a name for a limb, thus "one whose limbs are radiant. He whose back (*pṛṣṭha*) is ghee—that is, clarified butter—is "Ghṛtapṛṣṭha," drinking the ghee. Of what kind? The nectar-like, beautiful product of the cow (*gavya*), appearing in this ritual as the portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and so forth. Thus...

"O Being, now by this oblation of fuel-sticks, lead this young man to old age. Be firm; stand against those who attack; withstand those who seek to fight. The wealthy ones have woven you; the Kṛttikās have cut you. They spun [the threads]; they chose nine sheep; they covered [you] on all sides with a thousand ends. O Goddess, for the God, these enclosures were made for Savitṛ; that was great. (From the *Savyākhyānaikāṇḍa*).

"O Father, cause this son to reach old age; act in such a way that he becomes long-lived, just as a father causes his son to attain a long life in every respect. This is the application [of the mantra] according to the view that the preceptor is the speaker of the mantra. However, from the perspective of the student (*māṇavaka*), it means: "Lead me, this one, [to old age]. The placing of the stone (*aśmāsthāpana*) has been explained. 3. With the two following [mantras], there is the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the garment: "With the *revatī* verses... etc.

O garment! The Revatīs—by the rule *vā chandasi*, the *jas* ending takes the preceding vowel grade—the deities named Revatīs have "sharpened" (*vyakṣṇan*) you, meaning they have variously worn away the fibers while in the state of cotton for the purpose of removing the seeds. Through the metaphorical identification of cause and effect, it is said that they sharpened the garment itself. And the Kṛttikās have "cut" (*akṛntan*) you, meaning they performed the cutting of the threads. Here too, there is a metaphorical identification. The deities named Dhīs, having spun the threads together, have woven you into a garment.

And the village deities have chosen you; they have cut off the intervening spaces. Furthermore—other thousands of goddesses who were mentioned have stretched the ten threads at the ends on both sides, all around.

And the divine waters chose you for your greatness. Second Chapter, Second Section. 83. O Waters, those who flow within, those that run swiftly, and those divine ones that reach the horse—may those goddesses clothe you in this garment. Being long-lived, put on this robe! Clothe him, dress him in this garment; bestow upon him full life and long duration of existence. O Bṛhaspati, in the act of giving, may they grant him their refreshing power, having bestowed it.

The connection with the preceding [verse], "O divine goddesses, thousands... is as follows: "For the god Savitṛ"—that is, for the god Savitṛ—"the enclosures" (*paridhī*); *paridhi* means an enclosure or surrounding. [This is] the substitution of the preceding vowel for the locative singular ending. At the time of the enclosure (*paridhau*), that greatness (*mahitvanam*)—the majesty—of these goddesses truly became great; indeed, those goddesses were so great that they fashioned the garment for the god Savitṛ. And the purpose of the consecration formula is: "And you are such as this."

With the following three verses he causes him to put on the garment: "Those who cut [the cloth]... O divine ones, those goddesses who cut you, who caused you to be heard, who stretched you out, and who placed the ends and the fringe-sutras all around on both sides—those goddesses, beginning with Revatī, may they clothe you for old age; that is, may they cause you to wear it so that you may reach old age. And you, being long-lived, put on this garment.

"Put it on! Clothe him! O goddesses, Revatī and the others! Clothe this boy with a garment; cover him, clothe him—here too there is a repetition for emphasis. And as you clothe him, make him long-lived. This connects with what follows; and the expression "long life" (*dīrgham āyuḥ*) is used figuratively for its cause. [He becomes] one who wards off curses. Live known and renowned, full of luster, and clothe yourself in the increase of wealth.

"Put on this garment for well-being, O protector from curses, you who are like a boat in the waters. Live a hundred autumns; Bṛhaspati gave this garment as a sign of life. To whom? To King Soma. For what purpose? To be worn—for the sake of wearing it. And indeed, 'you shall go to old age. Put on this garment; having put it on, you shall go—you will reach—old age."

Be the protector—that is, the guardian and defender—against the curse of the *kṛṣṭīs*, meaning of human beings. "Go to old age" has already been stated; it is further specified: live for a hundred autumns, that is, years, having become possessed of excellent luster (*suvarcas*). And having approached the nourishment of wealth—the nourishment of riches (*rāyaspoṣa*)—clothe yourself in the garment upon this chariot so that you may possess the abundance of wealth.

He addresses the boy who has put on the garment with the verse: "Thou hast put on this garment. (*parīdaṃ vāsaḥ*). You have donned (*paridadhāḥ*) this garment; this is the form in the *luṅ* (aorist) tense from the root *dhā*, with the change of *th* to *dh* being Vedic. For what purpose? For well-being (*svastaye*). And having put it on, you have become a protector against the curses of those who are trustworthy, such as kinsmen and others (*apiyām āptānām*). May you live for a hundred autumns (*śataṃ ca jīva śaradaḥ*). [May you attain] many paths (*purucīḥ*), abundant movements, and riches among the people (*ākṛṣṭīnām*).

Second Khaṇḍa of the Second Prapāṭhaka Go around; seek [us] around... the far-reaching ones, destroying the demons, victorious... protected by you... autumnal, manifold, you distribute riches while living. This [goddess], warding off ill-spoken words, purifying our protection and shelter—may we not [be harmed].

85. O Noble One, having become the master, you shall divide; may you divide [the wealth] after having divided it, so that you may be endowed with life. For in this world, he is said to "live" who is truly endowed [with prosperity]. This is the mantra for tying the girdle of muñja grass: "This [girdle], from ill-spoken words... This girdle [protects] from ill-spoken words (*duruktāt*). [The substitution of *ś* for *s* occurs here. Thus also is the reading in the Śābaragṛhyasūtra: "...from ill-spoken words. It destroys [evil] on all sides, protecting the home, the refuge, the dwelling—the desirable one—cleansing and purifying.

"May she who is related to us, or who has come to us—*āgāt* being from *ā-gatavatī*—[endowed] with out-breath and in-breath (*prāṇa-apānābhyām*), this word ending in the dative case; and bringing [us] together, or bringing [us] hither through the fear of the gods—such is this girdle of mine, [invoked] with the words 'O Right' (*ṛtaye*)."

She is the guardian of *ṛta*—of truth or sacrifice—and the protector of austerity (*tapas*). The word *para* signifies excellence; thus, she is the preeminent protector (*pātrī*) through the excellence of her austerity, the one who guards. She is the slayer of demons (*rakṣas*), performing the destruction of the *rakṣases*, the subduer and overcomer of enemies (*aratīḥ*), that is, the various classes of foes. [The form *aratīḥ* is due to the preservation of the original stem. She who is thus... [the enemies]. O Haimavatī! Do not... [text fragment]. — With commentary, from the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa*. *Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 9.76.5.

Go around me on all sides with auspiciousness; O girdle, may we, your wearers, not come to harm. "The eye of Mitra, the supporter, powerful splendor, that which is most firm and well-kindled, the ageless garment that endures—this very skin-garment (ajina) do I put on. May I attain long life and prosperity. [May we] not come to harm; may we, as your wearers, not be injured. [The suffix -tṛ in *bhartāraḥ* is used for both the agent and the object according to the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.]

The *ajina-mantra* is: "Of Mitra... [etc. The eye of Mitra—that is, of the Sun—is the illuminator. For one who wears the skin of a conqueror (*jineottarīya*) becomes long-lived, and he beholds the Sun; therefore, it is his illuminator. It is a supporting (*dharuṇa*) power, being sustained (*dhāryamāṇa*), a most powerful splendor (*balīyaḥ tejaḥ*). Because it is the cause of glory for one who possesses it, it is itself glorious (*yaśasvi*). It is ancient (*sthavira*), fully grown (*pravṛddha*), well-kindled (*samiddha*), blazing (*dīptimat*), and invulnerable (*anāhanasya*). [The word] *āhanasaḥ* refers to rogues (*dhūrtaḥ*).

This is because we see [the term] in passages such as, "Those intoxications of yours which are *āhanasa*... The activity of those [intoxications] is *āhanasya*, consisting of sounds of cooing and the like. The *Baudhāyana-Brāhmaṇa* states: "*Āhanasyā dve retaḥ sicyate*" ("The two *āhanasyā* [songs] are emitted as seed"). The opposite of that is *anāhanasya*, meaning unsuitable for rogues.

The upper garment (*vasana*) is the upper cloth (*uparivāsa*), which is subject to decay; the root *jṛ* means "to decay," and here the agentive suffix is used in the sense of the object, meaning that which is to be praised. Or, it may mean "one who has reached old age" (*jarāyāḥ prāpitu*). O *vājin* (possessor of strength), you who are like food (*annavat*) or the giver of food (*annasya dātṛ*), I, being such a vessel, put on and cover myself with this. Thus ends the second section of the second chapter in the commentary on the *Ekāgni-kāṇḍa* composed by Śrī Haradatta. Third Section of the Second Chapter: "Come hither together; drive away death."

May we move about unharmed; may we proceed here with well-being, and with well-being reach our home. (87) May we attain immortality. These indeed are the rays of the sun, by which one crosses over the difficulties. This is the mantra for stabilizing [the student]: "O you who have come" (*āgantrā*). With the teacher who has come, we have come together; we have met.

"May we not encounter death together; may we not be separated. The root *yau* signifies separation; this is the third person plural form of the middle voice (*loṇ-madhyama-puruṣa-bahuvacana*), with the suffix *-tanap* applied, and there is an exchange of persons, where the middle person takes the place of the first person. "May we thoroughly and completely separate [from death]. May we move about unharmed. And may the teacher move about in well-being; may there be well-being for me here in this life of studentship (*brahmacarya*), until I reach the home—that is, until I enter the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*). This is the mantra for sprinkling: "From the ocean, the wave... (Samudrād ūrmir iti).

That drops of sprinkling water fall upon me—let that honeyed wave from the ocean itself lift me up; it has come toward me with its face turned upward. The connection [of the verb] is with *upetya* (having approached), as indicated by the verbal root *aś* (to reach). The reading with the grave accent (*anudātta*), however, is due to a metrical or grammatical anomaly; the Bahvṛcas, moreover, recite it as having the acute accent on the first syllable (*ādyudātta*). The word *aṃśunā* contains the suffix *-mat* in the sense of possession; thus, by means of that radiant, shining wave, may I fully attain immortality—may I truly partake of it.

The words "these" (*ime*) and "your" (*te*) are not meaningless; although the word "wave" (*ūrmiḥ*) was introduced in the singular, nevertheless, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "rays" (*raśmayaḥ*), the plural form "these" (*ime*) and "your" (*te*) is used. These are the rays of the Sun, [referring to] that wave which has reached me; this is a metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*) of cause and effect, as in the statement: "From the Sun rain is born" (Manu 3.76). Having bathed, O Fathers, come to us. He has grasped the heart. He has seized it.

Soma grasped your hand; the fearless Aditi grasped your hand; the womb-bearing Earth grasped your hand; Pūṣan grasped your hand; Aryaman grasped your hand; the Aśvins grasped your hand. "O Indra," [it is said]. The drops of water are the rays of the sun; by those rays with which our fathers, the Aṅgirases, drank together—that common draught—come hither. This is the speech of Vāmadeva, the son of Aṅgiras.

Aṅgiras is the friend of the gods; therefore, it is appropriate that he drinks together with the rays and the other deities. What is meant is this: those drops which, along with the rays, were drunk by our ancestors, the Aṅgirases, have fallen upon me for that reason, and through them I shall attain immortality. 5. "The mantras for taking the hand: *agniṣṭe* etc. This taking of your hand by me—let it be a taking by Agni and the others; such is the figurative expression. The *luṅ* (aorist) is used in the sense of the *loṭ* (imperative)."

He has seized, he seized, may he seize. Agni, Soma, and Sarasvatī are well-known [deities]. Savitṛ and the others are also among the twelve Ādityas. By virtue of *dharman* (the cosmic order), you are Mitra; as the god Mitra is, so are you. And of what nature is he? "The gods said, 'Let us kill King Soma'; he replied, 'I am indeed the friend (*mitra*) of all. Such a one is like a teacher (*ācārya*). Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita maintains that the word *anyatama* does not possess the status of a pronoun (*sarvanāma*).

Saṃhitā 6.4.8.2. Second Prapāṭhaka, Third Khaṇḍa. I honor you as the foremost according to the Law (dharma). "I entrust you to Agni, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Soma, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Savitṛ, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Sarasvatī, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Mṛtyu, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Yama, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Gada, O [Name]! "I entrust you to Avṛttaka, O [Name]! "May the Adityas protect you."

"I give you, O so-and-so, to the Uṣan-dhīs; I give you away, O so-and-so. "To the Earth, to her who belongs to all men (vaiśvānarī), I give you away, O so-and-so. "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ, I initiate you, O so-and-so. "May you be rich in offspring through your progeny," etc.—the mantras beginning with "To Agni," and so forth. Giving for the sake of protection is *paridāna*; these are the *paridāna* mantras. In every instance, in place of the word "so-and-so," the name of the *māṇavaka* should be specified in the vocative case.

The mantra for the initiation (*upanayana*): *devasya tvā...* "At the impulse (*prasava*)—that is, with the permission—of the god Savitṛ, I initiate you (*upanaye*), meaning I bring you near to myself, I lead you under my control. The mention of the name is as before. Some, however, because of the final acute accent (*antodātta*) in the recitation, maintain that the teacher’s name should be mentioned in the nominative case. Then the whispering into the ear (*karṇejapa*): *suprajā...* "O student (*brahmacārin*), may you be rich in offspring through progeny; rich in heroes through your heroic sons."

In this context, "heroic" (*vīra*) refers to the grandsons, as they are described as the progeny. "Possessing excellent speech through splendor" (*varcasā suvacaḥ*) and "possessing excellent nourishment through prosperity" (*poṣaiḥ supoṣaḥ*)—the phrase "may he be" (*bhūyāt*) is to be supplied everywhere. 89.12 [From] *Savyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*. — Anasuya Ram (talk) 11:41, 7 December 2016 (UTC).
[Regarding] the son.

The hero among heroes, the one of good speech, Varcalā; well-nourished among those who nourish. *Brahma*... [omitted] ... "What is your name? "I am named so-and-so. "To whom do you belong? "I belong to my teacher (*brahmacārya*). "I am a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) belonging to Prāṇa. "This is your dress, O divine Sūrya; as a student of sacred knowledge, may I not die. May Sūrya, Candramas, and [the other deities] grant me well-being. Now follows the mantra for the youth: "Brahmacarya. *Brahman* is the Veda; that...

"I have come for that vow, that holy life (*brahmacarya*). [The suffix] *luṅ* is used here in the sense of future time according to the rule "in the sense of expectation, it is as if already accomplished. [Thus, the meaning is] "may I attain it; initiate me," O you who are impelled and authorized by the divine Savitṛ. "What is your name?"—the teacher asks, "What is your name? What is your designation?"

"Such-and-such am I," says the student; this is the mention of his name in the nominative case. "Of whom [am I] the religious student? asks the teacher; this is the mention of the name in connection with the genitive case. "I am such-and-such, the religious student of Prāṇa," says the student; this is the mention of his name in the nominative case. Prāṇa is the Self (Ātman).
"This one," says the teacher—referring to this student, O divine Sūrya, yours!

O Brahmacārī, protect and guard him. Let him not meet death; O Sūrya, let this son of yours be long-lived, and let him not meet death in the midst of his long life. May that well-being which Agni and the others [attained] follow after the vital breath.

From the *Ātman*, Second [Section], Fourth Chapter, Section 91: "Those who move along the paths, may you move along them safely; O Asau (Name), in every undertaking, [be] most powerful for strength, for life, and for splendor. [The teacher says: "Move along by way of the path. [The student, the *māṇavaka*, replies: "O Sacrifice, for my protection! [The teacher says: "Of the paths... [The student, the *māṇavaka*, replies: "O Sacrifice, for my protection! *Note: The portion "adhvanām iti māṇavakaḥ" indicates the student's response to the teacher's instruction.*

When it is said "adhvapate" (Lord of the Path), it is understood that he is the lord of one particular path; therefore, the word "adhvanām" (of all paths) is stated again. O Lord of all paths, O Sūrya! by your grace, may I reach the *pāram*, the further limit, of the best and most beneficial path—the path of *brahmacarya*. The meaning is: O Lord of that path which is the means to happiness—a path where suffering (*dhvaṃ*) does not exist.

Thus ends the third section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. Now follow the *homa*-mantras; all of these belong to the student (*māṇavaka*) alone. According to some, the second and fourth [verses] belong to the teacher (*ācārya*). Regarding the phrase "yogeyoge gataṃ": here, *yoga* refers to exertion (*udyoga*) in ritual action (*karman*). Regarding the mantra "imamagre": O *Agni*, you [make] this student [prosper] for long life and splendor. He causes the student to recite [the mantra]. [The reading] "adhvanām" is a variant. [The meaning is] exertion in the duties of studentship (*brahmacarya*).
This mantra (10) is written on a leaf: *ḍumarmagra āyuṣe varcase kṛdhi priyaḥ retoṃ varuṇa*. [End of] the *Savyākhyānaikānnikāṇḍa*. [Note by] Anasūyā Rām. (Conversation).

Two verses: "O gods, grant us two years, three, four, five autumns, while we are still in the presence of our bodies and have not reached old age. Where sons become fathers—make it so, O Varuṇa, act so that this man may be long-lived and full of splendor. O Varuṇa, you again make his seed dear; grant him a beloved son so that he becomes a householder. And you, O King Soma, and you, O Aditi, like a mother, grant and bestow happiness upon us."

*dāṇ dāne*, *yaccha udaśaḥ*. O Viśvedevas! May you also grant us protection (*śarma*), so that this person may reach old age and become real (attain fulfillment). In the context of the teacher, this is straightforward. In the context of the student, it is an indirect reference to himself: "May this person [be] for this person; may this person reach old age and become real. *Śatam it śaradaḥ*. The word *it* has the sense of *eva* (indeed). The word *nu* is used as an expletive. Indeed, one hundred autumns is the maximum lifespan.

Of what sort is the "hundred"? It means "near," "proximate," or "small. O gods! In that hundred wherein you have brought about *jarasam* (old age) for our bodies—for the plural number is used here with reference to the body's constituent parts—both the body and its members. The lengthening of the vowel is an archaic Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

And in this world, where for some time sons become fathers, becoming protectors and preoccupied with the maintenance of the family—such indeed is life, which by its very nature is brief, overcome by old age, and a source of distress through the burden of supporting a family;
[yet] it is favorable for such maintenance.

O King Soma! O Aditi, grant us protection like a mother, so that all the gods may be long-lived. (Saṃhitā 2.3.10). Second Prapāṭhaka, Fourth Khaṇḍa. Do not harm us in our midst; do not destroy our life-force. May Agni bestow upon you extended life; may Agni provide for you increased prosperity. May Indra with the Maruts act according to the seasons, and may the Ādityas together with the Vasus grant it. May Prajāpati grant me intelligence; may Agni grant me intelligence.

Whatever wisdom is among the *apsarases* and whatever glory is among the *gandharvas*, may even that divine [wisdom] be ours; may our lifespan be full. Do not cause us harm, do not injure us in the midst of our journey—do not let us perish midway. [The root] *ruṣ* (in the form *riṣ*) means "to injure. The prefix *ā-* should be understood here as "until"; that is, until the end of the journey, until one goes by oneself, do not cause us harm. "O Agni!"—may Agni bestow (*dadhātu*), grant, or establish for you a longer, more excellent lifespan.

May that very Agni make your nourishment (*puṣṭam*) even more excellent, most preeminent. And may Indra, together with the Maruts, O you who abide in the cosmic order (*ṛtāvṛdh*), establish your nourishment according to the seasons (*ṛtudhā*). May that same Indra, together with the Ādityas and the Vasus, bestow nourishment upon you. This [explanation] is also easy to understand from the perspective of the teacher; however, from the perspective of the student (*māṇavaka*), the term *medhīm* refers to the distinction between the inner self (*antarātman*) and the bodily self (*śarīrātman*). The meaning is clear. [The verb] *daduḥ* means "may they give. Regarding *apsarāṃsviti*: it means "among the Apsarases. *Daivī* means "belonging to the gods" (*deveṣu bhavā*).

"May that wisdom which is human among men, which is *saṃsā* and *medhā*, and which is also to be regarded as *yaśas*—may that *medhā* enter into me in this rite. (94) "May that wisdom which is human enter into me here. "This I implore of you, O Varuṇa; you are our leader at the beginning"—thus [the verses] "sa tvaṃ no agre," "tvarmagre ayā," "rāṣṭrabhṛd asi," "ācāryāsandī mā tvadyoṣam," and "tat savitur vareṇyam" [are recited]. "Arvāṅ dham"—"this I [implore] of you," etc. Five [verses] have been completed.

The teacher ascends the seat with the mantra, "Rāṣṭrabhṛt" (O sustainer of the kingdom). O seat! You are the sustainer of the kingdom; you are the bearer of the realm and are highly praised. You are the teacher’s throne, the seat of teachers. From such as you, may I not fall away—may I not become separated or disunited from you.
Then follows the Sāvitrī mantra: "Tat savitur... (That [splendor] of Savitṛ...). Because of the hearing of the word "tat" (that), the word "yat" (which) is to be supplied.

It is to be taken away. That which is the object of meditation for all—that most excellent (*vareṇya*) light (*bhargaḥ*) of the divine Savitṛ, which is to be chosen (*varaṇīya*), the burner (*bharjana*) of sins, that form consisting of splendor (*tejas*), we meditate upon (*dhīmahi*); we contemplate it. Of what kind is Savitṛ? He who shall impel (*pracodayāt*) our thoughts (*dhiyaḥ*)—that is, our intellects regarding objects such as Dharma and the like—for it is said in the Brāhmaṇa: "Savitṛ indeed is the lord of all impulses (*prasava*). For only when permitted by Savitṛ does one perform even those actions.

And: *bhañjanam*. Saṃhitā 2-1-6. The fifth section of the second chapter. O gentle Prāṇa, protect my own [breath]. "The two leaders of the Brahman, you and I... (four verses). "O Suśravas, make me one who has heard well, as you, O Suśravas, [are]... [There is] the touching of the lips—"I have increased. "Vṛddhi" means prosperity (*śrī*). I am "vṛdha," one who has grown; I am born from the Sāvitrī, because of the grasping of the Sāvitrī: "the Ṛcs, the Sāmans, and the Yajus. For she is the immortal prosperity of the virtuous.

"Indeed, the Sāvitrī is recited from all the Vedas," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Here, "Asau" (that one) refers to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), because it is present within the body; "Saumya" is an address of kindness. Thus, the vital breath is the Self. "O you who are present within my body! O vital breath! O kind one! O my inner self! That which is now my own wealth called the Sāvitrī, which has entered into my mouth—that protect it, guard it; act in such a way that it does not go out. (Brāhmaṇa 1.2.1). "The touching of the ears—with the words 'of Brahman'."

"You two are the pins (āṇī) of the *brahman*, characterized by the *sāvitrī* mantra. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here in the sense of the imperative (*loḍartha*). "May you two be so. Thus ends the fourth section of the second chapter in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. [He] takes the staff [with the words]: "O thou of good fame (*suśravaḥ*). The *pālāśa* tree is called *suśravas*; for it is heard in scripture: "The gods, indeed, were conversing about the *brahman*. The *parṇa* leaf overheard it; hence its name is *suśravas*" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.1.10; Sūtra 3.5.7). [End of] the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* with its commentary.

O you who are of good renown, may I likewise be of good renown; O you who are of good renown, may I become one of good renown, just as you, O of good renown, are the guardian of the treasure of the gods, so may I become the guardian of the treasure of the Brahmins and of the Veda.

"That which is remembered by me and that which is not remembered by me—let both of those be my vow. That which is censured by me and that which is not censured by me—let both of those be my vow. Faith and lack of faith—in this regard, O Suśravaḥ! [addressing him], make me too one who hears well, a good listener. The repetition of "as you are" and so forth is for the sake of emphasis; its meaning is clear.

Just as you are the guardian of the treasure of the gods, and that treasure is the sacrifice which the Palāśa tree protects in the form of the *juhū* ladle and so forth, even so may I also, through my retention of you, become a guardian (*gopa*) of the treasure of the Brāhmaṇas—that is, a protector of the Brahman, the Veda. Here, the word *nidhi* (treasure), though subordinate, is construed with the word *brāhmaṇaiḥ* (with the Brāhmaṇas).
"Then he makes the boy recite: 'And remembered by me... [The word] *smṛtam*.

That which is thought, "This must be done," and its opposite, that which is not remembered due to incapacity and is undertaken in times of distress—both of these are my vow (*vrata*). Censure (*nindā*) concerns objects of censure; non-censure (*anindā*) concerns the Vedas and so forth. Faith (*śraddhā*) concerns what ought to be done; lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) concerns what is prohibited. Knowledge (*vidyā*) is the cognition of that which is to be known; ignorance (*avidyā*) concerns that which is not to be known. Learning (*śruta*) is the hearing of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; unlearning (*aśruta*) is the study of heretical scriptures and the like.

Truth is speech according to what has been perceived; this is obtained by its own nature. Untruth [is permitted] in cases such as when life is at risk. Austerity consists of wandering for alms and so forth. This is the fifth section of the second chapter.

Both knowledge and ignorance are my vow; both truth and falsehood are my vow; both austerity and non-austerity are my vow; both vows and non-vows are my vow. Whatever vow belongs to the Brāhmaṇas in the Brahman, to the king of the gods together with men, to the king of men together with his subjects, to the king of the fathers together with the Gandharvas and Apsarases—whatever vow is mine in myself, by that may I be consecrated.

May I become possessed of all vows (*vrata*). The non-performance of that [vow] when one is capable is a lack of austerity (*atapas*). A vow consists of the avoidance of neglecting Vedic study (*anadhyayana*) and so forth. Herein, the transgression of it occurs through fear and other such causes. And whatever other vow there is of the Brahmins regarding *brahman*—that is, concerning the Veda—and whatever belongs to Agni together with Indra and the others;

and whatever vow of mine, of my own self, within myself, conceived by me alone—such as acting for another purpose when sent by a teacher for a different task, and so forth—by means of all these types of vows, may I possess all vows.

In this regard, the function of the *Anuvrata* (guardian of vows) belongs to Agni, as seen in the mantra: "O Agni, you are the guardian of vows" (*tvam agne vratapā asi*). Indra possesses preeminence; Prajāpati possesses sovereignty (*khaṣṭratva*); the gods possess the quality of being givers; the king of the gods possesses the delighting of the gods; for humans, there is pleasant speech; the king of men possesses the protection of the subjects; for the ancestors (*pitṛs*), there is the procreation of sons; Yama, the king of the ancestors, possesses impartiality toward all; the Gandharvas possess the praising of the gods; and the Apsarases possess skill in attendance. This is the bringing of other matters [from the *Saṃhitā*, 1.2.3].
13. 98. [From] the *Sādhyākhyānaikāgnikāṇḍa*, Brāhmaṇa 1.5.8:

"Arise with life, with good life, O gods, through wisdom, through the essence, through the vigor of Parjanya! May we, as immortals, follow this [path]. That eye, established by the gods, in front... autumnal, hundredfold, may we be unaging for a hundred autumns; autumnal, hundredfold, may we long behold the sun."

The mantra for rising is: *uditi*. "The gods are immortal; following them, I rise; I arise. Therein lies the specific detail: "I stand up with life-force (*āyus*), together with life-force. With my own life-force, characterized by a full hundred years, I rise. With the essence of the plants—their essence being their strength, by which power is indicated—with that [strength] I rise. With the vigor (*śuṣman*) of Parjanya—"vigor" being a name for strength—with such strength as belongs to Parjanya, I rise. The phrase "I have risen" (*udasthām*) is to be supplied everywhere. The worship of the Sun begins with: "That eye... and so forth.

The word *tat* refers to what is well-known. "The eye" (*cakṣuḥ*) means that which stands in the place of the eye for the world; "beneficial to the gods" (*devahitam*) means placed by the god Indra, as seen in the text: "Indra raised up the sun in heaven so that he might see afar. "In the east" (*purastāt*), meaning in the eastern direction, "rising" (*udyan*), let us behold the "bright, pure light" (*śukraṃ pariśuddhaṃ jyotiḥ*) known as the sun. The optative suffix (*liṅ*) here expresses a prayer. The same applies to the subsequent instances where the optative (*loṭ*) is used. "May we live" (*jīvema*) means may we flourish for a full hundred and sixteen years.

May we rejoice, may we delight, together with our sons, grandsons, and others; may we be contented. May we become possessors of prosperity. [End of the sixth section of the second chapter. For the sake of seeing: "In whom the past and the future, and all the worlds are contained—by him I take you; for myself I take you. By Prajāpati I take you, O Aro. (5) "O well-stepping one, well-stepping one, be united. (5) "I cleanse you first with long life and with wealth."

May we hear words that are pleasant and beneficial; may we remain unconquered and unharmed, and may we be able to behold [the truth]—this is the connection. (99) May we speak, may we be performers of the sacred teaching, and may we long behold the sun for a great length of time. (18) The mantra for taking the hand: "In whom all beings exist, in whom, O Prajāpati, the past, the present, and the future—all worlds, including those existing now—are concentrated and supported; by him, and with his permission, I take you."

"I take hold of you so that you may not be separated from me; thus I take hold of you. The repetition beginning with "O Prajāpati" is for the sake of emphasis. The word "asau" (so-and-so) is the mention of the student's name in the vocative case. Thus ends the fifth section of the second book in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta, concerning the mantra for the placing of fuel and the wiping: "I wipe around you," etc. O Agni! I wipe around you; I cleanse you on all sides.
The word *pari* is heard twice; the verb is also repeated. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis (*ādarārtha*). [With] life and wealth... (100) ... [End of] Savyākhyānaikānnikāṇḍa.

May I be blessed with good offspring through my progeny; may I be blessed with brave sons through my heroes; may I be blessed with great luster through my splendor; may I be well-nourished through my possessions; may I be a good householder through my home; may I be a good husband through my wife; may I be wise through wisdom; may I be a master of sacred knowledge through my students. I have brought fuel for Agni, the vast Jātavedas, so that you may be kindled by this fuel. Even so, do you kindle me with long life, with luster, with gain, with wisdom, with progeny, with cattle, with the splendor of sacred knowledge, and with food—Svāhā! O Fuel, may we prosper through you—Svāhā!

"May I be united with and prosper through what is prayed for," and so forth; this has been explained. Here, the distinction is "may I be [thus]. The "Lord" (*pati*) is the protector, the teacher (*ācārya*). "Possessing good intelligence" (*sumedhāḥ*) means having an intellect endowed with the power of retention (*medhā*). "Possessing excellent sacred knowledge" (*subrahmā*) refers to one who studies together with excellent Vedic students (*brahmacārin*), according to the statement: "A quarter [of the merit] belongs to the fellow-students (*sabrahmacārin*)."

The mantras for placing the fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*) begin with "O Agni... [The mantra continues: "To you, the great, the powerful, the mighty, the one born with wealth (*jātavedas*), or the one born with wisdom, I have brought this fuel-stick; I bring it. And as you, O Agni, are kindled and made to blaze by this fuel-stick, so do you cause me to prosper and increase through long life and other blessings. *Saniḥ* means gain. *Annādya* means the eating of food. The rest is well-known. 'Thou art fuel' (*edho 'si*)—this is the response to the fuel-stick."
O Fuel! You are the fuel; [svāhā]. Second Prapāṭhaka, Sixth Khaṇḍa. "Light are you; bestow light upon me, svāhā! We have entered into the waters today with this essence.
O Agni, unite me first with splendor, with progeny, and with wealth, svāhā! May it turn back for my benefit.

The root *indh* means "to shine"; this fire is the instrument for that shining. May we also, kindling you, *edhiṣīmahi*—that is, may we flourish. Regarding the mantra "Thou art fuel" (*samid asi*): this has been explained by the *nigama* (Vedic citation). Regarding "Thou art luster" (*tejo 'si*): because thou art the cause of radiance, do thou also bestow and establish luster within me. Regarding "The waters, today" (*apo adya*): *āpaḥ* is a name for ritual action (*karman*). "Today I have performed," that is, I perform in due order, the action characterized by the placing of fuel. "With juices" (*rasaiḥ*): faith is the desire directed toward the object of action; with that juice we have united. The plural is used in place of the singular. The *luṅ* tense is used in the sense of the *liṅ* (optative).

"May I be united with him in the act of placing the fuel; may my faith also increase"—this is the meaning. Alternatively, "rasa" refers to Brahman, according to the Śruti: "He is the essence of essences. Thus, the meaning is: "By your grace, may I attain union with Brahman. "Payasvān"—here "payas" (milk) is an indicative term for the oblation (*havis*); having become possessed of the oblation, O Agni, I have come to you day after day. The *luṅ* (aorist) is used in the sense of the optative (*liṅ*). [Thus,] "I would come."

May He, who is thus constituted, unite me with splendor—O Agni! Unite me with splendor, with progeny, and with wealth. Svāhā! "May Indra, together with the seers, know my lightning; svāhā! To the other, the great firmament, svāhā! To Heaven and Earth, svāhā! "This is your fuel-stick, O Agni; grow and swell with it, and through it may I grow and swell; svāhā! "Whoever [attacks] me first, O winged one..."

Regarding the word *vidyut*: here the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative; thus, "may the gods know (*vidyuḥ*) me, this one"—the *t* is a Vedic archaism. The Rigvedins indeed recite it in this very way. The meaning is: "May the gods recognize me as performing such an action. And may Indra, together with the seers (*ṛṣibhiḥ*), know (*vidyāt*) me.

Regarding the word *agye*: "For the great, the powerful, or the vast *nāka*"; for the *Brāhmaṇa* states, "*Nāka* is indeed food. To that [Agni]. Regarding "*dyāvāpṛthivībhyām*": heaven and earth are well-known. Regarding "*eṣā te*": O Agni! This fuel-stick (*samit*) is given to you; by it, may you grow and may you swell—swelling means filling—and may you become full. May I also, growing and swelling by that fuel-stick, become full. Regarding "*yo mā'gre*": [and so forth].
"O Agni! He who, while I am a sharer—meaning one worthy of receiving a portion—desires to make me a non-sharer (abhāgam), that is, wishes to deprive me of my share.
(Brāhmaṇa 3.2.3, Sixth Section of the Second Praśna).

"O Agni, you who wish to make me a non-participant, place that [share] before me; make me a participant first, svāhā! Having placed the fuel-stick (*samidh*) before you, O Agni, may I become one who fulfills all vows, svāhā! O student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), eat your food, perform your duties, do not sleep; go for alms, remaining dependent upon your teacher. Whose first garment I take from you—that person I shall make a non-participant, but I shall make myself a participant. (108) For the sake of emphasis, the address "the fuel-stick" is repeated. O Agni! Having placed this fuel-stick before you, I— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "I—". The full ritual context would typically conclude with the student's declaration of intent.)

"May I be one whose vow is fulfilled. The instruction: "You are a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*). You have entered the stage of the student (*brahmacaryāśrama*). "Drink water"—meaning, "Having been permitted by me, drink only water. "Perform your duties"—such as the fetching of fuel and so forth. "Do not sleep during the day"—do not sleep in the daytime. For it is said: "He who rises first and goes to rest last, they say of him that he does not sleep. Or rather, such is the nature of [proper] non-sleeping.

"Go on your alms-round; even though you do not eat yourself, bring alms for our sake. Be dependent upon the teacher; without my permission, do not perform officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or similar duties for anyone. Regarding the taking of the garment: "Whose it is... We take this first garment—the very first cloth with which you were covered—may all the gods protect you. Furthermore: "Thee, growing, well-born (of auspicious birth), may many [protect]... (without my permission). "Drink only water" (ĀpDhS 1.4.28.104).

In the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*: "May they protect you... [The verse continues: "We fashion this hymn for Jātavedas, who is worthy of it, like a chariot; we do so with our inspired thought. "For auspicious is his providence for us. "O brothers, being well-increasing (*suvṛdhaḥ*)—that is, excellent increasers—may you be born after him; may you become such as he is. The meaning is: 'May your younger brothers also become such as you are.'"

Thus ends the sixth section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. Now, regarding the placing of fuel at the time of the *samāvartana*: "This hymn... (*imaṃ stomam*). We shall offer this hymn—this praise—to the one worthy of praise, to Jātavedas, who has acquired wealth or whose wisdom is born; for while the root *mahi* elsewhere means "to honor," here it should be understood in the sense of "to prepare" or "to refine."

We might be able to create or fashion [the self] by means of our own wisdom and intellect, just as a carpenter constructs a chariot, or as one desiring to travel repairs it; it would be just like that.

For what reason is praise offered to Agni? It is said: "For auspicious" (*bhadrā hi*); here the word *hi* has the sense of "because. Because his benevolent, auspicious, and excellent grace-bestowing wisdom (*pramati*) is present in our assembly (*saṃsadi*), that is, in the gathering such as sacrifices; therefore, in friendship with you, may we not suffer harm. [We take] the long life of Jamadagni, the long life of Kaśyapa.

"Whatever triple life-span belongs to the gods, may that be my triple life-span. You are auspicious by name; heaven-increaser is your father; homage be to you; do not harm me. [The mantra] "With warm water, O Vāyu... and so forth. "I here [perform this for] such-and-such a person, the descendant of such-and-such"—the meaning is that he is our benefactor. The subsequent quarter-verse, because it is addressed directly [to the recipient], constitutes a separate sentence.

O Agni! In your friendship—your friendship characterized by the state of being a praiser, which is worthy of praise by both gods and humans—may we, abiding therein, suffer no harm and may we not be forgotten by anyone. The consecration of the razor: "Vyāyuṣam" (Long life). Vyāyuṣam refers to the collection of the three lifespans: childhood, youth, and old age. May there be for me such a long life as was the long life of Jamadagni and others.

Since the act of shaving does not promote longevity, the razor used as its instrument is consecrated in this manner. He hands the razor to the barber, saying: "Thou art named Śiva. The word *nāma* is a particle used here for emphasis; it means "thou art indeed Śiva," because of the scriptural insight: "The axe is indeed the thunderbolt" (*vajra*). He is your father, because he is the foremost among all instruments. "Salutation be unto thee; do not harm me."—"With warm water, O Vāyu"—the meaning of these [verses] is already explained.

The embracing of the girdle with the mantra: "This, I... [and so on]. "The evil of this Yajñaśarman, of such-and-such a lineage, of the Vātsya or Vātsyāyana family—this, I... (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6.3.7; 4.11). These mantras are written in folios 78–80. 106.

"May this [person], having embraced the *pāpman* (evil), be superior to his enemies."—In the *Savyākhyānaikāśikāṇḍa*, "embracing" (*upagūhana*) means non-disclosure. That which is called "embracing" in the Sūtra is precisely this: the embracing of the girdle (*mekhalā*) is figuratively described as the embracing of evil itself. May this Yajñaśarman be superior—that is, greater—than his enemies.

The *ṛk*-mantras beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*: "O Waters! You are the sources of bliss (*mayobhuvaḥ*). *Mayas* is a name for happiness; you are the bringers of happiness. *Hiḥ* is used for emphasis. Therefore, O you, bestow (*dadhātana*)—that is, grant—food (*ūrjam*) for our nourishment (*annāya*). Grant us food. For the sake of great joy (*mahe raṇāya*), that is, for delightful pleasure."

"Of you"—that is, of your own—whatever essence (*rasa*) exists most near [to you], [the genitive case] here stands in the sense of the instrumental; with that essence, "make us share," meaning act so that it may partake of us. In this world, like longing mothers—that is, just as affectionate mothers, being full of love, cause their milk to flow for their offspring—so [be to us].
(18) "To him": for that essence, "araṃ" means quickly or sufficiently.

Let us go to you, let us approach you for the sake of drinking that essence; not [for any other purpose], but for great joy and for skillfulness. May he here cause us to partake of that most desirable essence which is yours, like longing mothers [partaking] of their son. Let us go sufficiently to you, for whose abode you quicken us, O Waters, as a people [is quickened]. (Saṃhitā)

5-6-1. Second Prapāṭhaka, Seventh Khaṇḍa: [The verses] beginning with *hiṣṭhā bharmā yo-bhuvaḥ*—three [verses]; and [the verses] beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayo yaḥ pāvakāḥ*—three [verses]. [In the phrase] *annādyāya vyūhadhvaṃ*, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the dative (*tṛtīyārthe*). [The word] *kṣayāya* means "for a dwelling" (*nivāsa*), because it is accented on the first syllable; thus, the dative (*caturthī*) is used in the sense of the accusative (*dvitīyārthe*). [The meaning is: "O waters, you who are radiant, purify us for the sake of food; gladden (*jinvatha*), that is, delight, our dwelling (*kṣayam*), which is our home."

And by which [power], O Waters! you cause us to be born—make us procreated through sons, grandsons, and so forth. 16—"The golden-hued, the pure ones... has been explained. Even that which was not previously mentioned is now clear. Indra is Parjanya; because he manifests within the clouds, his nature is "born of the waters" (*apsujā*).

Regarding the brushing of the teeth with the mantra *annādyāya*: "For the sake of eating food (*annādya*), for the purpose of consuming food, arrange yourselves—*vyūhadhvam* means 'arrangement' or 'separation'; O teeth, become separated from impurity! "Honey-colored, pure, and purifying are those [teeth] in whom Kaśyapa was born, in whom Indra was born; they, of diverse forms, have conceived the embryo" (RV 6.49.1).

Varuṇa moves in the midst, beholding the truth and the falsehood of men. May they be gracious! Those waters which the gods create in heaven, those which exist in the intermediate space in many forms, and those which moisten the earth with their milk—may those bright waters be gracious to us. (108) May I be one who eats food day after day.

"King Soma shall tell me the path by which my face shall instantly become endowed with luster. "Soma, you are this body; protect my body. Enter into me as my body. "Homage to the seizer and to the one who causes seizure; homage to Śākajañja. "Homage to those deities who are the seizers. [From the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikāṇḍa*, Brāhmaṇa 2.2.5]

"Be [present]. And may I, through you, become pure, long-lived, and an eater of food. This is said because the King (Soma) has arrived at the place where the tooth-stick stands, and because trees are presided over by Soma; thus he is called "the one who has come. And having arrived, he shall speak into my mouth along with fortune (*bhaga*), good luck (*saubhāgya*), splendor (*varcas*), and radiance (*dīpti*). It is said that when the teeth are cleaned, the mouth becomes exceedingly beautiful. Immediately thereafter, he puts on a garment with the mantra: "Thou art the body of Soma."

"Thou art the garment; thou art the body of Soma"—for thus says the Śruti: "The garment is indeed auspicious. Being such as this, protect my body; for when covered by thee, the body becomes protected. It is not only the body of Soma, but rather my own body as well that is so addressed because it is equivalent to a body. And so another mantra says: "The self is the father's body, the garment is vigor, and the ointment is strength. Being such as this, enter into me.

The offering of sandalwood to the deities, titled [thus]. There are three mantras beginning with *namaḥ*. The deities are those indicated by the words of the mantras (*māntravarṇika*): the *graha*, the *abhi-grāhya*, the *śākajañjabhī*, and the *abhigrāhiṇyaḥ*. These approach a man at the time of adornment; to them is the offering of sandalwood. (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 8.3.24). Second Prapāṭhaka, Seventh Khaṇḍa: "The fragrance that is among the Apsarases, and whatever glory is among the Gandharvas, the divine fragrance of men—may that fragrance, well-guarded, delight me."

"This [plant] is from the *uṣadhi* family, the protector, the victorious, the powerful. May it make me radiant with gold and endowed with the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*). You are the essence of the waters; do not harm me, O Urvaśī; do not stand over me.
With the following verse, he anoints himself: "Of the Apsarases... [the enjoyment of the Apsarases].

May that fragrance which is fit for the Gandharvas, and whatever fame and renown exists among the Gandharvas, and that well-known fragrance by virtue of which they are called Gandharvas—those who possess fragrance (gandhavantaḥ)—and whatever divine fragrance and whatever human fragrance there is, may all of it, being a fragrant scent that gratifies the sense of smell, attend and delight me.

He heats a golden jewel in a vessel of water, saying: "This is the herb. This is a praise of the earthly gold by way of its being the earth: "This earth is the herb; [it is] herbs" (the elision of the case-ending is Vedic). The meaning is that she is the *trāyamāṇā* (protecting/sustaining) one, the support of all herbs. "Sahamānā" means capable in all undertakings; "sahasvatī" means powerful. May such an earth make me possessed of golden luster—that is, radiant like gold—and may she make me one who possesses the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcas*), endowed with the power of the Veda.
"Thou art the neck-fastener, not a noose"—thus [he says]. That by which a thief or the like is bound is a *pāśa* (noose);

thou art not that. And therefore, do not injure my chest, the breast-region; for there is a fear of injury to the chest due to falling while being bound by the neck. "Be auspicious unto me, for long life"—for what kind of life? For a hundred autumns, for long life, for a hundred autumns. "For a hundred autumns, for life, for luster, for living, for merit"—[these are the verses] beginning with "The wealthy ones have covered thee. 7.

"May there be for me prosperity of wealth (*rāyaspoṣa*) and that longevity which occurs in the autumn (*śaradaḥ*)—for that [longevity], [may there be] a hundred [autumns]. Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the dative; "for a hundred autumns" means for the sake of a lifespan lasting a hundred years, for the sake of that life which occurs during those hundred years. "For splendor (*varcase*), for vitality (*jīvātve*)," where *jīvātu* means living—that is, for the sake of that merit and excellence, [may you] stand auspiciously for me. The repetition of "life" (*āyuṣaḥ*) is for the sake of emphasis.
"The wealthy ones (*revatīḥ*) have anointed you," and so forth—these have been explained. With those very [verses], the second [rite is performed].

"Put on the garment. Thus ends the seventh section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. Having tied a fringe (*pravartī*) to its hem (*daśā*), he offers an oblation with the mantra: "Life-prolonging" (*āyuṣyam*). That which is the cause of life is "life-prolonging"; that which is the cause of splendor is "splendid" (*varcasyam*). "Possessing good heroism" means endowed with excellent strength. "Nourisher of wealth" means the nourisher of riches; gold is the root of all wealth. These mantras (82–84) are written in the *Pṛṣṭas*.

The eighth section of the second chapter. May this gold enter into me for victory! It is the loud speaker, the conqueror of armies, the overcomer of terrors, the winner of wealth. All auspicious verses are contained within this gold. "I have grasped the great name of gold as if it were that of my father. Regarding the term *audvidya*: because it pierces upward (*udbhinatti*) and shines forth (*prakāśate*), it is called *udvit*; thus, by means of *udvit*, it is *audvidya*, meaning "glorious."

"May this gold, being thus, for victory—that is, the cause of victory; *jaitryam* means that very thing which is victorious, the act of winning—for that purpose, for the sake of the oblation and for victory itself, enter me, let it enter. *Um̐ carvādi*: "He causes to sound loudly," thus he is *ucairvādi*. For those possessing gold indeed speak aloud. *Pṛtanāji*: the absence of the *tuka*-suffix is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). [It means] a conqueror of armies (*pṛtanājit*).

*Satrāsāha*: *satrā* is an indeclinable meaning "truth"; thus, he is the name of Truth itself, the conqueror of enemies. *Dhanañjaya*: the victor even over the wealth belonging to the enemy. What more need be said? Of what kind are all these prosperities (*ṛddhi*)? They are *samṛddhīḥ*, meaning fully developed and complete; such is the reading of the Vājasaneyins. *Hiraṇye’smin samāhitāḥ*: they are perfectly placed within this gold. Regarding *śunam aham*: *śunam* is a name for happiness.

I have grasped the name of gold; I have taken it up just as a son repeatedly pronounces the name of his father. Make me, who thus proclaim that name of yours, endowed with golden luster—O Gold, make me shine like gold! Furthermore, among men—"pūru" is a name for "man," as explained in the *Nirukta*, in the section on synonyms (Ekānnikāṇḍa). Make me a beloved man of golden luster. Make me dear to the two worlds; make me dear to the Brahman.

Make me beloved among the Vaiśyas and Śūdras; do not make me beloved among the Rājanyas. You who lie down among the animals, thinking "I am the supporter"—you, as such, I worship with a stream of clarified butter. To you, the goddess who supports, *svāhā*! To you, the one who adorns, *saṃdīrghatvam*. [The word] *pūruṣu* is used in the locative case with the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe saptamī*). Make me beloved among many, among the many; act in such a way that I may be beloved by all. This is precisely what is meant by: "Make me beloved."

In all instances, the locative case is used in the sense of the genitive. They explain it as "for the Brahmin" (*brahmaṇe*) or "in the Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇe*). The shortening of the vowel in the word *brāhmaṇa* is Vedic; the singular number is used in the sense of the class (*jāti*). [Similarly,] "among the Vaiśyas" (*viśyeṣu*) means "among the Vaiśyas" (*vaiśyeṣu*); the shortening of the vowel is Vedic. "Among the kings" (*rājasu*) means "among the Kṣatriyas. O Hiraṇya! The meaning is that through the oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) touched by you, these [beings], beginning with the gods, become dear. Regarding the verse "yā tiraścī": there is a deity named Saṃrādhanī, and some say she is the Earth; others say she is Speech abiding in the intermediate space.

O Saṃrādhani! O you who, being *tiraścī* (transverse), lie down as the *śeṣa* (remainder); in the case of the Earth, this is with the thought: "I am the supporter (*vidharaṇī*), the ordainer (*vidhātrī*) of every living being. But in the case of Speech, it is with the thought: "I am the warder-off (*nivārayitrī*), the one who restrains those who cause harm"—thus, for their non-entry, you who lie transverse at the doorway as the *śeṣa*; you, I worship here with a stream of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

The following two [verses] are clear. *Prasādhani* is also that very same *saṃrādhanī*, meaning "she who accomplishes excellently," or it may refer to another deity. Second Prapāṭhaka, Eighth Khaṇḍa: "To the Goddess, Svāhā! To the Sovereign (*samrāj*) and the Radiant One (*virāj*), to the Prosperity (*abhiśrī*) that is in our home, and to the Fortune (*lakṣmī*) that is at the head of the kingdom—with her, may we unite. O *Śubhikeśī*, ascend to my head; beautifying, adorn my face."

"Make my mouth indeed a vital point (*marman*) that is imperishable, and make that [mouth] my fortune. [The mantra continues: "O you who crush the enemy of Yama, for the sake of faithless and lustful women, cleanse me thoroughly! In the fourth quarter of the first line, there is a connection with the word *me* (of me). "I unite you both—the sovereign (*samrāj*) and the radiant (*virāj*)—with me. The plural number is used in reference to a single entity; thus, it means "I unite. By what? By that prosperity (*śrī*) which is directed toward me (*abhiśrīḥ*) in my house. The particle *ca* (and) is used in anticipation of what is to be stated next.

And with that Fortune which is at the head of the kingdom, may you unite me. A *samrāj* is one who shines perfectly; a *virāj* is one who shines diversely. With the following two verses, the binding of the garland takes place: "O auspicious one, ascend my head... *Śubhikā* means simply "auspicious" (*śubhā*); the suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense. O *śubhikā*, O auspicious one! Ascend my head, becoming one who adorns my face. It is stated again for the sake of emphasis: "Do thou indeed adorn me. The word *hi* is a filler (*pādapūraṇa*).

"Make [her] more fortunate and blessed. Regarding the phrase "yāmāharat" (whom he brought): Jamadagni brought that *khajā* (churning vessel). For whom? For the goddess Śraddhā. Of what kind? For her who desires (*kāmayānyai*), that is, for her who longs [for him]. "I too bind this such *trajā* upon our head with fortune (*bhagena*)," [meaning] for one who desires. [This is from] the commentary on the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa*.

"Bring this river here along with its splendor in an instant! When the *traikakuda* [ointment] was produced upon the Himalayas for the Jina, by that [power], grant me brilliance, splendor, and fortune. May I possess the essence of the mountain, may I possess the splendor of the mountain, may I possess the medicine of the mountain, may I possess the longevity of the mountain. Whatever splendor has gone before me—the *añjana* mantra: 'That which is the *añjana*...'"

There is a mountain named Trikakud; that which grows thereon is *ekakuda*. And with that *añjana* (ointment) produced upon the Himavat, [the seer] anointed your two eyes, O [Goddess]. For what purpose? For brilliance (*tejas*), for radiance (*prakāśa*), for luster (*dīpti*), and for fortune (*bhaga*) and good luck (*saubhāgya*). Thus ends the eighth section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. — [The mantra: "In me [are] the mountains and men... etc.

May that manliness, virility, and power of endurance which is in Parvata be in me; and whatever radiance and smoothness belongs to Parvata, and whatever healing power is in Parvata, and whatever longevity is in Parvata—the life of Parvata—may all that be in me. First, the mantra for the inspection: "Whatever luster is in me... [The text continues: "Whatever luster is mine, [he] approaches himself. [End of] the ninth section of the second recitation.

I take back this very luster for long life and splendor. You two are the foundation of the deities; may you not cause me to fall. You are the refuge of Prajāpati, the covering of Brahman, the shadow of all people. O Earth, protect me. I approach the Self that has come forth from the god, emerged from me, and stands upon the surface of the mirror—this very luster I take back for long life and splendor.

The mantra for putting on sandals is: *pratiṣṭha stha*. The word *prati* means "in response" (*śabdāthe*). O sandals! You two are *pratiṣṭhe*, the means for setting forth; this applies even to the deities—so it must be supplied—that they are the means for the deities' setting forth, how much more so for us. *Mā mā saṃtāpsīḥ*: do not cause me distress through the production of wounds, or distress caused by thorns and the like; the meaning is that no such distress shall befall me. The mantra for holding the umbrella is: *prajāpateḥ*.

O umbrella! You are the refuge and the home of Prajāpati; you are the roof of Brahman—the meaning is that you are indeed a protective covering, a layer of shelter. What more need be said? You are the shade for all people; you perform the function of shade. Being such as this, protect me from all sides. The mantra for taking up the staff: *devasya tvā...* ("By the impulse of the god..."). This means: at the impulse (or with the permission) of the god Savitṛ, being true, [I take you] by the arms of the Aśvins—that is, by my own arms presided over by them.

Thus, "from the two hands of Pūṣan": the upper portion of the middle joint is the *bāhu* (arm), and the lower portion is the *hasta* (hand). "I take thee for the slaying of the enemy; let it reach the dog-eater. [This is from] the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*. "I take thee for the slaying of the enemy; thou art the thunderbolt of Indra; O food, grant me protection; ward off whatever sin there may be."—"O six goddesses, wide ones..."—this is the verse.

For the sake of driving away, like Indra’s thunderbolt—just as Indra’s weapon is [the slayer], so are you my protector against the enemy; "Vṛtra" is a name for the enemy, and "Vṛtrahan" is its slayer. Being thus, like the Vṛtra-slayer, be my refuge (*śarma*); be the bringer of happiness to me. Ward off whatever brings harm, such as dogs and the like. The invocation of the directions: "O Goddesses, six... There are three invocations of the directions: "O Goddesses!"—O divine ones! The four principal directions, beginning with the East, and the zenith.

And Dharā—these are the six! O Uvaḥ! O Urvyas! O you who are wide! Make for us—that is, for us—*uru*, which means "wide," "extensive," or "abundant," wealth. O Viśve Devāsas! O all you gods, the lords of those directions, Indra and the others! May you also perform heroic deeds (*vīrayadhvam*)—that is, perform acts of heroes—and make me possessed of heroes or possessed of sons. [The prayer] "May we not abandon the constellations, nor the moon"—here, by the word "O King" (*rājan*), the constellations are indicated.

O King among the constellations, O Soma! By your grace, may we not be abandoned by our progeny—*hāniḥ* meaning abandonment; may we not be forsaken. May we not be abandoned by our bodies—the plural is used here with reference to many bodies, such as sons and so forth. May we not fall under the power of the enemy (*mā radhāma dviṣate*). The word *rādhiḥ* refers to the act of subjugation; the dative case is used here in the sense of the object of that subjugation. May we not become subject to those who hate us. "O Viśvedevas, make Varuṇa our protector; O All-Gods, display your heroism here!"

May we not be abandoned by our offspring, nor by our bodies; may we not fall into the power of the enemy, O King Soma. (Saṃhitā 4.1.14). This is the eleventh [section], the ninth section of the second prapāṭhaka. 12. Rāṣṭra.

117. "O imperial throne (*samrāḍ-āsandī*), do not fail me! O royal throne (*rāṣṭrabhṛt-sadhipahnyā*), do not fail me! May the feet of the Ṛṣis protect me; may they destroy my enemies. May there be Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcas*) in this family. In me be greatness, in me glory, in me sensory power and vigor. [Bring it! Now follow the mantras for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*): 'O sustainer of the kingdom' (*rāṣṭrabhṛt*), etc. [This is understood. Imperial throne: the consecrated Kṣatriya; the seat corresponding to that is the *samrāḍ-āsandī*."

The presiding deity is the Lord of the Maṇḍala (*maṇḍalādhipati*), who has not yet been consecrated; his seat is the *ādhipatryāsandī*. There is no [need for] the *kāra-chāndusa* or the *upajjana*. The consecration of the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) is as follows: "O waters, may you destroy my enemy. Those waters by which the two feet are washed—that is, cleansed—are the *pādāvanejanī* waters. [The mantra is: "May those waters destroy my enemy. In this family, may I become possessed of Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasī*). The self-consecration (*pratyabhimarśa*) is: "In me, greatness... (*mayi mahaḥ*).

*Mahas* is great honor; *yaśas* is renown; *indriya* refers to the eye and other senses; *vīrya* is semen. The word "let it be" (*bhavatu*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having been touched on the foot by a Brāhmaṇa, one prays thus out of fear that these qualities might depart. The consecration (*adhyabhimantraṇa*) is: "Come to me" (*ā mā ganna*). O water (*avyo*), you [come] to me!

Come, O Āgama! Or rather, come hither. Having come, unite me with glory (*yaśas*), with speech (*vaca*), with milk (*payas*), and with splendor (*tejas*). Furthermore—with these [qualities]—make me beloved by the subjects and the lord of cattle. "Thou art the milking of Virāj; may I obtain the milking of Virāj. May my Virāj be established. I release you like a seal; go back to your own womb. May I be unbroken in my progeny; may I not perish.

What is the meaning? || 9 || There are six [verses] beginning with *arvāk*. || 9 || Make me, who have been created by you, dear to living beings (*prajā*) and the lord (*adhipati*) of cattle (*paśu*), such as cows and others. Regarding the *adhvaryu* priest when he is being brought [the water] in his joined palms (*añjali*), he recites: "O Virāj. Here, *virāṭ* refers to the entrails (*antra*); "the entrails are the Virāj. You are its milking (*doha*), that is, its flowing forth (*kṣaraṇa*). Therefore, through your acceptance, may I obtain and attain the milking of the Virāj.

"My *padya*": a place or station is *pada*; that which exists therein is *padya*. To my son who is *padya*, who has not fallen from his station (*mat-sthānapanna*), "to him, the radiant one (*virāj*),"—make him also such as this. He consecrates with the following verse the remainder being carried forward: "O ocean, you... O Waters! I send you forth to the ocean; may you go back to your own source, the ocean. The ocean is the source of all waters.

"By your grace, may I also be unbroken and continuous through progeny; may my progeny not be cut off. And may no milk be spilled from me. "Spilling" (*parāsika*) refers to pouring [the milk] in such a way that it does not become suitable for use again. Thus ends the tenth section of the second chapter in the *Ekāgrikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. (ŚB 2.5.10).

"From the threefold knowledge, [I take] the glories; from the glorious ones, the glory; from the Brahman, the radiance. Make me dear to the subjects, prospering for the sake of cattle. 'May it come to me'—this is the formula. It is the under-layer of immortality; it is the covering of immortality. That which is the supreme food and the vigor of the honeyed honey—with that, with the honeyed honey, the supreme, he consecrates the *madhuparka* with the two following verses, beginning with 'From the threefold knowledge.'"

The three Vedas are the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*); for that [knowledge], the fourth case ending is used in the sense of the sixth. You are the glory (*yaśas*) of that [knowledge]—that is, the fame [derived from it], as in the saying, "He who studies the Veda is worthy of cows and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). Furthermore, you are the glory of glory, meaning the highest degree of praise, just as one speaks of "the ornament of ornaments. You are the radiance of Brahman, that is, of the Veda. The passage beginning with "Make me beloved" (*taṃ mā priyam*) has already been explained. "Come to me" (*ā mā gann*) has also been explained.

He sips water with the formula: *amṛtopastaraṇam asi* ("Thou art the underlayer for the nectar"). Thou art the underlayer for that which is like nectar, just as there is an underlayer for the portions of sacrificial food. Afterwards, he sips water with the formula: *amṛtāpidhānam asi* ("Thou art the cover for the nectar"). Thou art the cover for the nectar. He eats the *madhuparka* with the formula: *yan madhunaḥ* ("That which [is] of honey"). That which exists in honey is *madhavya*; just as in expressions such as *gavāṃ gopatiḥ* ("lord of cows") or *vasupatiḥ* ("lord of wealth"), where the term *pati* does not in reality exceed the meaning of the preceding word, yet both are employed together, so it is here with "of honey."

Regarding the term "madhavyam": the meaning of this mantra (117), written on the leaf, is as follows. [Verse 2-9-16]: "The Lord of Wealth (*vasupati*), by means of food and vigor, is the supreme eater of food; he is Madhavya. O Gauri, you who are free from evil, strike away the evil of both me and that person. Let Agni eat first, for he knows how the oblation is; making it inexhaustible for us, may the Brahmin [bestow it] upon the Brahmins. The sacrifice is simply "madhavyam" to this extent.

What, then, is that? It is supreme food; for this eating of honey is indeed supreme food, being heroic and bestowing heroism. With such "honey-like" [substance], with that honey-like [essence], with supreme food and heroism—following the previous [formula]—the *yājyā* is recited: "May I also become a supreme eater of food and honey-like; may I be honey-like, one who consumes honey. He consecrates the cow offered [to him] with the mantra: "Thou art a cow."

"O Cow! You are free from evil; therefore, drive away evil—from whom? From me and from this donor. Regarding the mantra for the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) on the occasion of the ritual slaughter (*ālambhana*): "Agni... This Agni is the first; let him eat. For what purpose? Because he knows whether the oblation (*havis*) is properly prepared or improperly prepared. And as he eats, let him make it unfailing for us; let him eat so as to leave a remainder for us.

Of what sort is he? He is a Brāhmaṇa even among Brāhmaṇas; the meaning is that he is a Brāhmaṇa in the highest degree. Alternatively, "brāhmaṇebhyaḥ" is used in the sense of the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhyarthe caturthī): performing for us Brāhmaṇas what is not lost, and being himself a Brāhmaṇa. This is the tenth section of the second prapāṭhaka. O Vaidhartr, you are the filler of the sacrifice; may you increase. You are the healer; do not deprive me of my healing. May I be a healer among men.

"The cow, the milch-cow, the ox—the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality. May I speak forth for the one who knows; do not slay the sinless cow, the Aditi. In the case of the *utsarga* (the ritual release of the cows), the recitation is: "The sacrifice. May this human sacrifice, characterized by our worship, increase; even in the case of the *utsarga*, may there be no deficiency.

Following the increase of that sacrifice, O Cow! you too should increase; for you are *apaciti* (honour), because you are the means of its accomplishment, so make me an object of honour (*apaciti*). What is the purpose? By releasing you, may I become honoured among men.
"—*gaurdhenubhavyā*. This cow is a "cow that will become a milch-cow" (*dhenubhavyā*), meaning it is destined to become a milch-cow;

this is said for the sake of praise in the case where she is released (*utsarga-pakṣe*), for once released, this cow will become a milch-cow and thus yield great fruit. In the case of slaughter (*ālambha-pakṣe*), however, the satisfaction is merely momentary. Furthermore, she stands in the place of a mother and so forth to the gods such as Rudra, since all [the gods] partake in the sacrifice, and that [sacrifice] is accomplished by means of products of the cow, such as clarified butter (*ājya*). She is the "navel" (*nābhi*)—the principal constituent part—of "immortality" (*amṛtasya*), that is, of the sacrifice which is the cause for attaining immortality, because of the Vedic text: "This indeed is the sacrifice, namely clarified butter. (*Eṣa vāva yajño yadājyam*).

"Thus named," [is] this praise; and therefore I speak the *praṇava* (*om*) for the sake of speed, that is, I speak with swiftness and excellence. For the one who knows—*kituṣe* (from the root *kit*, meaning "to know")—for the person who understands. What shall I say? "Do not let her go"—[meaning] this innocent, blameless cow. [Let her eat] the grasses. *Om*, release her! "She is the Virāj. May I not be deprived of that; may I partake of its essence; may you bestow strength upon me. *Om*, arrange it! 10. And eight [verses] ending with *bhayāsam*. 10.

"Do not kill the cow, the unbroken Aditi. Let her drink water as she desires and eat grass. Om! Release her, release her!"—the prefix *pra-* has two meanings here; *om* is a word of permission, so [the meaning is]: "Release her who has been permitted by all. "When the food is prepared, he says, 'It is ready' (*bhūtam*). 'Ready' (*bhūtam*) means it is prepared. Saying 'So be it' (*tathāstu*), he mutters the subsequent [verses], beginning with 'She is Virāj. Because the word *virāj* is feminine, it is referred to as 'she' (*sā*). She is called *virāj* because she shines (*rājate*) in various ways (*vi-*) upon that food."

"May it not perish; may it not be exhausted. [The word] *tasya* [is used] for you; the second [word] is in the genitive case. "May I partake of that; may I eat that. "Grant that to me; bestow strength and power upon me. *Oṃ* is used as an expression of assent. "Prepare it! Bring it here, O attendants! Thus ends the tenth section in the commentary on the mantras of the Ekāgnikāṇḍa composed by Śrī Haradatta. This is the eleventh section in the second chapter.

"May Dhātṛ grant us wealth"—these four verses [beginning with] *iya* (RV 10.184.1–4) are the *mantras* for the *Sīmantonnayana* sacrifice, starting with "May Dhātṛ grant... Dhātṛ—the Lord (*īśāna*) and Protector (*pati*) of the moving world (*jagataḥ*)—may he grant us (*naḥ*) wealth (*rāyiṃ*, i.e., riches). And may he, while granting it, favor (*vāvanat*) us with our desires fulfilled. The root *vana* (in the form *vavaṇa*) means "to partake of" or "to enjoy"; this is the fifth *lakāra* (the subjunctive mood). Thus, he should favor us in such a way that our desire is fulfilled. (2) "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth, the Lord, the Master of the moving world."

May he favor us with fullness. Dhātṛ rules over progeny and wealth; he has generated this entire world. Dhātṛ shall grant a son to the sacrificer; to him we shall offer oblations rich in clarified butter. "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth and long, undecaying life. May we obtain the benevolent favor of the god whose bounty is true. "May Dhātṛ grant riches to the donor who desires offspring within his home, O bounteous one."

"May the immortal gods, all the Viśvedevas, and Aditi, acting in harmony, bestow their favor upon him. (Saṃhitā 2.3.11). "He who, thinking of you with a humble heart, invokes you as a messenger—O Jātavedas, bestow glory upon us; may we attain immortality through progeny, O Agni. (124) "He is the Ordainer (Dhātṛ). He alone is the Ordainer of progeny and also the Lord (īśe) of wealth (rāyaḥ).

The Creator alone has generated this entire world; here the root *jan* (to be born) carries the sense of the causative (*ṇyartha*), meaning "he caused to be born. He is the Creator who is also the giver to both the son and the sacrificer. This word [dhātā] ends in the suffix *tṛn*. To such a Creator, we shall offer oblation accompanied by clarified butter (*ghṛtavat*). Elsewhere the root *vid* means "to serve," but here it should be understood as "giving"—that is, "we shall give. Or rather, there is a shift in case endings: "with oblation accompanied by clarified butter, we shall serve him. The particle *u* is meaningless. Regarding "the Creator": may that very Creator grant us wealth. Of what kind?

"Prācīm" means the eastern [direction]; "prācīṃ prācālabhavaṃ" means that which has come down in succession from the ancestors, being of such a nature as they were—this is the meaning. "Jīvātuṃ" means sufficient for life; "akṣitām" means undecaying, free from destruction. "Vayaṃ tasya devasya dhātuḥ sumatiṃ" means we meditate upon—the word "dhīmahe" meaning we contemplate—the beautiful intention (sumati) of that divine Creator (dhātu), which consists of grace toward His devotees. "Satyaradhasaḥ" means whose wealth is truth. Regarding the word "dhātu": [it refers to the Creator].

He alone is the Ordainer for the donor—*dāśuṣe* means for the one who gives—at the act of giving; for whomsoever, O Jātavedas, you have first made a pleasant world with the *caru*, the *puroḍāśa*, and other offerings.
