Through the Aśvins, he attains well-being: wealth consisting of sons, heroic progeny, and cattle. "In thee, O Indra, the lords of power have fulfilled their desire through good sons; no one exceeds thee, O Indra. "Verse after verse, O Soma, has exhilarated Indra; at every ritual station, the pressed juices belong to the Bountiful One (*maghavān*)."

When the sons, though capable, do not honor their father while he is still living, they do not find favor [with him]. (The eleventh section of the second chapter. May the Giver grant me riches and treasures; by the statement "for one desiring offspring," it is intended here that offspring constitute the treasure. For the bountiful one who desires offspring, the shedder of seed, in the dwelling—*durona* is a name for the house, but here it is not so.

According to the maxim, "They say 'house, house,' yet it is the wife who is called the house," the word refers to the wife. The collective meaning is: "To me, who, desiring offspring, pour my seed into the wife, grant offspring. Therefore, may even the gods—who are immortal, possessing the nature of immortality—bestow [it] upon me; "saṃvyantām" is from the root *vi*, used in the sense of giving. To prevent the term "gods" from being restricted to only a few, he says: "O all-gods (*viśve devāsaḥ*)."

"And Aditi, being well-pleased, sharing the same delight. [Regarding the verse] "He who thee with the heart": O Agni! O Jātavedas! I, a mortal, thinking you—who are yourself immortal—to be a mortal, thinking that I, subject to death, am capable of protecting myself, call upon you repeatedly with a humble mind; for "kīri" is a name for a hymn, meaning one who praises. Since the word "yaḥ" (who) is heard, the word "saḥ" (he/that) must be supplied.

In that [world], for us—there is a transposition of words (*vacanavyatyaya*)—in that world, in me, place and establish glory or fame. Furthermore: "Through offspring may I attain immortality; you are born again following your offspring; that is your mortal [nature], while that [offspring] is your immortality," according to the Śruti. To whomsoever—O Agni, O Jātavedas!—to whichever person of good deeds you shall make a pleasant, blissful world, the word *u* being meaningless, he [shall attain] abundance.

[He is] joined with horses, possessed of sons, and endowed with sons who are heroes, as well as with heroic attendant men or grandsons—since the word *vīra* (hero) here refers to grandsons, it is stated [elsewhere] that he is "possessed of sons. And he attains, that is, reaches, abundance of cattle and wealth (*rāyaḥ* = *dhanaṃ*) safely and properly. In the *Savyākhyānaikānika-kaṇḍa*: "O son of strength! (*tve ṭu putra*). O son of *āvasa*! *Śava* is a name for strength; thus, "son of strength" is intended to demonstrate an excellence of power.

Even for one who is strong, a son may be strong; how much more so, then, for the son of Strength itself? Such a designation of Indra is seen elsewhere as well, namely: "O Suta, I consider him born of vigor. Regarding *tve*: it means "in you" (*tvayi*). From the root *vṛt* (to turn), in the *laṅ* tense, with the suffix *aṅ* due to its belonging to the *dyutādi* class, and the augment *ruṭ* added by the rule "often in the Veda" (*bahulaṃ chandasi*), the form *vṛtran* is produced. It means "they turn well" (*suṣṭhu vartante*).

What are they? They are the "desires for objects" (*kāmakātayaḥ*). "Objects" (*kāmāḥ*) are those things which are desired; their "desires" (*kātayaḥ*) are the longings for them. Thus, they abide in the very longings for all objects. The meaning is: "You alone are the giver of these. And therefore, no one surpasses you, O Indra; the sense is that there is no one whatsoever superior to you. Regarding the phrase *ukthaukthe*: *uktha* is the name of a liturgical recitation (*śastra*). At every limb of the recitation, Soma has exhilarated Indra at each *uktha*. The *liṭ* (perfect tense) is used here in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*), and the root *madi* carries an implied causative sense.

Let him exhilarate himself at every song, at every chant, at every completion, and at every conclusion. O worm, [praise] Indra, the possessor of wealth—*maghavān* being a name for wealth, meaning "possessing wealth"—with these pressed juices. The plural number is used for the singular. The *sutas* are the Soma juices pressed by us. For what purpose? Solely to exhilarate Indra. As for the word *yat*, it is used in the Vedic language (*chandas*) in the sense of *enam* (him).

These [Maruts], who are closely united, having common afflictions, common skill, and common strength, invoke him for their own aid and protection, just as sons invoke a father. Since they, though mutually contending, invoke this very one, therefore let Indra alone be the exhilarator of them all.
(Ṛgveda)

1.0-73-1. Second Pravāha, Eleventh Section. Regarding the *sīmanta-unnayana* (parting of the hair) mantras: "I invoke Rākā," "O Rākā, as the sky [is to the Gandharva]," and "Like a king for us"—the *vyāhṛtis* have been explained. "I invoke Rākā": Rākā is the full-moon night (*paurṇamāsī*) when the moon is full; her I invoke, she who is easy to call upon (*suhavā*), she who is well-invoked. "With good praise" (*sumutī*): this is the *pūrvasavarṇa* substitution for the third case singular. With beautiful, excellent praise, I call upon her. And may she hear us.

From the mention of the genitive case, "invocation" is the understood remainder [of the sentence]. "Subhagā" means endowed with good fortune; "having heard, may she afflict herself"—that is, may she perceive it within her own heart and bring it about. And immediately thereafter, "may she sew the waters. "Apas" (waters) is a name for the ritual action (*karman*); may she sew this rite characterized as the *sīmantonnayana*, performing it well by closing the opening with her own [needle], which serves as the needle.

"May she grant a hero—a son who is the giver of a hundred, a donor to many—by means of her intellect (*buddhi*) which is being cut [in the act of giving] yet remains unobstructed anywhere. [Grammatical Note: The suffix *aṇ* occurs after a word ending in long *ā* in the sense of the object (*karman*). Thus, [the form] will be [formed]. [The son is] *ukthya*, meaning praiseworthy. "I invoke Rākā, who is easily invoked, with beautiful hymns. May the fortunate one hear us and may she herself prosper. She sews the wound with a needle that is never blunted; may she grant a hero, a giver of a hundred, who is worthy of praise."

"O Rākā, those benevolent thoughts of yours which are well-formed, by which you grant riches to the donor—approach us today with a gracious mind, O auspicious one, bestowing thousands of nourishments. (Saṃhitā 2.3.11). "The Sālvas, the Arvādis, and others spoke of the nature of the *sūca*. 'The Brahmins said, "He alone is our king," as they sat with their wheels turned back along the bank of that river. Regarding this, [the verse begins] 'yāste'..."

O Rākā! O thou of beautiful form, with those gracious intentions—that is, those benevolent thoughts by which thou quickly bestowest gifts upon the sacrificer—come hither to us with those gracious intentions, being well-disposed toward us. O Subhagā! Bestowing, that is, granting, manifold nourishment that sustains thousands. [This is the mantra for the lute-singing of the inhabitants of the Yamunā banks: "Yaugandhari."]

The country named Śālva; the subjects dwelling in its territory are the Sāṭṭhīs, the Śālvīs. "The son of Yugandhara is Yaugandhari. "He alone is our king," they declared. Having become such that their kingdom (cakra) has turned in various ways (vivṛtta), they say: "O Yamunā! Seated upon your bank (tīreṇa = tīre). This is the mantra for the lute-song of all those Brāhmaṇī subjects: *soma eva*.

The Brāhmaṇas say that the people born of the Brāhmaṇa caste are indeed the *Sāman*, not the *Rājana*. [The passage beginning with] "with wheels turned away" (*vivṛttacakrā*) and so forth has been explained. Regarding the word "this one" (*asau*), it refers to a region by the name of a river, which they address in the vocative case, as in: "O Kāverī, on your bank. [Regarding the ritual: "With the *Puṃsavana* rite, he pours the juice of the *nyagrodha* shoot into the right nostril, saying: 'Thou art the male-creating essence' (*puṃsavanaṃ asi*). That by which a male is brought forth is the *puṃsavana*; "Thou art that," O Juice! The eleventh section of the second chapter.

15. For the binding of this [child] for its manifestation: "Just as Soma flows upon the mountain, just as he flows in the ocean, so let your embryo flow; having emerged together with the placenta, may it be established in long life, in Vedic splendor, in fame, in heroic sons, and in the enjoyment of food! Having lain for ten months, for thus has the Creator ordained: "May the embryo come forth uninjured, living from the living mother. 129. The touching [of the womb] with the *kṣiprasavana* formula: "With this [formula], 'I [have seized] thee... etc.

Because of the feminine gender in the expression "with ten," it is understood that the gender refers to the fingers. With these ten fingers, I touch you for the sake of the ten-month [embryo]. The dative case is used in the sense of the accusative: for the sake of bringing forth quickly the fetus that has been carried for ten months. [The mantras for the sprinkling are: "Just as... and so forth.

Just as Soma, when pressed, flows through the ten-fibered filter (*daśāpavitra*), and just as the ocean trembles and quivers by the force of the wind, even so let your embryo quiver; let it move from its place. Having moved and emerged outside along with the *jarāyu* (the fetal membrane), let it be established in long life and other blessings. "Ten"—having lain for ten months, let this embryo of yours, being uninjured, come forth from you alive, as if living, breathing.

"For it was thus ordained by the Creator. Indeed, the ten-month gestation was ordained by the Creator, the Divine; therefore, [the phrase] "having lain for ten months" is used. Here, the elision of the letter *ś* (in *daśa-śaya*) is to be understood. 17.130: "O divine waters, O Sarasvatīs, you have fashioned this embryo with strength and vigor. May the unharmed, living soul enter the living womb. O sesame-seed, descend like a lotus-petal—do not be fleshy, nor be thin. [May it settle] in the marrow, in the joints, in the bones, and in the sinews. May the speckled placenta come out for the dog to eat."

Regarding the word *āyamanī*: they say that the root *yam* is used in the sense of drawing or pulling, as in the example "āyaṃsta pādam" (he drew his foot). O *āyamanīs*! O *āyamanīs*! You who draw forth the embryo, do you cause it to be drawn forth (*yamayata*). Here too, the elision of the prefix *ā-* is to be understood. "Cause it to be drawn forth," i.e., pull it out, O embryo! O sinless ones! O goddesses! O divine ones! O Sarasvatīs—those belonging to the rivers such as the Sarasvatī and others! Let the embryo come; let it proceed. Regarding the sprinkling with water while reciting the *yajus* formula "tiladve" during the downward delivery along with the placenta: this is a name for the placenta (*jarāyu*).

"O thou who art full of fat (tilade)! Fall down, fall down! For you are not flesh, nor fat, nor even the belly. [Note: there is no distinction between *ra* and *la*. You are full of fat (sthavitrī), having become thick and indeed unimpaired, fall down! You are not bound within the muscles (*māṃsa*), you are not bound within the sinews (*srāvadhakṣu*), nor are you bound within the veins (*sirāsu*), nor are you bound within the marrow (*majjā*) which is the essence of the bones. The meaning is: let there be no attachment to the flesh and other parts even by a single portion. "Go forth! (niraitu).

Let it go forth, let it come out—the placenta, which is like moss (pṛś), having the form of moss; for *śek* is a name for happiness (*sukha*), and *lo* is a suffix denoting possession. Let the afterbirth come out as if it were a face. For what purpose? To be eaten by a dog, for the sake of a dog’s consumption.
The placenta does not fall from there; [this is] by means of the Ṛg and Yajus verses. This is the coarse form in the eleventh section of the second chapter.

131—"From heaven" (*divaspari*): this is the section (*anuvāka*). "On this day, a thousand..."—then follows the birth-rite (*jātakarma*). He touches the newborn boy with the section beginning "From heaven," which was seen by the seer Vatsapra; that is, the verse beginning *divaspari*. The word *pari* expresses the sense of the ablative case. This Jātavedas, Agni, was first born from heaven, either in the form of the sun or in the form of lightning. From us (*asmatpari*), he was born second, produced from the sacrificer.

"From me you two shall be born in the morning; once you two are born, you shall bring forth progeny"—from such a vision [it is known]. He was born third in the waters in the form of speech (*vāk*). Of what nature? *Nṛmaṇāḥ*: one whose mind (*manas*) is directed toward men (*nṛṣu*) as their benefactor is *nṛmaṇāḥ*. A person of self-mastery (*svādhīḥ*), being one of good meditation (*svādhyānaḥ*), having become one who kindles him incessantly (*ajasramindhānaḥ*), praises (*jarate*) this one who is thus constituted; but the dull-witted do not do so. "We know of thee..."—O Agni! We know thy own natures which are threefold, in three places...

We know, we perceive, the three forms—namely fire, wind, and the sun—which abide in these three places: on earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven. Likewise, those three abodes have been distributed; that is, they are maintained separately. [The change to *bha* follows the rule *hṛgrahorbhaḥ* in the Vedic language. They are spread out in many ways—that is, in various manners—as the *gārhapatya*, *āhavanīya*, and other sacrificial fires.

Thus has your supreme name entered into the cave, hidden and unknown by those who do not know the Veda. Since it is such as this: "From heaven was born your first [birth], O Agni; the second from Jātavedas; the third in the waters, he whose mind is set on man. The pious one, kindling him, praises him unceasingly. "O Agni, you know the three triads in three ways; you know the dwelling that is spread out in many places."

We know your name; we also know that very name from which you have come—that Immovable One (*acyuta*). *Utsa* means a spring or fountain, and since it is the source of waters, it indicates the place of origin. "In the ocean... [so it is said].

O Agni! Varuṇa, whose mind is intent upon men—that is, whose heart is devoted to bestowing grace upon men—kindles you who abide within the ocean and the waters in the form of the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*). Likewise, in the udder of heaven—the cloud or the solar orb which serves as the udder of the celestial world—he kindles you, the "beholder of men" (*nṛcakṣas*), through his constant observation of all beings. Who, then, is this? It is Sūrya; for he is the witness of all actions, and it is he who kindles you.

Likewise, in the third realm, the world of heaven—of what nature?—in the womb (*yoni*) of *ṛta*, that is, water or truth; you, who abide in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) in the form of lightning as the place of your birth, were perceived by the *mahishas*, the great ones. The root *hi* means "to go," and roots meaning "to go" also mean "to understand. They understood. The suffix *laṭ* indicates the present tense.

"The forest fire has been praised; it has cried out. It cried out, it cries out like a wild beast, like thundering Parjanya, like the sky. [The nominative case is used here in the sense of the locative. "In the light of heaven, upon the earth"—*kṣām* is a name for the earth. At the time of the *padapāṭha*, the word *vasu* [is used] as a Vedic archaism; this form, lacking its case-ending, serves the purpose of the accusative. "Licking the earth," that is, tasting it. "O Ocean, you who are manly-minded, you who look within the waters, I have kindled you at the summit of heaven, at the udder of the sky. Standing in the third realm, like a driver controlling a chariot, licking the earth, you anoint the plants."

This is the eleventh section of the second chapter. (Verse 133): "Burning the ground," is the meaning. "Smearing the shrubs"—that is, moving thoroughly over them, or alternatively, consuming them for the purpose of eating. Furthermore—"Jajñānaḥ" means born; as soon as he was born in the forest, "sadyaḥ" (immediately), at that very moment, "iddhaḥ" (kindled) and blazing, "vyakhyat. Here, by a grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*), the agentive suffix is used in the sense of the object. He is "vikhyāyate"—he is specifically seen even by those situated at a distance. "Im" is an expletive used to fill the meter. Between heaven and earth, he has shone with "bhānunā"—with your radiance—and he shines forth intensely on all sides.
"Uśik"—from the root *vaś*, "uśika" means one who desires or one who is desirable;

he is the purifier (*pāvaka*), the cleanser (*śodhayitā*), the one who moves (*arati*), and the one of excellent wisdom (*sumedhāḥ*) among mortals, that is, among men or in the world of men. O Agni, you who are immortal (*amṛta*), whose nature is deathlessness, have been established (*nidhāya*) as the Gārhapatya and other fires.

And that [verb] *iyarti* (he sends forth) requires the word *ut* to be supplied as will be mentioned later: he sends up, he causes to rise, the ruddy smoke—this is a name for the great; that is, the great *rocana*, or the light. What? The world. For he who causes this smoke to rise becomes a cloud and rains; and the stability of the world depends upon rain. With his bright, shining, glowing luster—that is, with his splendor—he reaches toward, or illuminates, the sky (*dyām*). There is a change of gender: *inakṣat*. The root *nakṣ* has the sense of pervading; the vowel *i* is a secondary suffix (*upasarjana*).

"Of the universe... [The verse continues: "The banner of the universe, the knower of all, born of the world, he, the most excellent sacrificer, has looked upon the two worlds with his light; the immortal one has been established as the foremost of lights. Bearing aloft the ruddy smoke, he sends it upward; with his bright flame, he has gazed toward heaven. "The banner of the universe"—[this occurs] in the *Bhūta-nātasya* section of the *Savyākhyānaikānnikāṇḍa*. Agni, in the form of Vaiśvānara, is the embryo of the born world. Being such, even as he is being born, he fills and pervades the two worlds (*rodasī*) with his own splendor.

Furthermore, "vīram" means "courageous," and "vīḷu" is a name for that which is firm—meaning even a firm *adri*, whether a cloud or a mountain, he strikes down and shatters as he goes forth, moving away. When people—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth—worship him (*ayajanta*), that is, worship him while taking up the oblation (*havir*), then he goes forth, having shattered even the Paveta mountains and so on; this is the meaning. Regarding "śrīṇām": he is the generous one, the one who causes prosperity to rise, the giver of riches (*śrī*).

The supporter of riches (*dharuṇo rayīṇām*), the sustainer of wealth; the bringer (*prāṣaṇaḥ*)—one who causes to reach—the objects of the senses for those possessing wisdom and intellect (*manīṣāṇām*); the protector of Soma (*somagopāḥ*), the guardian of the Soma; [the term] *vasoḥ* is used in the genitive case with the sense of the nominative (as is the reading in the Rigveda). He is the excellent (*vasuḥ*) son of strength (*sūnuḥ sahasaḥ*). *Sahas* is a name for power (*vala*); he is the son of power, born from the churning of strength through the vital breath (*prāṇāt*). He is the king in the waters, shining within the waters, in the form of lightning or as the submarine fire (*vaḍabā*).
He shines forth at the approach of dawn, kindled here by the three Agnihotras.
"Whoever [offers] to you... O God! O Foremost! O Auspicious One! O Radiant One!

Whatever person today prepares for you a cake mixed with clarified butter and a sacrificial oblation (*puroḍāśa*), his embryo, being brought forth, shall fill the two worlds. Even the firm mountain, when Agni goes forth, the five tribes of men worship as he departs.
He is the bestower of glory, the supporter of riches, and the impeller of inspired thoughts.

The protector of the hymn, the son of Vasu, the victorious one, shines as king within the waters, kindled at the forefront of the dawns. Whoever today should perform [this] for you—O Rudra—he should do so, he should give; [lead] that devotee of the gods toward better, toward more excellent, toward prosperity (*vasīyaḥ*, *śreyaḥ*). Lead him forward, lead him on; the meaning is: cause him to attain prosperity. Lead him toward splendor (*dyumna*)—be it wealth or fame—even further, lead him to greater distinction, O youngest one, O most youthful one!

"Ā tam. O Agni! Grant a share to that giver of the cake among the *śravases*. *Śrava* is a name for food; [grant him a share] in the sacrificial performances (*yogas*) endowed with excellent offerings such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*, at every hymn (*uktha*) being recited—that is, at every recitation (*śastra*). Grant him a share. And by your grace, may he become dear to Sūrya, and may he be dear to food and to you. Furthermore, "with what is born"—the singular is used for the plural—may he cause those who are born, his sons, to shine forth (*udbhinadat*), that is, to attain manifestation.
It burst open with sons who had been born and those yet to be born.

"Tvāmagra" (To you first). O Agni! Following after you day by day, the sacrificing persons have maintained (*dadhire*) all desirable and praiseworthy riches (*viśvā vāryāṇi vasūni*). [The form *dadhire*] is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *dhā*, meaning "to hold" or "to maintain," signifying that they hold or obtain them. "Together with you. Regarding this, they relate an ancient history: formerly, the Asuras, having carried off the cows of the gods, placed them in a mountain fastness and closed the entrance. To him [Agni], who possesses the sacrificial cake (*apūpa*) and the *dhṛtavrata* [the one whose vow is firm], O God Agni... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

Lead him further forward; may he be dear to Sūrya, dear to the quarters. Having known [him], he has shattered the unknown with his knowings. At the beginning, the sacrificing [sages] followed you, O Youthful One; having known all things, the gods went forth with Aṅgiras and Bṛhaspati. Having conquered the Asuras for the sake of the cows and having broken through the mountain-fortress, they brought back the cows. This very thing is here.

"O you who desire the wealth of cattle, the Asuras have fallen away along with your riches. The Uśijas—the wise ones, such as Aṅgiras and others—have opened the cow-stall, which is rich in cattle and densely packed with cows; they have made its door wide open. *Dṛśāna* means being visible, seen even by those standing at a distance; [it refers to] the golden ornament (*rukma*)."

Having the nature of *rocanas* (shining ones), he shone, he blazed with great splendor, as if becoming difficult to behold. For the sake of the life and for the sake of the prosperity of living beings—he who shines, who is radiant—such as he became, or let him be, together with the *vayas* (vital forces) and the *atrāṇi* (sacrificial offerings).

That which the two [worlds] generated—namely, this [fire]—as lightning; for the sky is "suretāḥ," meaning she whose seed is excellent, characterized by rain. (39) With the following *yajus* formula, he places the boy upon his lap with the words, "In him, I... In this boy, I shall nourish (*puṣyāmi*)—that is, I shall cause to flourish and attain—a thousand desires, while increasing and growing, standing under my own control; the meaning is that I shall remain independent. [From] the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikāṇḍa*: 1. "The seekers have opened the cow-filled pen."

"Shining like gold, spreading through the wide atmosphere, he bestows an irresistible life-span and glory. (*Ṛgveda* 4.2.2). Second Prapāṭhaka, Twelfth Khaṇḍa. "I nourish you while growing; I am under my own control. From limb after limb you come together; from the heart you are born. You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns! (11) "Become a stone, become an axe, become unassailable gold.
Then follows the consecration with the mantra: "From limb after limb... [and so on]. [Regarding] union with a woman by one who is powerful...

Through diligent effort, semen is emitted from all the limbs; this is what is meant by the words, "Thou art born from limb after limb. The heart is the seat of desire; therefore, it is mentioned again: "Thou art born forth from the heart. The prefix *adhi* here reiterates the sense of the ablative case. Being such as this, O son, thou art my very self (*ātman*). The word *vai* indicates well-known fact. Therefore, live for a hundred autumns!

Thus ends the eleventh section in the second book of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. [The teacher] smells [the child] on the head: "Become a stone; be firm like a stone. Become an axe; be as unassailable as an axe. Become gold, uncovered by impurity; become austerity."

With that same *hiṅkāra* by which mother cows smell their calves, with that *hiṅkāra* of cattle, I smell you, O [Name], [the name of the lunar mansion being indicated in the vocative case, such as] "O Jhātika," "O Rauhiṇa," and so forth. (From the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa* with commentary: "With the *hiṅkāra* of cattle, I smell you, O [Name]. "May Savitṛ bestow intelligence upon you; may the goddess Sarasvatī bestow intelligence; may the two Aśvins, the gods adorned with lotus-garlands, bestow intelligence upon you."

May Savitṛ bestow intelligence upon you; may he bestow offspring upon you; may he bestow splendor upon you. May Savitṛ bestow intelligence upon you; may he bestow offspring upon you; may Indra bestow power upon you. May Savitṛ bestow intelligence upon you; may he bestow offspring upon you; may Sūrya bestow radiance upon you. I release you from the field-spirit, from the house-spirit, from malice, and from the noose of Varuṇa. I make you sinless before the Brahman. May both Heaven and Earth be auspicious for you. [The recitation] in the right ear is: "May intelligence be yours. May the god Savitṛ bestow intelligence upon you.

Likewise, may the goddess Sarasvatī and the two divine Aśvins—wearing garlands of lotuses (*puṣkarasrajau*)—bestow and establish [wisdom] within you. (The *prāśana* mantras beginning with "In you, wisdom... are self-evident through their recitation. *Bhrājaḥ* means radiance. The mantras for the ritual bathing are: "From *Kṣetrī*, from thee... *Kṣetrī* is an incurable disease. Here, the fifth case-ending is used in place of the fourth. From *Śyāḥ* (dark) pains, from the incurable disease, I release thee. Likewise, from *Nirṛti*, from Nirṛti, I release thee.

May Nirṛti, the presiding deity of the Rākṣasas, Śācas, and others, [protect you]. I release you from the malicious and from those who seek to harm you; likewise, I release you from the noose of Varuṇa. Thus, [you become] sinless. [From the second Prapāṭhaka, Twelfth Khaṇḍa: May these fires be auspicious for you; may Heaven and Earth grant you peace. May the four quarters be favorable to you. Those four divine quarters which Vāyu, Pūṣan, and Sūrya behold.

I place you among them until old age; let consumption depart, let destruction go far away. You have been released from evil; I make you worthy of the Veda for the sake of the sacred knowledge (*brahman*). I make both these, heaven and earth, auspicious for you—the meaning is "I make. "May there be peace for you": may food, together with water, bring you peace and grant you well-being. May heaven and earth, together with the plants, be peaceful. And may the intermediate space, together with the wind, be peaceful for you.

And may those four principal directions be auspicious for you—those divine (daivī) directions belonging to the gods beginning with Indra, whose paths are the wind, and which the sun surveys from all sides. For as long as those directions endure, for that length of time I establish you.
From you, thus established, let consumption (yakṣma), disease, and destruction depart far away, turning their faces back.

"He has been released. This youth has been released from consumption (*yakṣma*) and from misfortune (*durita*). Likewise, he has gone forth; he has been freed here from sin and from calamity (*āpatti*). Likewise, he has been released from the enemy (*druh*), from the snares (*pāśa*), and from destruction (*nirṛti*). He has abandoned them; he has abandoned consumption, misfortune, the enemy, the snares, and destruction. He has abandoned the enemies; he has become one who possesses a pleasant dwelling in the auspicious world of good deeds. "As the gods released the sun, the truth, from darkness and from the grasp [of the demon], so did they release him from sin; even so do I release this man from hereditary disease (*kṣetriya*), from the curse of the *jāmi*, and from the enemy's malice. [This concludes] the section on the single fire (*ekāgnikāṇḍa*) with its commentary.
