Having ascended, being formidable—that is, unassailable—and shining brightly, drive away the enemies.

In the *Savyākhyānakāgnikāṇḍa*: Jña and Dakṣiṇa are in the south; iṣa and ūrja are in the west; Mitra and Varuṇa are in the north. "Dharma is your king-post, Śrī is your pinnacle. While being raised up, he says: "O evil one, whatever sin I, ignorant of the sacrifice, have committed while knowing it—whatever sin has been committed by him during the day, and whatever sin has been committed by him during the night—may all that be removed from me. He consecrates the sacrificial post with the verses beginning with "sammitam" and ending with "brahma ca."

May *brahman*—the class of Brahmins—and *kṣatra*—the class of Kṣatriyas—protect your two eastern pillars, O house! May sacrifice (*yajña*) and sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) protect the southern pillar. May food (*iṣ*) and strength (*ūrj*) protect the western pillar. May Mitra and Varuṇa protect the northern pillar. (The word "pillar" is to be supplied everywhere). May Dharma be the king of your pillars, the principal pillar. [And may] Śrī [be so].

That [stūpa] is the spine. Regarding the phrase "the fire lifts up" (*agnir udharati udvīyamānaḥ*): "O Agni! Being lifted up by me, lift me up from evil. [The change in gender is for metrical reasons. "That evil which I, being ignorant, have done unintentionally, and that which I, being knowledgeable, have done intentionally"—this is the distribution and manifestation of that very evil: "By day, with my foot, I have committed such-and-such evil."

Because it has been stated as "ena," this word denoting action (*kriyāvācaka*) is a qualifier of the mind (*manas*). [The root] *u* means "to dry up" (*śoṣaṇe*); thus, it dries up the agent. From whatever sin or evil (*enas*) has been committed during the night (*rātryām*), release me from all of that, having risen up. Fifteenth Section of the Second Chapter. Release me from that! "I, being well-disposed, enter those dwellings of Indra, which are rich in wealth and provide protection."

"I offer this immortal oblation, which is itself immortal, upon this earth for the winning of immortality; through it, may I win infinite desire—desire which Prajāpati won first. (153) He causes [the bride] to enter the house with the mantra: "Of Indra... The houses of Indra—that is, of the Lord—are mine. The use of the plural in reference to a single [house] is as in the expression "the waters" (*āpaḥ*) or "the wife" (*dārāḥ*). They are "possessing wealth" (*vasumantaḥ*) and "possessing protection" (*varūthinaḥ*). *Varūtha* is also a name for a house, but here it should be understood as referring to a part of the house.

"Possessing those [qualities], with their limbs praised"—[this refers to] those houses; "sumanasaḥ" is a transposition of the case-ending (va canavyatyayaḥ); thus, "I, being well-minded, enter them. He establishes [the offering]: "Amṛtāhutim. I offer this oblation (*āhuti*) which is the cause for attaining immortality (*amṛta*) upon this immortal earth (*pṛthivī*); I establish it for the sake of the eternal victory of immortality (*amṛtatva*). By means of that oblation, may I conquer—that is, may I win—the infinite desire for food.

Whatever desire the first *Prajāpati*, the Golden Embryo (*Hiraṇyagarbha*), conquered—that is why this [fire] is called *Agni Vaiśvānara* on earth, according to the Vedic revelation: "This indeed is Agni Vaiśvānara. Because of the dual and seventh case endings in the scripture, it requires the verb "I offer" (*juhomi*). The mantra for sowing rice and barley is: "O Lord of Food (*annapati*)!"—here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object. "Give us food; give us that which is free from disease (*anamīvam*), which brings health, and which is powerful (*śuṣmiṇaḥ*). *Śuṣma* is a name for strength.
Therefore, give such food as you have for the sake of one who desires it; and protect me, the giver, [from the consequences]. (3.9.17)

20. 154. In the *Savyākhyānaikānnikāṇḍa*, [the verse] beginning with "Gāyatrīnirmāu svāhā" follows. This [verse] begins with "O Lord of Food (*annapati*). "May our heroes be unharmed; let my wealth not be poured away. The Earth has gone to the Earth, the Mother has gone to her Mother. May we abound in sons and cattle. May he who hates us be shattered—[shattered] by the enemy (*riṣaḥ*)! Cause [us] to increase exceedingly. Furthermore, bestow (*dhehi*) nourishment (*ūrja*), food, or strength upon our bipeds and quadrupeds."

At the oven (uddhāna), he brings water-jars [with the mantra], "May they be unharmed" (*ariṣṭā*). May our heroic sons be unharmed, meaning uninjured; and may my wealth not be poured away—that is, let it not be poured out in vain. This refers to the drops being poured. He consecrates the cracked [spot] with the following verse: "The earth" (*bhūmiḥ*). The earth has gone to the earth; the oven, which is a modification of the earth, has returned to its own original nature, the earth.

The mother is the intermediate space; she has gone to the sky situated above, to the mother who is the external space. *Apyathaḥ* means dissolution (*pralaya*). She has dissolved right there; the meaning is that she has become one with it. "And may we be with cattle," that is, may we be abundant. "May he who hates us be split asunder, not the hearth. The oblation mantras begin with *vāstoṣpate*. O Vāstoṣpati! Do you recognize us. The prefix *prati* restates the root meaning of the verb. Recognize us as your devotees.

"O Lord of Food, grant us food that is free from disease and full of vigor. Further those who give to us; bestow strength upon our bipeds and our quadrupeds. (Saṃhitā 4.2.3) ... [End of] the fifteenth section in the second prapāṭhaka.

And having known us as your own, O you who dwell in the house of the mouse, become one who brings health to us. Furthermore—whatever we entreat or beg of you, please us with that; reach us and be gracious. Be a source of well-being (*śam*) for our bipeds and quadrupeds; be a bringer of happiness. "O Lord of the Dwelling (*vāstoṣpati*): with auspicious power (*śagmayā*). [The word *śagmayā* is derived from the root *śak*, meaning "to be capable" or "to help."]

Thus, O you who are named "Bliss"! May we also be able to sit together with your assembly—that assembly which is blissful in form, delightful, joyous, possessed of movement, and moving along the path of the righteous. [The root] *ghas* means "to assemble. The meaning is: "May we enter into and become part of it. *Kṣema* is the preservation of what has been obtained; *yoga* is the acquisition of what has not yet been obtained. The locative case is used here in the sense of the instrumental. [May you] protect us (*naḥ*) by means of *kṣema* and *yoga*. [The suffix] *-avaḥ* is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*). *Varam* is an adverbial modifier of the action.

I have invoked [you] in the most excellent manner. The word *uta* has the sense of "also. The fourth quarter-verse constitutes a separate sentence due to the difference in deities. O Viśvedevas! May you always protect us with blessings.

Homage to you, O Blind One! Whatever we entreat of you, be pleased with that; grant well-being to our bipeds and well-being to our quadrupeds. "O Lord of the Dwelling, may we ever abide in your auspicious protection. Grant us a path that is easy to traverse. Protect us in peace and in exertion; guard us always with blessings. (Saṃhitā 2.4.10) "Be present with cattle and horses, O Indu! May we remain unaging in your friendship. Like a father toward his sons, be gracious unto us."

"O Vāstoṣpati, drive away disease; entering all forms, be auspicious to us in our dwellings! Be auspicious, be auspicious! May he protect us from misfortune! [15] In the *Savyākhyānaikāmikāṇḍa*, verse 2: "O Vāstoṣpati!"—O Lord of the Dwelling! Be for us our protector, our deliverer, and our prosperer. With cattle, with horses, and with wealth—O Indu! (The word *indu* signifies the act of bestowing sovereignty); O Lord! Or [the root *ud*] signifies the act of cutting away [misfortune].

O you who are cut down by the rain! Furthermore—may we be ageless in this friendship characterized by the relationship of the praised and the praiser; that is to say, may our union be undecaying. Why say more? Just as a father delights his sons, so may you delight us. "O Lord of the Dwelling! [Thus ends the verse.]

O Vāstoṣpati! You are the dispeller of *amīvā* (diseases), the destroyer of ailments. Entering—that is, pervading—all forms (*viśvā rūpāṇi*), you become the dispeller of disease by entering those forms employed for the alleviation of illness, such as the forms of physicians, medicines, and so forth. Being thus, may you be our most excellent friend (*sakhā su-sakhīṣu śevaḥ*) among our friends; be so. The sprinkling with a water-pot: "May it be auspicious" (*śivam*). May this dwelling (*vāstu*) be auspicious. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

Thus ends the fifteenth section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. The sixteenth section of the second *prapāṭhaka*: "Kūrkara, sukuṃra, kūrkara—the tetherer of the hair; that which stirs from above, from the third station, from here, from heaven. The dog, the son of Saramā, runs downward from here, looking toward the ocean. These are the mantras for the sprinkling of one seized by the *śvagraha* (dog-seizure): "Kūrkara," etc. Kūrkara, sukuṃra, kūrkara—these are names of the dog (*śvan*).

*Sukūraḥ* means one who makes the sound *sukūkara* very well; such is one kind. Another is *vālabandhalaḥ kūkuraḥ*, a dog that binds others with its tail. Regarding *upariṣṭāt*: from the upper world; the *su* [ending] becomes *luk* by the rule *supāṃ suluk*. He goes (*ejjāya*); the *ja* is a Vedic form for *ya*. He comes (*eyāya*) toward us. From where, from above? From the third heaven from here—from the middle of this world, the third sky, which is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). [The word] *aulava*... [Note: The provided text appears to be a commentary on the Rigveda (10.108.2), explaining the names of two dogs and the movement of the third dog from the heavenly realm.]

*Aulaba* is the offspring of *Ulaba*. The singular number is used because the relationship applies to each individual. The particle *iti* is meaningless here. "Having summoned that dog"—here the present tense (*laṭ*) is used in the sense of the imperative (*loṭ*). The prefix *upa-* has the sense of *apa-*. Thus, "he summoned away" (*apāhvayata*). "In such a way that he goes away from here," so you should utter sounds, O attendants!—meaning those belonging to me. He also summoned away other arrows (*ājīn*), namely the feathers (*parṇān*) of the *ṛji* [reed]. Who, then, are they? They are those which are black at the lower part.

Ulumvala, Urubala, R̥du, and Jai—these four are the sons; such are their names according to the *Anvṛthanī*. Now, she who is the divine dog named Saramā, her offspring is the *sārameya*, the "son of Saramā," another name for the dog (*aparaśvā*). The particle *ha* is meaningless. He runs, he rushes toward the ocean, gazing intently at the mid-air (*antarikṣa*). [The rest of the text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on the preceding section.]

That is the truth which Candra said: "Lie down in the lap. Having lain down in her lap, he went away. He said to you: "I have found (avindam)!"—thus [he said], "I have found" (avibhram). Carrying and holding the *niṣka* and the *rukma* as ornaments, [he said] "at the head of the dogs, prospering, with good heroes"—that is his name.

In response to that, he says: "O Subīriṇa! O Sūjasṛja! Erbha! O Bāla! O Śunaka! O Atibhakṣaka! Release, let loose! O Ekatrātya! O leader among the pack of dogs! These are indeed epithets of Subīriṇa. 'Sṛja' means release; 'visṛja' means let loose; 'chat' is a word used for reviling, just as 'chi' is used in common parlance."

"That is the truth. Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend: the Asuras, having carried off the cows of the gods, established them in a mountain fastness and closed the entrance. Then Indra, having summoned Saramā’s son Suvīriṇa, said to him: "O Suvīriṇa, go and inform the people."

The cows were bound by the Asuras; Indra said to them, "O cows, you are bound; stay! [The root] *spāś* means 'to bind' and 'to touch,' but here it should be understood in the sense of acquisition preceded by binding. Having bound them, acquire them; having bound them and acquired them through that binding, return to Indra. He said to you, O cow, "Stay! (the elision of the visarga is Vedic). Having eaten [them], [this concludes] the sixteenth section of the second chapter.

"Choose a boon," [the father] said. "I choose this very boy as my boon," the son replied, stretching out his arms and speaking with firm resolve: "I shall go to heaven, wearing a golden necklace and a breast-plate, with a beautiful chariot yoked with dogs. O you who possess a beautiful chariot, let the dogs run; O you who possess a beautiful chariot, let them run; O you who possess a beautiful chariot, let one run; O you who possess a beautiful chariot, let the hundred run! That is the truth: Saramā is the mother, Lohita is the father. You have found me. *Hā* is an interjection used to indicate a question; its meaning is "O, son! [Thus he spoke].

Then you said to Indra, "I have found him" (*avidaṃ hi*). "I have found" means "I have obtained"; the particle *hi* indicates acceptance. Indra spoke again: "Choose a boon. And you spoke again: "I choose this boy himself as my boon. "May I oppress the boys," you said. All of that is true, in that you now oppress this child; for you come pressing down upon him, having seized and drawn out his arms, whether crossing the sky or a river, coming from heaven.

And thus it is recited by the followers of the Ṛgveda regarding Saramā: "How did you cross the waters of the Rasā? The Rasā is the celestial river. "Looking down" means looking toward the sky. "Wearing a golden ornament" has already been explained. "That is the truth": that is the truth, namely, that Saramā is your mother by name and Rohita is your father by name; whereas these other dogs—those of yours—are merely some who dwell in the lake (sarasyakāḥ), and they run away together with what is savory (rasena), such as meat and the like.
There is an inversion of the verbal suffix (*lakāra*). Go with faces turned downward. Why? From the third heaven from here.
(Ṛgveda 10.108.1). [End of] Savyākhyānaikānneika 9, 3.

"Chadapehi" [is explained as follows]. This section is concluded. All these are dogs: Teaka, Naśa, Lohita, Dulāhu by name, Pātā, and Manthaka—these are your names. "Chadapehi, Sīsarā, Sārameya; homage be to you, Sīlara! The dogs that have run about like stallions and bulls, do not let them loose. "Chadapehi, Sī, Sārameya; homage be to you, Sīlara! Who, then, are those dogs? They are: Teaka, Sasaramataṇḍa, Tūla, Vitūla, Arjuna, and Lohita—these are the six.

"Your mother is named Dulā and your father is named Manthāka. Our attendant, the carpenter Takṣaka, armed with a wheel and weapons in hand, will strike you properly—he will kill you—so do not cry out and do not approach! These two others, Sīsarama and Sīsara, are the sons of Saramā. He says to them, "Hide yourself!"—"O Sīsarama! O son of a bitch! Go away, depart! O Sīsara! O son of a bitch! Homage be to you!"

The word *sam* is connected with the verb. My horses—stallions capable of raining [semen], powerful ones—should *saṃsīsarīdat*, like feet. There is a transposition of persons (*puruṣavyatyaya*). Let them creep together; let you two creep together; go toward [him]. He replies: [From the second section, sixteenth division of the *Dhānamita*: "O man, look at this! These two are your rivals; these two are equal in strength; both are winners."]

"May Mātariśvan carry you away with his swift wind; may those vital breaths of yours return to you. Do not fear. It was only a dog—a dog that has come here—that bit me. This is the word of reproach. "Do not eat this man"—this is the mantra for consecrating one seized by *kuśaṅgraha*. These [are the words].

These two, well-known as the mothers of the *śaṅkagrahas*, are seen and observed wearing identical garments and having similar forms. Having placed them upon the mortar, I thresh them with a pestle made of *sāra* wood—a solid and firm one. "Hataśśāḍa!"—the *śaṅkha* (conch-demon) or *śaṅkagraha* is slain; the father of the *śaṅkha* is slain. *Śaṅkakuturvaka*: he is a *kuturvaka*—a harmful and contemptible *turvaka*; being both a *śaṅkha* and a *kuturvaka*, he is called *śaṅkakuturvaka*, and he too is slain.

"Has even the master, the owner of these conchs, been killed? With the following verse, he pours water from a water-pot over the head [of the boy]: "The seer Bodha... He whose lineage is Bodhāyana is the seer Bodha. *Prabodha* means awakening; *prabuddhatā* means the state of being awake; *svapra* means sleep; *mātariśvā* is the wind. These—these shall protect (*spariṣyanti*) your vital breaths; therefore you shall not die. So, do not fear, O boy! You shall not die. 162. You shall not die.

"Devoured is Māṅka, devoured is Vitṛṣṭi, devoured is Vyadhvara—Svāhā! Devoured is Vyadhvara, devoured is Maśaṅka, devoured is Vitṛṣṭi—Svāhā! Devoured is Vitṛṣṭi, devoured is Vyadhvara, devoured is Maśāka—Svāhā! (16). "I drive away the father into the mortar"—and five [more]. (16). In the *Savyākhyānakānnikāṇḍa*: "Kill Indra with the *danduśūka* [insect], the one who is *pṛkṣiṇa*, he who is a reptile."

"O Indra, crush all those—the Daikṣṇanta and the Dṛśanta. (1.13) The mantras for the *kiṃśuka* oblation of the "Serpent-force" (*sarpabala*) begin with "jagdha" (eaten). *Jaladhaḥ* means one who has swallowed; it is a serpent named Maśaka. Likewise is *vyadhvaraḥ*. *Vitṛṣṭiḥ* is a serpent. The rest is clear. Thus ends the sixteenth section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. [Regarding] the *samidh* oblation: "Indra... etc.

O Indra! Slay our oppressor—the biting serpent, the bird provided with wing-like sides, and that which is a *sarīsṛpa* (a crawling creature) by nature—whether it is about to bite (*dekṣantam*) or is currently biting (*daśantam*). O Indra! Crush (*jambhaya*) all such beings; paralyze them. [End of the seventeenth section of the second chapter.]

*svāhā!* Born in the waters, grown in the lake, and held in the hand of the gods—O Agni, sent by Indra, do not harm us; *svāhā*. You are the protector from debt, you are the protector from the flood, you are the enclosure. You nourish humans with food, cattle with grass, and all creatures with pits; you protect the gods with sacrifice in the waters. Born in the waters! O you who have grown in the lake in the form of lightning, and in the ocean in the form of the submarine fire (*bāḍaba*), you who are held in the hand of the gods—the particle *api* serves to complete the meter.

O you who have become thus! O foremost one! You perform actions sent by Indra, and we are the devotees of Indra; therefore, do not harm us—meaning, act in such a way that the injury caused by serpents does not befall us. (Manu 3.76) Regarding the phrase "trāṇabhāsī": it is not merely protection, but you are the complete protection, protecting from all sides.

"Obeisance! You are the enclosing-stick (paridhi); you are that which is placed on all sides for protection, and you are indeed that. By means of food, you give birth to men; as fire, you cook the external food and digest what has been eaten in the form of Vaiśvānara. With grass, you protect cattle, for fire produces grass since it is dependent upon rain, as seen in the scriptural statement: 'The oblation cast into the fire [reaches the sun]' and so forth. By means of pits, you protect all beings; a pit is a hole."

For the earth, scorched by the rays of the sun, reveals its cavities, and the sun is as if split apart by food; indeed, having set, he enters into them. And for all serpents that have emerged from their holes, death is certain. Therefore it is said: "By the hole you protect all beings. You protect the gods through sacrifice because you are the bearer of oblations (*havyavāhana*); you protect the ancestors through *svadhā* because you are the bearer of offerings to the ancestors (*kavyavāhana*). Thus, in this manner, [you protect] the Ājyeyas... [or] the ancestors with *svadhā*, [and] the [gods] with *svāhā*.

"That is the truth, for on that [night] of the new moon, in the section concerning the single offering with its commentary, they offer oblations of water and clarified butter. They flow forth into you and enter into you; therefore, from you, grant us safety from the rains. These are the mantras for the offerings of clarified butter—"That is the truth"—wherein the Lord of All is praised. On that night of the new moon and the full moon, humans offer a *bali* of poison; they offer this *bali* for the sake of averting the danger of poison.

And all those serpents that crawl upon the belly—those very ones send forth their tribute from you and pursue it; having reached you, they enter into you and abide by taking refuge in you—this is the meaning of "that which is yours" (*sayam*). Therefore, for the sake of protection, entrust us who dwell in you—that is, us who have you as our refuge—to all those who dwell in you, so that they may not harm us; and entrust us to the rains (*vapābhyaḥ*), for during the rainy season the serpents multiply; this is the entrusting of them specifically.

By means of the season (*ṛtu*), the year (*saṃvatsara*) is indicated. From "from the rains" (*varṣābhyaḥ*), the suffix *ṭā* is used in the sense of "for the sake of. [The meaning is: "In such a way that they may not harm us (*naḥ*) in the course of the year, so do thou entrust us to all [the serpents]. "Salutation be to all serpents" (*namo astu sarpebhyaḥ*): whatever [serpents] there are, however many, who have taken refuge upon the earth (*pṛthivīm anu śritāḥ*), those who have taken refuge in the intermediate space (*antarikṣe*) and those who have taken refuge in heaven (*divi*), salutation be to all those serpents. (5) "Those here" (*ye 'daḥ*): [this refers to] all those [serpents]. There is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending. "Salutation be to those serpents over there (*amuṣmin*) who have taken refuge upon the earth."

And those who are in the intermediate space and those who are in heaven—to those *tarpaṇas*, obeisance! In the seventeenth section of the second *prapāṭhaka*: "Obeisance be to all," thus three [verses]. "Obeisance be to all the seers (*ṛṣis*)—those who are on earth, those who are in the intermediate space, those who are in heaven, and those who are in the sky. To them I shall offer this oblation (*bali*). To them [I offer it] in this radiant place belonging to heaven, or in the rays of the sun, or in the waters where the seat of the serpents has been prepared."

Homage to all those arrows! Regarding the word "yā" (those which): since it is used in grammatical apposition with the word *iṣavaḥ* (arrows), it takes the feminine gender. Homage to all those arrows that belong to the *yātudhānas*, or those that rest upon the trees, or those that lie in pits and holes—to all those arrows, homage! The mantra for the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*) is: "Homage be... Those who are terrestrial (*pārthivāḥ*), existing on the earth; those who are atmospheric (*āntarikṣyāḥ*), existing in the intermediate space.

Regarding the form *bhave*, the suffix *yat* is applied according to the rule *bhave chandasi*; because it is Vedic (*chāndasa*), there is an initial *vṛddhi* strengthening. To those who are divine (*divyāḥ*), existing in heaven (*divi bhavāḥ*), and to those who are directional (*diśyāḥ*), existing in the quarters (*dikṣu bhavāḥ*), to all of them, to the serpents (*sapebhyaḥ*), let there be [this offering]; I shall take this oblation (*balim*) for them. Thus: "To those who are in the bright realm of heaven, or those who are in the rays of the sun; those whose dwelling (*sardaḥ*) is made in the waters—to those who are to be satisfied, obeisance. "Those who are the spirits (*irṣavaḥ*) of the sorcerers (*yātudhānānām*), or those who are in the trees (*vanaspatiṣu*); or those who lie in pits (*avaṭeṣu*)—to all of them, obeisance. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā)

(Śaṅkhāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.2.8) 166. "O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, O Ārāvat, O Takṣaka Vaiśāleya, these living beings of ours have come to you; do not deliver them to the Sadryas or to the rains. O Ahi Sātivala, these living beings of ours have come to you; do not deliver them to the Sadryas or to the rains. [This concludes] the *Atisavyākhyāna-kāśmakāṇḍa*, up to the Mārgaśīrṣya. But from those [spirits], I have taken this away during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.

10. *Valaṃ* 2: The mantra for attendance begins with "O Takṣaka! O Takṣaka! This is a specific qualification. "O Vaiśāleya!"—O offspring of Viśālā! "Dhṛtarāṣṭrāirāvata"—this is the name of a serpent; Dhṛtarāṣṭra who is also Airāvata. That serpent named Airāvata is your life-force (*jīva*), your vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The plural number is used because of the multiplicity of the vital breaths. The serpent called Airāvata is your life-force. It has already been understood that "he dwells within you. The specific distinction is: "for the sake of the living beings dwelling within you."

"Thus, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Rāvata, Takṣaka, Vaiśāleya! These living beings are yours," and so forth. By these two mantras, there is a mutual entrustment (*paridāna*) between the two. Regarding "O Ahiṃsa": that is indeed named Ahiṃsa. Likewise, "O Atibala! [the mantra says], "O Ahiṃsa! These living beings of yours are exceedingly powerful," and so forth; and also, "O Atibala! These living beings of yours are harmless," and so forth. Here too, there is a mutual entrustment. Regarding "Those which": those snakes (*dandaśūka*) that are on the earth—addressing the King of Snakes (*sarparāja*), he says, "I have taken them from here, from this house, beyond the distance of a *gavyūti*."

The seventeenth section of the second chapter. "Entrust us to the rains! Those biting serpents that dwell upon the earth—drive them away from here beyond the distance of a *gavyūti*. There are indeed those with feet like hooves, there are those with staves; let them not lead you toward us, nor do you drive us out from here. The pasture named *Samīcī* faces eastward; its extent is two *krośas*. Beyond that, settle them! He says 'there are' regarding every single one of them. *Vai* is used in the sense of what is well-known."

In our house, may those hoofed animals—oxen and the like—that might trample you, and those staff-bearing men with sticks in their hands who might strike you, neither those hooved ones nor those with staffs in their hands shall harm (*hinásāt*) you; they shall not harm you at all. [The *yakāra* is a Vedic form. You must not harm us; if you do not harm us, then they too shall not harm you—this is the meaning.

The fifth *lakāra* (the imperative mood) is used in the sense of a formal agreement (*upasaṃvāda*). A formal agreement is a verbal instruction or a binding contract regarding what must be done. [The mantra says: "Thou art Samīcī by name. This means: "Thou art the eastern direction named Samīcī; since thou art the eastern direction, thou art Samīcī by name."

Of that [direction] Agnidhipati is the lord. ("The eastern direction is named Samīcī; of that, Agnidhipati is the lord—[that is,] he who is the overlord and he who is the protector—to those two, salutation! May they both be gracious to us. Whom we hate and whoever hates us, him I place within the jaws of you two. 1.68, with commentary from the Ekāgnikāṇḍa). He is named Asita; he is the protector, he who is the overlord, and Agni is the guardian—he is Asita. To those two, salutation! May they both be gracious to us, may they bring us happiness.

This much [of the mantra] is performed indirectly (*parokṣakṛta*) because of its connection with the third person (*prathamapuruṣa*). The remainder is performed directly (*pratyakṣakṛta*) because of its connection with the word *vām* (you two). "We, who hate whom, and he who hates us—him, that man, I place in your jaws. The singular number is used for the plural; "in the jaws," meaning in the teeth. There is a change of verbal number (*vacanavyatyaya*); "I place" (*dadhāmi*) means "we place" (*dadhmaḥ*), i.e., we set him there for the purpose of devouring. Regarding "Ojasvinī" and so forth: everywhere, the lords are well-known. The protectors are the serpents (*sarpa*).

The phrase "rakṣitā" (the protector) and so forth is to be supplied throughout all [the following]. Ojasvinī is the name of the southern direction; its lord is Indra, and the viper (*pṛdākū*) is its protector. Prācī is the name of the eastern direction; the goat (*svaja*) is its protector. Avasthāvā is the name of the intermediate direction; the transverse line (*tiraścīnarājī*) is its protector. Adhipatrī is the name of the white (*śvitra*) direction; the bear (*rīkṣa*) is its protector. Vaśinī is the name of the spotted-necked (*kalmāṣagrīva*) direction; the spotted-necked one is its protector. Bṛhatī is the name of the upward direction (*ūrdhvā dik*). This [verse] is as follows: "Ojasvinī is the name of the southern direction; its lord is Indra, and the viper is its protector... I establish."

"Thou art named Prācī; the eastern direction is thine; Soma is thy overlord, Svaja is thy guardian... I place [thee]. Thou art named Avasthāvān; the southern direction is thine; Varuṇa is thy overlord... Thou art named Adhipatrī; the western direction is thine; Bṛhaspati is thy overlord, Citra is thy guardian... I place [thee]. The seventeenth section of the second prapāṭhaka. 169. 'The twelve cycles are named Ṛtvidhetayaḥ. 'The upward direction, the downward direction. 'Asita and the others are conventional (rūḍhi) terms.'"

They should be applied in whatever way is appropriate. Here, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* and the *ap* affix have not been applied because they belong to the Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage. The "weapons" (*heti*) are indeed the *sthapati*s (chieftains). Some say they are the Gandharvas. [The mantra says: "You are indeed weapons; yours are the houses in the eastern direction; fire is your arrows. *Salila*, *sagara*, *gaṅkara*, *samudra*, *avasvān*, and *nimiṣa*—these six are all names for the sky (*ākāśa*). Their etymologies, however, may be explained in any suitable manner.

The winds are the eaters of water. Of that wind, this quarter is named *Vaśinī*; its overlord is Yama; its protector is Kalmāṣagrīva... I place [him] within you. "Your names are *Hetayaḥ* (Weapons); *Iṣavaḥ* (Arrows) are your front; *Gṛhāḥ* (Houses) are your head; *Agniḥ* (Fire) is your vigor; *Salilaḥ* (the Water) is your name. To them, I bow; do not strike us. Whomever we hate, and whoever hates us—him I place within your jaws.

"Ye are named *Nilimpas*; for you, O Fathers, I assign the southern caves as your dwellings, and *Sagara* as your wind-name. Ye are named *Vañcins*; for you, O Fathers, I assign the western caves as your dwellings, and *Gahvara* as your wind-name. With white feet, I strike [the enemy] from the front and from behind. And seven, O Manu!

The wind is established as "nameless" because it originates from space (*ākāśa*). It is neuter in gender because it begins with a common [non-specific] term. Homage to you, those destructive powers (*haiti*). May you grant us happiness and comfort. As for him whom we hate and whoever hates us—him I place within your jaws, in your teeth. There is an inversion of case endings; thus, *dadhmaḥ* [is used instead of *dadhāmi*]. By this, the five subsequent mantras are explained. And the phrase beginning with "O Wind, nameless" is to be supplied everywhere.

"Ye are the *nilimpas*, the whirlwind named after the wind; ye are the *vatriṇas*, the hollow named after the wind; ye are the *avasthāvānas*, the ocean named after the wind; ye are the *adhipatis*, the downward-blowing named after the wind; ye are the *kravyās*, the blinking one named after the wind.
Having returned, [he performs] the sprinkling of the house with the mantra: "Away, O white one! This is the *cata* [rite].

The Lord of the Storms (*sapaṇiāmadhipatiḥ*). O Śveta! Drive away, destroy with your foot (*padā* = *pādena*). "Ye are the 'Abodes' by name; among you I place the Northern Quarter, the Waters, and the Arrow named Vāta. Ye are the 'Lords' by name; above you I place the House, the Rain, and the Arrow named Arvāsvān, [the Wind] named Vāta... I place. The three 'Arrows', the 'Blinkers', [the Wind] named Vāta... I place. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.10). This is the eighteenth section of the second chapter.

171. And there are three *ṣīrimā* verses concerning royal kinsmen (*rājarbandhu*). "He indeed did not slay anyone during his conduct at Śveta" (*na vai śvetasyāṃ dhyācāre'hni jaghāna kaṃcana*); [this refers to] Śveta Ārya Vaidarbha. There are two verses for the *diśyā* [section] concerning royal kinsmen (*rājarbandhu*). "You are the Supreme Being (*parameṣṭhin*); lead me to supreme glory" (*paramāṃ mā śriyaṃ gamaya*). "With the front foot and with the hind foot" (*pratyavaṃ pūrveṇa ca padā apareṇa ca*). This is said in the state of walking, for in that state there are indeed the front and hind feet.

He states what is to be removed: there are seven species of serpents belonging to the Brahmins—one *tila* [unit] for Brahmins, two for Vaiśyas, and two for Śūdras; and three belonging to royal kinsmen—that is, three related to kings—making ten species of serpents. Or rather, not so: in the case of the conduct of Śveta, the king of the Nāgas, it is *ādhi*...

The serpent *ahi* did not indeed kill any person whatsoever; therefore, homage to Śveta, the son of Vidarva! The repetition is for the sake of emphasis: "Homage to Śveta, the son of Vidarva! Thus, in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta: "Having formed the remains of the *āgrayaṇa* offering into a ball, [he places it] on the roof-peak of the house with the *yajuṣ* formula beginning 'ud divaḥ,' and with 'parameṣṭhy asī.'"

O lump of water! You are the Supreme; you are now established in the highest place. Lead me to supreme prosperity. The winter has descended upon us. I am firmly established in the ruling power (*kṣatra*), I am firmly established in the kingdom (*rāṣṭra*), I am firmly established among the horses, I am firmly established among the cattle, I am firmly established in my offspring, and I am firmly established in what is to come. Here is stability, here is support, here is delight, here is enjoyment. O Earth, be pleasant to us, as you are for the mountains.
[This concludes] the descent for winter: "He has descended," it is said. By us—by us, the winter... [has descended].
The winter season has descended; [the meaning is] that we descend to the earth in order to lie down upon a new layer of grass for the sake of the winter season. Thus it is said:
"The mantras for lying down" begin with *pratikṣatre*. Lying down upon the new layer of grass...

The meaning is: "I shall firmly establish myself among the Kṣatriyas and others. *Bhavyam* means auspiciousness. On this sacrificial bed (*svastara*), there is *dhṛtiḥ* (steadfastness), *prītiḥ* (affection), *vidhṛtiḥ* (sustenance), *svadhairyam* (self-composure), *rāntiḥ* (tranquility), *ratiḥ* (delight), and *ramatiḥ* (sporting with sons and others). With the next two [verses], he touches the earth: "O Earth, be pleasant (*syonā pṛthivi*). This has been explained. "Baḍittha..."—*baṭ* means truth; *itthā* means in this way, by the manner about to be described. You bear, maintain, and effect the *rivadraṃ*—the fissure, the opening, or the breaking—asunder of the mountains and the clouds.

"O Earth! O Ground! O thou who art vast! O thou who art full of slopes!"—this mantra (150) is written on the leaf. (9) "Thus, O Earth, thou bearest the hollow of the mountains; thou, O Ground, full of slopes, dost expand with thy greatness. (Ṛgveda 2.3.12). This is the eighteenth section of the second prapāṭhaka. [The verses] numbered 178 are two: "May the wise bay horses carry thee hither, together with the white-hued steeds, to the mountain that bestows joy."

O Vāta, come with the Añjīs; may Śarva touch our oblations. Svāhā! May he touch Mīḍhvān; svāhā to Mīḍhvas! Svāhā! May he touch Mīḍhuṣī; svāhā to Mīḍhuṣī! Svāhā! May he touch Jayanta; svāhā to Jayanta! Svāhā! To the god Bhava, svāhā! Svāhā! To the god Śarva, svāhā! Svāhā! To the god Īśāna, svāhā! Svāhā! To the god Paśupati, svāhā! Svāhā! To the god Rudra, svāhā! Svāhā! To the god Ugra, svāhā! O Bhīma, by your own greatness you cause them to rejoice—you satisfy whom? The gods.

"O Earth! O Great One! By means of herbs and animals, the gods are worshipped, and by them the kings; those satisfied gods split the clouds for the sake of raining. In this manner, you sustain the hollows of the mountains. Then follows the *īśānabali*. He invokes Īśāna with the verse beginning, "Come hither... (*ā tvā*).

Let the bay horses, green-colored and of one mind, knowing your intention, carry you; come with white horses that possess banners, joined with a standard and flag, swift as the wind—[the root] *aja* meaning "to go" or "to throw"—come with the speed of the wind. For what purpose? For my oblation (*havya*), for the enjoyment of my sacrificial offering (*havis*). O Śarva!

He causes [the sacrificer] to touch the rice-oblation, saying: "May he touch it"—that is, may he accept it. Regarding the term *mīḍhvān*: the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*) say it is Rudra, the one who dwells in the intermediate region (*madhyamasthāna*), the nourisher. The followers of the Purāṇas (*paurāṇikāḥ*) say it is the essence (*sattā*) of his own power, which is the material cause of the universe. To that *mīḍhvan*—regarding *mīḍhuṣī*, the etymologists say she is Vāk, the wife of Rudra, who dwells in the intermediate region; the followers of the Purāṇas say she is the form of the reflection of the universe. "Oṃ svāhā to the god! Svāhā to the great god! Svāhā to the wife of the god Kṣava! Svāhā to the wife of the god Śarva! (174)

"Oblation to the leaf of the god Śāna; oblation to the leaf of the god Paśupati; oblation to the leaf of the god Rudra; oblation to the leaf of the god Agni; oblation to the leaf of the god Bhīma; oblation to the leaf of the great god; oblation to Jayanta—these are the eight [offerings]. To her, the bountiful one (Mīḍhuṣī). Jayanta is Skanda; to him [is the offering]. Bhava and the others are the eight forms of the Blessed One. And they are: Water, Earth, Wind, Fire, Sun, and the Initiated (Dīkṣita) as well."

"Ākāśa," "Candra," and these three are known as the presiding deities (adhiṣṭhātṛ). Such is the method of the Purāṇas. Alternatively: he brings beings into existence (*bhāvayati*), thus he is *Bhava*—the causative sense being inherent. He is the creator of the entire world. *Śarva* is the destroyer; from the root *śṝ*, meaning "to injure. *Īśāna* is the Lord of all. *Paśupati* is the protector of "paśus"—both bipeds and quadrupeds. *Rudra* is the one who causes weeping at the time of dissolution. *Ugra* is the unconquerable.

"His kingdom becomes fierce and unshakable. [This is] because of his being known and seen. He is "Bhīma" (the Terrifying) because all beings are afraid of him; he is "Mahān" (the Great) because he is greater than all. The names beginning with "Bhavasya devasya" (of the god Bhava) are also understood by this same principle.
The *sviṣṭakṛt* mantra is "O Agni... Rudra is the *sviṣṭakṛt*. This is the eighteenth section of the second chapter.

To the fulfiller, Svāhā! May he of full countenance step forward for our well-being. "Touch the Gṛhapas, Svāhā to the Gṛhapas! "Touch the Gṛhapyas, Svāhā to the Gṛhapyas! "Touch the Ghoṣins, Svāhā to the Ghoṣins! "Touch the Śvāsins, Svāhā to the Śvāsins! "Touch the Vicinvats, Svāhā to the Vicinvats! "Touch the Samadbhas, Svāhā to the Samadbhas! "Touch the Devasenās, Svāhā to the Devasenās! [Those] who are named and those who are unnamed... 38.

He offers what is well-offered; thus he is the "well-offerer. To that Agni, who brings about the fulfillment and increase of the oblations and desires, or who causes them to reach their goal—Brāhmaṇa 3.7.9.

"Upasthānaṃ svāstana iti": O God, with these oblations, may you stride forth and move about so that there may be well-being (*svāstana*) for us. "Parṇadānaṃ gṛhapa iti": He who protects the house is the *gṛhapa* (house-protector) god, as seen in the scriptural passage: "*Namo rudrāya vāstoṣpataye*" ("Salutation to Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling"). Or, the *gṛhapa* of the god is the protector of the dwelling—namely, Nandīśvara Kumāra. O *gṛhapa*, O house-protector! Touch this offering; I give it to you, the house-protector, with the cry of *svāhā*.

Gṛhapi is the wife of the householder (gṛhapati). O Gṛhapi! "Ghoṣiṇaḥ" means those possessing sound; "śvāsinaḥ" means those possessing breath. "Vicinvantaḥ": the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *vi-* has the sense of searching; thus, they are searching.

In the *Prapāṭhaka* 176, within the section on the single-stanza hymns (*ekānikāṇḍa*), the *Devasenā* (the Army of the Gods) is proclaimed: "To the *Urpaspṛś* [those who touch from afar], to the *Devasenās*, Svāhā! To the *Dvārā* [the gatekeepers], to the *Urpaspṛś*, to the *Dvārās*, Svāhā! To the *Dvārā* [the gatekeepers], to the *Urpaspṛś*, to the *Dvārās*, Svāhā! To the *Anvāsārin* [the followers], to the *Urpaspṛś*, to the *Anvāsāras*, Svāhā! To the *Niṣaṅgin* [the quiver-bearers], to the *Urpaspṛś*, to the *Niṣaṅgins*, Svāhā! Those who bow down, those who purify, those who come together, and those who move in unison—these are all the hosts of the God.

O divine armies! Touch [this water]; to you, the divine armies, svāhā! Those who are mentioned in this collection of mantras, and those who are not mentioned—those are you, O divine armies. O gatekeepers of the god! O female gatekeepers of the goddess! The *anvāsāriṇas* are also his attendants, appointed over the inner apartments. O quiver-bearer! O bow-case bearer! This is an address to Jayanta. [As it is said: "He hangs the carrying-net on the tree, saying: 'Homage to the quiver-bearer!'"

*Ipudhi* and *niṣaṅga* are synonyms; however, here *niṣaṅga* refers to the place where weapons other than arrows are kept. This much alone is the *yajus*, and it is not a citation of the opening words (*pratīka*) of that which is recited among the Rudras. If it were indeed so, one would have said: "The formula 'Homage to the quiver-bearer, the arrow-holder'. For example, as in: "The verse beginning with 'āśāsāna' [is for the waters], and the verse beginning with 'tat savitur vareṇyam' [is for Sūrya]. Here, one should mutter the Rudras. The Rudras have been explained elsewhere. Regarding the mantra for the worship of the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*), beginning with "of the field": "May we, by the Lord of the Field..."

With [the help of] Mitra and others who are indeed well-wishers, we conquer what is to be conquered; and may that Kṣetrapati be the nourisher of our cattle and horses—there is a change of gender [in the original], meaning he is the nourisher and the guardian of the door, and his followers. (1-2-7, 2-4-13)

In the second prapāṭhaka, the eighteenth section (177): "To the one with the quiver, to the one with the arrow-case... two verses beginning with "We [worship] the Lord of the Field. (18) "Parameṣṭhyati" [refers to] the eight supreme [verses]. (18) The word "ā" is used for conjunction; this [deity] has the action of "mṛḍ" as his function—meaning he is one who brings happiness (*sukhakarmā*). When such an action is performed, he would "mṛḍāti"—that is, he would cause happiness. O Lord of the Field! [Grant us] the wave (*ūrmi*) rich in honey—that is, endowed with the sweet taste of milk and so forth—the collection of cows.

Its qualifiers are "flowing with honey" (*madhuśruta*) and "well-purified like clarified butter" (*ghṛtam iva supūtam*). There may be something that possesses honey but does not flow with it, such as a sturdy jar; there may be something that flows with honey but does not possess honey, such as a hole in a honey-vessel.

Therefore, the two phrases "full of sweetness" (*madhumantam*) and "flowing with sweetness" (*madhuśrutam*) are employed; just as one might say "full of honey," "flowing with honey," and "possessing honey," so too [the ghee] is characterized by both qualities. Like clarified butter (*ghṛtam*), it is well-purified (*supūtam*), thoroughly cleansed by means of cloth and other filters. Being thus prepared, milk this out for us from the udder of the cows—pour it forth like a cow pouring milk, just as a cow yields her milk. Furthermore, through your grace, may we attain the mastership of *ṛta*, the sacrifice; may they show mercy to us and grant us happiness.

Thus ends the eighteenth section in the commentary on the Ekāgnikāṇḍa composed by Śrī Haradatta. "Like a well-plowed field, we win the Lord of the Field; may he, who nourishes cattle and horses, be gracious to us for our protection. O Lord of the Field, milk for us a wave rich in sweetness, as a cow yields her milk—sweet-flowing, well-purified ghee, the essence of Truth. May the Lords of Truth be gracious to us. (Saṃhitā 1.1.14). "That which my mother, following her own inclinations, caused me to be confused while she wandered..."

"May my grandfather choose that seed for me; let it not perish, and let another descend upon such-and-such [person]. Svāhā! Those who stand, those who run, those who have come from afar, and those who dwell around—the waters, with all their threefold powers, have brought me away; I have set aside the sin of my father for such-and-such [person]. Svāhā! That which my grandmother, following her own will, has lusted after while she wanders—may my grandfather choose that seed for me; let it not perish, and let another descend. [The *Śrāddha-homa* mantras begin: "That which my mother... [and so forth].

As for that seed belonging to another which my mother, being unfaithful and unyielding toward her husband, wandered about and intensely desired—this is said because even among virtuous women, mental transgression is possible. May my father seize and take that seed for himself, so that there may be no confusion of seed caused by such mental deviation.

"Ābhu" means "he who has become manifest. By this much [of a name], may no other person, manifesting toward me as a father, descend upon me; let him be one whose hope is in vain, and let him not obtain the oblation (*havis*) being given by me. *Svāhā* to that [name] of my father Yajñaśarman! "That which my grandfather... and so forth, as before. "Yā" (those which...)—[as follows].

The waters stand in tanks and the like, those that flow in rivers, and those that are *paritasthūṣīḥ*—those standing all around; they are *ādrotriyaḥ*, meaning they move toward the moist regions such as the banks and so forth. With those waters, which are the mothers of the universe (*viśvastha-bhartṛbhiḥ*), I exclude (*antardadhe*) from this rite another father who has come here as a claimant of a share; I place him out of reach. The rest is explained.
[End of] the nineteenth section of the second chapter.

"O my great-grandmother," and so forth, as before. Regarding "I place between": *ṛtu* and the others are well-known. [The meaning is] "among *ṛtu* and the others. By means of these, I place another person between [myself and] my great-grandfather. "May it be offered to such-and-such; Svāhā! I place [him] between by means of the mountains, between the great earth, and between these infinite directions; I place another person between [myself and] my grandfather for such-and-such; Svāhā!"

"Whatever my great-grandmother, being infatuated, moved about following [another's] vow—that seed of mine may my great-grandfather take; let no other fall upon it. To such-and-such, Svāhā! I have placed a barrier between [him and her] by means of the seasons, days and nights, the junctions, the half-months, and the months; I have placed another barrier between [her] and my great-grandfather. To such-and-such, Svāhā! Those ancestors who are here and those who are not here, whom we know and whom we do not know—you know them all, O Agni Jātavedas. With that *svadhā* offering, [do thou satisfy them]."

"I concealed him" means: I concealed [him] from the mountains, such as Meru and others; from the great earth; and from these directions—east and so forth—which are infinite in terms of space and time, being hidden from all quarters. "I concealed him who is other than the Grandfather. "And their very junctions": those ancestors who abide here in this world, and those who do not abide here, and those whom we know—that is, we recognize—and those whom we do not know (the particle *u* is expletive). I concealed him from all of them.

O Agni! O Jātavedas! If you [accept] the *svāhā* offering... *svāhā* to the Father! To the Father, *svāhā*! "To the Father, *svāhā*! "To the Father, *svāhā*! "Svadhā, *svāhā*! To Agni Kavyavāhana, *svadhā*, *svāhā*!

"This honeyed, swelling wave, resonant with *svara*, as great as heaven and earth are—of that [heaven] this is the measure; so much of that measure do I give to you, so that it may be for my father inexhaustible and undecaying. As it is for him, so let it be for me: *svadhā*. Live on together with them upon that *svadhā* food, O Great One! This honeyed, swelling wave, resonant with *svara*... of that [Vāyu] this is the measure; so much of that measure do I give to you, so that Vāyu may be inexhaustible... *svāhā*."

"To the father, [belongs] the foremost of the ancestors. You know them; you understand them. To them, do you yourself present [the offering] as is appropriate. And they shall eat with that. There is a change of gender and case-ending [in the text]. "May they rejoice with the offered *svadhā*; may they be satisfied"—these and other such phrases are established by the *nigama* (Vedic recitation). "Kavyavāhana" [is the deity].—"One should touch all the food with the subsequent [mantra]: 'O father! This is your wave (*ūrmi*), possessed of waves, rich in honey, endowed with honey and other [flavors], full of essence, an ocean of *svadhā*. And this...'"

That [offering] should be considered small, because: "As great as fire and earth are in extent, so great is my grandfather's inexhaustible, unfailing greatness. This honeyed wave of yours, O Great-grandfather, is full of vigor and sweet. As great as the sun and the sky are, so much is its measure; so much of that measure do I give to you, so that it may be for me as inexhaustible and unfailing as the sun. (Second Prapāṭhaka, Nineteenth Khaṇḍa)

"O Grandfather, may you be inexhaustible and undecaying; *svadhā* be for such-and-such, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*—and one [offering]. (19) The measure and extent of this [food] is just that much; I give this much measure to you. Then he says in response: "Just as the fire, once kindled, is never deficient and is undecaying—free from consumption—so too, O Grandfather, may you be inexhaustible and undecaying for my father; may you become *svadhā*, the food of the ancestors."

Now it is said in response to the father: "O Father, you shall subsist upon that *svadhā* together with those [offerings] beginning with the *agrāyaṇa*. Although fire and earth are the two primary elements (*prakṛti*), nevertheless, by the use of the plural "those" (*taiḥ*), the sense of "beginning with" (*ādi*) is understood. "The *ṛc*s are your majesty": all the *ṛc*s residing in all the Vedas constitute your greatness. By this, the two subsequent mantras are explained.

Thus ends the nineteenth section of the second chapter in the *Ekāgnikāṇḍa-vyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. [The mantra: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is your lid; I offer you into the mouth of Brahman; I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. You are imperishable; may you not perish for them there in yonder world. He causes [the sacrificer] to touch [the water] with the *Yajus* formula: "The earth is yours... and so forth, [saying] "May my fathers cleanse me; may my grandfathers cleanse me. [The ritual action: He causes [him] to touch [the water] with the *Yajus*: "The earth is yours... and so on.

"The earth is your vessel; shine forth, O you who are named so-and-so! You are indeed great. As it was stated previously, "As great as fire and the earth are," so too the sky is your lid; the meaning is that your lid must likewise be of immeasurable extent. That which stands above is the lid, and that which stands below is the vessel; such is the arrangement of the sky and the earth. I offer you, [O Soma], into the mouth of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa.

In this context, the ancestors (*pitṛs*) are the deities, while the Brāhmaṇas serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. As the Smṛti states: "The gods always consume the sacrificial offerings (*havya*) with his mouth; the ancestors consume the ancestral offerings (*kavya*) in three ways. What being could be greater than him? Thus it is said that one offers into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of the ancestors. Now, saying "may there be satisfaction even for those who are eating," he says: "I offer you into the out-breath and in-breath of the Brāhmaṇas. O food! You are imperishable (*akṣita*). This means, "O food, you are inexhaustible."
"May there be no exhaustion for these [ancestors] and for the Brahmins; may you not go to destruction—there in the other world for the ancestors, and here in this world for the Brahmins.
At the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he pours water upon the *darbha* grass with the words, "May they cleanse themselves. He cleanses.

"For this very reason, all the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* enjoin [the following], such as: 'At the end of the sacrifice, one should satisfy the Brahmins with water offerings,' and so forth. (2-19-14). This is the twentieth section of the second chapter. "May my great-grandfathers purify themselves; may my grandmothers purify themselves; may my great-grandmothers purify themselves."

"O father, N.N., and those who follow you; O grandfather, N.N., and those who follow you; O great-grandfather, N.N., and those who follow you; O mother, and those who follow you; O grandmother, N.N., and those who follow you; O great-grandmother, N.N., and those who follow you—may they purify me. O my fathers, may those who are here among you, and those who have departed from us, and those who are yours..."

"May those [streams] which flow toward us and those which flow away carry [the offerings]; may you sirs be satisfied, may you ladies be satisfied; may they be satisfied. May my ancestors become pure through this water. The subsequent [verses] are to be applied in the same way. 5. The offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*): "This is for you, O father [named] Yajñaśarman, who are called 'Tata'! And for those living beings who follow after you. The subsequent [verses] are to be applied in the same way. "The worship with the following [verses]: 'Those who... etc.

O Fathers! Those among you who desire this rite, and those who desire us; O Mothers! Those women in our family who have died and desire you, and those who desire us—let those men attain the *svadhā* offering, and let those women also attain it.
In this sentence, some do not recite the word "mine" (*mama*). 184

In the *Savyākhyānakāmikāṇḍa*: "Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied! May these waters, which satisfy sons and grandsons, flow for us with splendor. May they, yielding the *svadhā* offering and immortality to the ancestors, may the divine waters satisfy both [the gods and the ancestors]. Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied!
Having entered into the vital breath (*prāṇa*), I offer immortality; my self is in Brahman."

For the sake of death: "The night which people welcome—may the men here be satisfied, and may the women here be satisfied. O fathers and mothers, be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied! You both [fathers and mothers], [offer] both types of *piṇḍas* to those who have passed away, to sons and grandsons. Sons and grandsons...

One meaning of the sentence is: "These waters—scorching, satisfying, honey-sweet, full of honey, and joined with honey-sweetness—are such as these. Those waters, for the fathers (*pitṛbhyaḥ*)—where *pitā* [father] and *mātā* [mother] form a *ekaśeṣa* compound—yielding the *svadhā*, which is the nectar in the form of *svadhā*, may those goddesses (*devīḥ*) satisfy both the fathers and the mothers. O fathers! O mothers! Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied. Regarding the consumption of the remainder: "In the *prāṇa*," etc.; established in the *prāṇa*, [he satisfies] the *prāṇa* and the others.

Abiding by presiding over the five vital airs (*pañca vāyūn*), I offer the nectar—the means of immortality—into the Brahman. Into what? Into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For the sake of my own immortality, I, whose self is the Supreme Self, [offer this]. Now follow the mantras for the *Aṣṭakā* rites. Therein, on the seventh night, there is an offering of cakes (*apūpa-homa*) with the verse: "The night which people celebrate... That night which people celebrate—that is, honor—with offerings of cakes (*apūpahavyā*)—[is the one intended]. (End of the twentieth section of the second chapter. ...the night that is celebrated.

May she who is the mistress of the year be auspicious for us; Svāhā! "Carry the omentum, O Jātavedas, to the fathers where you know them to be placed in the distance. May the streams flow for them from the banks; may these prayers be true according to our desires. Svāhā! Just as people rejoice when a cow comes toward them for milking, so [should they rejoice]."

Furthermore, regarding the verse: "The wife of the year, named Ekāṣṭakā—this Ekāṣṭakā is indeed the wife of the year. This is a praise of the Aṣṭakā; the praise of the seventh [lunar day] is based precisely on its proximity to that. May that night be *sumaṅgalī*, auspicious for us. On the following day, the mantra for the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) is: "Carry the omentum (*vaha vapām*). O Jātavedas! Carry the omentum to the ancestors; bring the omentum to the ancestors.

Wherever you know these ancestors to be placed or situated—whether near or far away—when the omentum (*vapā*) is being offered, let those ancestors flow toward them like rivers of fat; for "rivers" (*kūlyāḥ*) means artificial streams. May these blessings (*āśiṣaḥ*) of these ancestors be fulfilled along with their desires; "blessings" refers to prayers, while "desires" (*kāmāḥ*) are so called because they are objects of longing.
With the [verses] beginning with "māṃsaudanam uttarābhiḥ" and ending with "yāṃ janāḥ pratinandanti kheṣeti," she has gone.

*Oṃ, this indeed is...* This very *Aṣṭakā* is that Dawn (*uṣas*) which first shone forth before the Sun; having shone forth and entered the Sun, she moves within this earth in the form of its rays. And she who is the bride is the Dawn who is born (*jāyate*). [The mantra continues: "Her whom people welcome with joy. This same [passage] occurs in the section on the *Sādhyas* in the *Ekāṣṭakā-kāṇḍa*. She who goes to a new husband is the "new-goer" (*navagat*); she is the progenitor (*janitrī*), the mother of sons.

And those great ones—the three Āreikas and the two Aśvins—attend to and partake of this Dawn; these are the gods who delight in the sacrificial fat (*vapā*). As the *Bṛhad-Āraṇyaka-Upaniṣad* states: "The two Aśvins, who travel at dawn, [partook] of the sacrificial fat. Such is that Dawn; the meaning is that she alone is the Ekāṣṭakā. There are two Dawns: one belonging to the middle region and one belonging to the heavenly region; of these two, the latter is the one characterized by meters (*chandasvatī*).

"Rich in meters, accompanied by meters, they go with meters: 'This is she who first shone forth; within her the rains and the summer were born. She, the mother of nine sons—three greatnesses attend her. Rich in meters, the two Dawns, adorning themselves, moving toward a common womb, move along together. The two wives of Sūrya shine forth, making all things known. 'Three have come along the path of Ṛta; three heats have come along with the light.
One protects my offspring, one protects my strength, and one protects the vow of those seeking the gods' (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.3.11)."

Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.5, twentieth section of the second prapāṭhaka: "She who first shone forth..."—thus [the text speaks of] three. Two Dawns (uṣasau) are praised: they are beautifully adorned (pepiśāne), shining brightly (dīpyamāne), moving along the same single path, following after the Sun (ādityam). Moving along, entering into the day, they are the two wives of Sūrya; he whose wife they are is Sūrya, the protector (patiḥ pālayitā); as such, they move about (vicarataḥ) in various ways. They are wise (prajānatī), making a banner (ketum) for all the world. They are ageless (ajare), free from decay, and possessed of abundant seed (bhūriretasā).

The dual ending is replaced by *ā*. "The two with abundant seed" (*bhūriretasau*) refers to the two Dawns (*uṣasau*) who possess copious mist and water; these too are to be understood as being this very same [Dawn], following the same logic. Regarding the phrase "the path of *ṛta*": the three Dawns follow along the path, the way, of *ṛta*, which is sacrifice (*yajña*). Their number is three due to the distinction of their functions. As it will be stated: "Being one, O Dawn, you shine forth in many ways. They have followed (*anvāguḥ*), that is, they follow (*anvāyanti*). And there are three *gharmās*. The root *ghṛ* means "to flow" and "to shine."

These radiant fires have followed this Dawn with their light; they follow her. He shows their distinction: among them, one protects the offspring of those "devayus"—that is, the sacrificers who desire to worship the gods. One, however, protects their *ūrj* (vital energy) and strength. And one protects their *vrata* (vow), that is, their ritual acts such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) and the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*). These three are also to be understood as being this very [Dawn] herself.
"Ekāṣṭakām" [means]: O Brāhmaṇas! Behold this Ekāṣṭakā—of what nature is she? She is one who milks out food for the ancestors. What kind of food? It is meat.
(Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.3.11). Behold her as she milks out food, which contains all the seasons and is accompanied by the *svadhā* offering.

In the *Savyākhyānaikāṣṭakāṇḍa*: "May there be prosperity for my ancestors, Svāhā! The mortars and pestles, making the oblation fragrant, have encompassed that which has lasted for a year. The Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance with austerity throughout the year—may that [oblation], rich in clarified butter and accompanied by the *svadhā* offering, which is indeed the milk, meat, and so forth due to the ancestors, being purified and thoroughly cleansed by the Brāhmaṇas, becoming infinite and inexhaustible—that food may go to increase the prosperity of my ancestors in that world."

"O *aulūkhalāḥ*! [This is] a primary derivative (*svārthika-taddhita*) suffix; thus, *aulūkhalāḥ* refers to the mortars and the pressing-stones (*grāvāṇaḥ*), as well as the grinding-stones and so forth. They have made a sound, they produce noise, performing the oblation (*haviḥ*) by means of threshing, grinding, and so on. "Belonging to the year" (*parivatsarīṇam*) means occurring year after year. O *Ekāṣṭake*! O *mujāḥ*—there is a change in the grammatical number (from singular to plural). "Possessing good offspring" (*suprajāḥ*), "possessing heroes" (*vīravantaḥ*)—meaning being endowed with brave men—and through your grace, may we become lords of riches (*rayīṇām patayaḥ*). [Regarding the verse beginning with] *māṣādi*: "O Ekāṣṭake... *oṃ ekāṣṭake*. *Note: The term *aulūkhalāḥ* is derived from *ulūkhala* (mortar) with a primary suffix indicating the object itself.*

This Ekāṣṭakā, performing penance, the mother and protector of the year, yields her milk—she who is full and flourishing. That milking consists of the striking, the threshing, and the grinding. Svāhā! To that thousand-streamed [offering] in yonder world. 20. [End of] the twenty-first section of the second Prapāṭhaka.

The Ukthya, the Atirātra, and the Sādyaska along with the Chandas—these are known as the Sadyaskrī. Anasuya Ram (sambhāṣaṇam), 12:26, 7 December 2016 (UTC)_____________________________________________________

189. O Fathers! You who subsist, may you subsist a thousandfold in that world, the world beyond. Thus ends the twentieth section in the second book of the commentary on the *Ekāṣṭakā-kāṇḍa* composed by the venerable Haradatta. With the next verse, he offers an oblation of ground-grain (*piṣṭānna*), [reciting]: "And the *ukthya*... O Ekāṣṭakā! You are the *ukthya* sacrifice and the *atirātra* sacrifice; and the *sādyaskrī*—the *sādyaskrī* being the name of a seasonal sacrifice (*ṛtu*), where the vowel *ī* is used for metrical reasons (*chāndasa*).

Together with *chandas*, the term *chandaḥ* does not refer merely to a portion of the Vedic meters. It is an address to her whose offering consists of cakes (*apūpa*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*). O you whose offering is cake and butter (*apūpadhṛtāhuti*), let there be salutation to you! O you whose *pippala* is flesh (*māṃsapippalā*)! For it is seen in scripture that "one of them eats the sweet *pippala*" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1), and thus the *pippala* is the sweet fruit; she whose *pippala* is indeed flesh is addressed as "O you whose *pippala* is flesh! (*māṃsapippale*).

"The subsequent oblations of clarified butter [are made] with the words: *bhūḥ pṛthivī* (Earth, the earth). The *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ*, are beneficial by their mere utterance; they do not denote a meaning through the combination of other words. *Bhūḥ! With the earth, with Agni, with the Ṛgveda, I bind this desire upon me—Svāhā!* *Bhuvaḥ! With Vāyu, with the intermediate space, with the Sāmaveda, I bind this desire upon me—Svāhā!* *Svaḥ! With the heavens, with Āditya, with the Yajurveda, I bind this desire upon me—Svāhā!* *Janat! With the mountains, with the Ṛṣis, with the Atharvāṅgirasa, I bind this desire upon me—Svāhā!*” (Puruṣasūkta 2.3.1.190)

To the radiant one, the foremost of wealth, born of the gods, Svāhā! To the banner, the mind, the sacred word (*brahman*), born of the gods, Svāhā! *Svadhā* and *svāhā* to Agni Kavyavāhana; [the form] *pṛthivīm* is the single word in the third case with the preceding vowel lengthened (*pūrvasavarṇa*). By means of these—by the world of earth, by the god Agni, by the *ṛc*, and by the Veda—as the instrumental causes, I bind and establish that desire residing in my heart within myself. By this, the subsequent [formulas] are explained. [The phrase] "janadadbhiḥ" [is used].

*Janat* is the fourth *vyāhṛti*, as recited in the *Atharvaveda*. The word division is *janat* | *adbhiḥ*. However, in the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, it is recited with a final *visarga* as *janaḥ*. Regarding *rocanāya*: for the shining (*rocana*), for the impetuous (*ājira*), for that which has the nature of motion (*ana*)—that is, of going—or for the field (*kṣetra*) of darkness; for Agni of such a kind, who is born of the gods (*devajātave*), the knower (*ketave*) of the gods who are to be sacrificed to, or the source (*yonibhūtāya*). [As it is said: "The Brāhmaṇas are indeed born of Agni. Regarding *svadhā*: *svadhā* and the others have already been explained.

Saṃ. 2-1-2. *Svadhā*! *Svāhā*! "May I be like food for you to behold; may I be like clothing for you to behold; may I be like a dwelling for you to behold. [End of the twenty-first section of the second chapter. May the quarters and the great ones grant me prosperity; may all my desires be fulfilled; may my beloved ones protect me, may my beloved ones protect me. One should mutter the verse beginning with "May food be mine" (*annamiva*) after the *sanimittātara*.

"May I be like food for your two eyes to behold; as much joy as there is in seeing food, let that same joy be yours toward me. This is a statement addressed to the giver regarding oneself. The same should be applied to the subsequent [verses] as well. Regarding the verse beginning with "āśāḥ saṃsravantu": "Let them flow together"—let the great quarters (mahīḥ) flow together, meaning let all the vast directions flow; let whatever is to be given by you come to me from all directions. Let the *sūnṛtāḥ*—pleasant words such as "welcome" and so forth—converge upon me.

May all beloved desires come toward me and approach me; may they protect me—this is the very purpose of my being beloved. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. "O Yaśas" means you are glorious, and I too am glory in you.

"May I be famous, may I become renowned; grant this to me"—this is the meaning. For in this way, the glory of the petitioner becomes his own. "Asau" (that one) is the mention of the giver’s name in the vocative case, such as: "O Yajñaśarman! When the chariot has been obtained, he touches its two wheels or its two sides, saying: "The two flanks. [Regarding the word] *dhvāntam*: from the root *dhvan* in the sense of sound; the absence of the augment *iṭ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It refers to the wind at the front that has resounded. "Thou art fame; may I become fame in thee, O [Name]! This is the verse beginning with: "The two flanks, bent down on both sides."

"O path, O lord of the path, lead me safely across. May this chariot of yours, O Aśvins, suffer no harm in either sorrow or joy. Unharmed, may it go in safety. [The root *gam* means 'to go']. Moving like the wind, following after such a chariot on both sides are two beings named Aṅka; likewise the two named Nyaṅka, Yakṣa, and Dareha; and he who is possessed of sense-power, strong, and winged (patatrī), who is prone to flying."

These specific beings are the presiding deities of the chariot; they are the foremost. *Agra* is derived from the root *ag*, meaning "to go"; thus, they are the goers along with the chariot. *Pamayah*: from the root *prā*, meaning "to fill"; they are the fulfillers of our desires. May they carry us across (*pārayantu*), may they lead us to the further shore, may they cause us to reach our desired destination.
With the Yajus formula, "Of paths, of the path," he mounts [the chariot]. O chariot! Of paths... [of the path].

"O protector of the path, protect the path"—this is the meaning. It is just as in the expression "lord of cows" (*gopati*). "Svasti"—in whatever way is auspicious—lead me, *mā*, safely across; that is, lead me properly to the further shore. With the following verse he proceeds: "This [chariot]," etc. O Aśvins! O Ashvinau! This chariot is your own; therefore, on the path, whether in sorrow or in joy, let it not suffer harm (*mā riṣat*); let it not be ruined. Let it go safely, unharmed. [The form] *vivibhrān*: the doubling of the word *vi-* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage.

What various kinds [of enemies] are they? Those who are *pṛtanāyat*, desiring to fight. O you two who run on both sides of the chariot with your limbs, you whose tips are like darkness, moving through the atmosphere, far-reaching, possessing swift senses, and winged—may those foremost ones carry us across and bring us to the further shore. (Saṃhitā 1.7.7). In the twenty-first section of the second prapāṭhaka: "Thou art a steed (*aśva*), thou art a courser (*hayas*), thou art a racer (*atya*), thou art a manly steed (*nara*), thou art a runner (*arvan*), thou art a winner of prizes (*sapti*), thou art a stallion (*vṛṣan*), thou art one whose mind is directed toward men (*nṛmaṇas*), thou art the path of the Ādityas; follow after their flight!"
"Hastiyaśastvam asi; may I become Hastiyaśas. O carrier of time, bring me prosperity.
(1983) Regarding the horse obtained, the mantra for mounting is: "Aśvo 'si" (You are a horse). One hears the path.

*Na* means "not. *Haya* comes from the roots *hi* (to impel) or *haya* (to go); from *hi* in the sense of going, or *haya* in the sense of going—one who is habitually moving. Hence, *asyuḥ*. From *nṛt* (to dance), *naraḥ*. Hence, *arvā*. From *sṛp* (to glide), *saptiḥ*. From *vaj* (to go), *vājī*. From *vṛṣ* (to rain), *vṛṣā*, meaning one capable of sprinkling. One whose mind (*manas*) is directed toward men—that is, toward enemies or human beings—thinking "I shall slay them," is *nṛmaṇāḥ*. *Yātuḥ* means "one who goes," namely the horse of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. *Nāma* is used in the sense of well-known renown.

O you who are the flight—the one characterized by the act of flying—of the Ādityas, the sons of Aditi, and the gods; as such, follow me, come after me; do not pass me by. [Regarding the mantra for mounting an elephant: "Thou art the glory of elephants. You have become the glory (*yaśas*) of elephants. And may I, through you, become possessed of the glory of elephants (*hastiyaśas*). O Kālavaha! O Kālaskandhavaha! Carry me; bring me to prosperity; cause me to attain prosperity.

With the thunderbolt of Indra, with a goad similar to it, I bind you; that is to say, I place such a goad upon your head. O Airāvata! O Supratīka! [The word] *nara* means "man" (*narati*), and from those two, in the sense of "afflicting," one should touch the earth as before with the mantra: "O Earth, be pleasant. (*Syonā pṛthivī*)

[The previous section] has been explained. [End of] the additional reading 2.5. In the *Savyākhyānaikāgnikaṇḍa*: "O Vaha! With Indra’s thunderbolt, I strike you down, O so-and-so! You who are crooked-tongued, you who are double-tongued—I worship you with oblations. That which I speak is the truth: 'May this one be lower than you, svāhā!'"

"I have taken your speech from your mouth, from your mind, and from your heart. Wherever your speech has gone, I have brought it back here. That which I speak here is the truth; fall down beneath me, O [Name]! (21) I shall worship with an eternal oblation. (21) ... He offers a handful of chaff as an oblation during the dialogue, saying: "O downward-tongued one... etc.

"O you whose tongue is turned downward—addressing him thus: 'O Avajihvaka! likewise, he whose tongue is bent down is *nijihvaka*; 'O Nijihvaka! I shall sacrifice to you with this oblation consisting of a handful of husks, so that you may become speechless; I worship you in such a way. Let that which I speak be true. What is it? May this Yajñaśarman, my rival, speaking against me, be rendered inferior to me and speak [in defeat]."

The recitation (*japa*) in the presence of the opponent is: *ā ta iti*. I take your speech (*vāc*) that resides in the mouth (*āsya*), and with the mind (*manas*), I take the speech intended for utterance that resides in the mind (*manas*). I take that speech which is above the heart (*hṛdaya*). Furthermore, wherever your speech is located, I take that which belongs to you. May that which I speak come true. What is it? O [Name], such as Yajñaśarman, may you fall lower than me (*mat*); that is to say, may you be defeated or ruined.

Thus ends the twenty-first section in the second chapter of the *Ekāgrikāṇḍavyākhyāna* composed by Śrī Haradatta. The twenty-second section in the second chapter. 195. That glowing form of yours which destroys the madness of the mind—that may the wise gods, the students of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), discipline. That which they pierce with a sharp instrument in your mouth—[we remove] your anger from there; we lead it away like the fetus of a mare.

Desiring to remove the anger of the bow, he bends the bowstring; then, wishing to take away its wrath, he consecrates it with the two following verses beginning with "yā te. That form of yours which is on the forehead, O Manyu—that manifestation of anger consisting of the frown and so forth—is the destroyer of softness. "Mṛdhra" is a name for softness, and it emphasizes the state [of being soft]; for prosperity indeed causes one to abandon softness.

O gods, may those who practice sacred knowledge (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*), moving within the Veda (*brahmaṇi*) as that which is to be realized through mantra, and being well-endowed with wisdom (*sumedhasaḥ*), discipline—that is, remove—that body of wrath (*manyos tanūm*). Regarding the phrase "that which": this refers to that which is in your mouth, which is disagreeable (*amataṃ*) to the virtuous; it is as if it were tearing open the forehead (*rarāṭim udvidhyati*). This intends the throbbing of the *kudu* (the lower lip) and the pulsation of the channels (*nāḍīnām*) on the forehead. Because the word "yat" (which/that) is heard, the word "tat" (that) must be supplied.

We subdue that anger of yours; we subdue it, just as one [subdues] the pregnancy of a she-mule. The taking of pregnancy is a cause of death for a mule; therefore, it must be subdued. One who desires the impossibility [of union] with others should have coarse *āḍhārikā* seeds made into a powder and, while she is asleep, scatter it into her private parts with the following verse: "Away, O bowstring. O woman! From your heart—from the heart—[I remove] *manyu*. By the word *manyu*, desire is indicated here due to the similarity of its nature as a modification of the mind.

I willingly cast down, I draw away, I remove from my heart the passion directed toward another man. O Indra, I turn back this longing from other men; let it not be for anyone else than me. Since I move about seeking wealth with my riches, O Gods, desiring wealth, may Soma bestow radiance upon that [wealth], and may Agni, Indra, and Bṛhaspati [bestow it]—Svāhā! I have taken you away from the mountain, away from your brother, away from your sister, and away from those who explain the Savya hymns.

Just as those desiring to make a bow fit for its purpose lower the string of the bow, so too, O Indra! you should remove this man’s *pāliṅga*—that is, his generative organ—from other men, acting in such a way that they do not enter it. Forward, the two radiant ones of him who is meditating; forward, the well-being! This one named *Prācī* (eastward-moving) is present; she is entered into the breath as *Pratīcī* (westward-moving)... The morning meal, Indra in the morning, the fierce and upright Bhaga in the morning... May he release me, dear among the gods; may he release me from the bond. Thus stands the mantra-opening of the purifiers.

May we not be abandoned by our offspring, O Mitra; you have grasped my hand. You are the friendship through the sacred law (*dharman*). The eye of Mitra, the support... May the gods and the seers first consecrate you. They have consecrated you; touch it! You are a kindling-stick; may we prosper through you. You are named *Samīcī* (the Uniter). I send you forth to the ocean; from the ocean, rich in sweetness, [bring] me [strength]. With the waves of the ocean, may Sarasvatī, whose mind is fixed on man, protect you. Sarasvatī has taken your hand; Savitṛ has taken your hand for an easy path. May she deliver you across here. You are the *Virāj*; you are the *Sic* (the binding cord); the thunderbolt is in your nose. [I take] the *Sukiṃśuka* and the *Śalmali* tree.

I have ascended the path, O bride named Sumaṅgalā, who possesses beautiful feet. Of the plants, [I am] the one who brings forth well; Svāhā! ... May we be well-hearing and of good fame, [may we be] immortal from darkness... Soma was the first to find her; Soma is the long-lived one. Soma indeed is our king...
